attribution: Synthetically generated calibration instrument for a personalized, human-aligned PR-review pipeline (Tier 3 gating + Tier 4 persona synthesis). Items are behaviourally anchored; no option represents an objectively correct engineering answer.
changes_from_v1: Every item carries pr_context (title, author description, size, CI status, author note) as real reviewers and agents see it.
Options are scenario-specific mechanisms rather than a fixed rung ladder, and presentation order is shuffled per item (canonical_rank preserved) to defeat self-image answering.

Each option records the verbatim review comment, review state, follow-up mode, test request and suggestion-block use the developer would actually produce, plus a first-person rationale and an agent_behavior directive.
Eight extended behavioural signals for Tier 4 (comment density, suggestion blocks, test insistence, scope discipline, verification effort, praise, follow-up tracking, escalation).
Likert items gained behavioral_indicators: observable PR-telemetry signals for validating scored profiles against real review history.
Diffs lengthened with context lines; Category 5 comment lengths equalised (spread <= 8 words) to remove the length cue; hedged variants no longer downgrade blocking defects with nit: tags.
Boilerplate notes replaced by item-specific discriminates / bias_control statements.

categories.format: 4-option action choice (ignore / nit / discretionary ask / block)

categories.name: Category 4: Gatekeeping & Blocking Policy
categories.format: 4-option choice mapped to APPROVE / APPROVE+note / COMMENT / REQUEST_CHANGES

technical_debt_tolerance.semantics: 0 = blocks all architectural shortcuts; 1 = accepts pragmatic compromise routinely

pedantry_level.semantics: 0 = suppresses all cosmetic findings; 1 = blocks on stylistic hygiene

blocking_threshold.semantics: effective severity S_effective at which the reviewer switches from advisory to REQUEST_CHANGES; low = blocks early

kai_index.semantics: Kirton Adaption-Innovation: 0 = strong Adaptor (optimise inside the paradigm), 1 = strong Innovator (reframe, introduce new patterns)

regulatory_focus.semantics: Higgins: 0 = Prevention (defensive, bug-averse), 1 = Promotion (velocity, accepts manageable risk)

phi_framing.semantics: Phi_framing for the Tier 4 synthesizer: 0.0 = Direct_Imperative, ~0.5 = Balanced_Inquisitive / hedged, 1.0 = Strictly_Socratic

use_negative_politeness_tags.semantics: probability mass for explicit face-saving prefixes (nit:, optional:, fyi:); binarised at 0.5 for the boolean profile field

topic_weights.semantics: W_topic multiplier applied as S_effective = sigma * W_topic

aggregation.likert_5: value = points[selected_anchor]; reverse_scored items already encode the inversion in the points map
aggregation.choice_items: value = mapping[attribute] of the selected option
aggregation.attribute_estimate: arithmetic mean of all item-level values contributing to that attribute
aggregation.topic_weight_estimate: mean of contributing option values, defaulting to 0.5 for any topic with no contributing response
aggregation.safety_floor: no aggregate profile value may suppress a candidate with sigma >= 0.80; Tier 3 clamps S_effective >= sigma for those candidates
aggregation.extended_signals: mean of extended_signals values on selected options; default 0.5 when no contributing response; consumed by Tier 4 only, never by Tier 3 gating
aggregation.presentation_order: options are presented in the shuffled label order stored per item; scoring reads the selected option's own mapping, so the shuffle never touches values; canonical_rank records the original A-D position for analysis

comment_density.semantics: 0 = a few high-value comments only; 1 = comments on nearly every observation

suggestion_block_usage.semantics: 0 = describes the change in prose; 1 = always supplies a concrete code suggestion / diff block

test_insistence.semantics: 0 = rarely asks for tests; 1 = routinely requires a test for the changed path before merge

scope_discipline.semantics: 0 = also comments on pre-existing code adjacent to the diff; 1 = strictly confines review to the changed lines

verification_effort.semantics: 0 = reads the diff only; 1 = checks out the branch, runs it, reproduces the issue, inspects call sites

praise_frequency.semantics: 0 = never acknowledges good decisions; 1 = regularly calls out well-made choices

follow_up_tracking.semantics: 0 = never files follow-up tickets; 1 = files a tracked ticket for every deferred concern

escalation_propensity.semantics: 0 = resolves everything inside the PR thread; 1 = pulls in code owners, security, or architecture review

agent_behavior_guide.purpose: How the aggregated profile drives agent behaviour. Tier 3 consumes core scalars and topic weights deterministically; Tier 4 consumes framing scalars and extended signals for style only. Nothing here may suppress a candidate with sigma >= 0.80.

tier3.rule: Emit REQUEST_CHANGES when S_effective = sigma * W_topic >= blocking_threshold; emit COMMENT when S_effective is within 0.15 below it; otherwise emit an APPROVE-scoped note or drop per pedantry_level. Clamp: any sigma >= 0.80 is REQUEST_CHANGES regardless.

For findings tagged architectural_shortcut, multiply sigma by (1.4 - 0.8 * technical_debt_tolerance) before gating; when tolerance >= 0.6 prefer 'tracked_ticket' follow-ups over blocking for sub-0.6 findings.

Drop cosmetic findings (sigma < 0.3) when pedantry_level < 0.3; emit them as nit: when 0.3 <= pedantry_level < 0.7; allow them to reach COMMENT state when pedantry_level >= 0.7 (never REQUEST_CHANGES on sigma < 0.3).
W_topic scales sigma per finding topic; weights are estimated per topic from Categories 2-4 and default to 0.5 where unobserved.

tier4.rule: phi < 0.33 -> Direct_Imperative; 0.33-0.66 -> Balanced_Inquisitive (hedged statements with a question); > 0.66 -> Strictly_Socratic (lead with the question that exposes the edge case).
>= 0.5 -> prefix non-blocking observations with nit:/optional:/fyi:; on blocking findings never attach an optional tag to the required fix.
Low -> collapse minor findings into one summary comment; high -> one inline comment per finding.
High -> always attach a GitHub suggestion block with the remediation diff; low -> describe the change in prose and anchor to file:line.
High -> every REQUEST_CHANGES on a logic path names the specific test to add; low -> tests requested only for sigma >= 0.6.
High -> suppress findings on unchanged lines; low -> permit findings on adjacent pre-existing code, tagged fyi:.
High -> the agent states what it ran or traced (call sites, tests executed) before asserting a defect; low -> reasons from the diff alone and says so.
High -> one specific acknowledgement of a well-made decision per review; low -> none.
High -> every deferred concern becomes a named ticket in the review summary; low -> TODO-in-code or nothing.
High -> tag code owners / security on tenant-boundary, auth, or migration findings; low -> keep everything in the PR thread.

quality_assurance.schema_gate: 95/95: IDs, counts, option counts, mapping vocabulary and values (within ±0.05 of v1 canonical values), extended-signal vocabulary, review states (Category 4 one-to-one with GitHub states), comments present on COMMENT/REQUEST_CHANGES options, grounded @@ coordinates, Category 5 length spread <= 8 words; Category 6: target extended signal present on all four options and spanning the range
quality_assurance.consistency_audit: independent per-item audit of code/scenario/option/pr_context agreement after enrichment; 9 items repaired and re-audited, 3 with a second directed pass; 1 option hand-corrected; Category 6: 3 of 10 flagged on first audit (HAB-01, HAB-06, HAB-09). HAB-01 and HAB-06 repaired and passed re-audit. HAB-09 required five passes: scenario grounding for the call-site list, an inverted diff rewritten, a review-state confound removed, an unsupported reviewer-side 'independently verified all seven call sites' claim removed from the option text/comment/rationale, a severity-wording mismatch aligned to the scenario, and a contradictory '// proration flag intentionally untouched' line removed from the diff. The final HAB-09 audit pass still returned objections; on direct reading they assert the fix should not be placed in cancelMidCycle because that method never touches the flag, which is the defect the item describes, and were judged auditor misreadings. HAB-09 is therefore shipped on author judgement, not on a clean automated pass.
quality_assurance.accepted_conventions: regulatory_focus 0 = Prevention / 1 = Promotion, and blocking_threshold low = blocks earlier; two audit flags (DEBT-11, GATE-13) were dismissed as misreadings of these conventions

pr_context.description: This introduces a lightweight static query helper for tenant-scoped invoice lookups instead of threading the change through InvoiceRepository and InvoiceService the way the other twelve modules do. This PR adds tenant scoping for one new query using a static helper method that reads the tenant ID directly from a ThreadLocal, bypassing that chain. CI is green, the query is correct, and the deadline for this billing cycle feature is two days out. No other PR currently touches this file.

pr_context.title: Fix stale balance read in reconciliation worker when ledger entries are backdated
pr_context.description: This closes the gap where a backdated ledger entry written after the reconciliation sweep started could cause the worker to compute a settlement delta against a stale account balance. I added a version check on the account row and a retry when the version has advanced mid-sweep. Tested locally against the replayed incident dataset from last quarter and against the standard reconciliation fixture suite; both pass. I did not have a way to reproduce the original race under load, so I can't confirm the retry loop behaves correctly above our peak sweep concurrency.
pr_context.author_note: Left the retry cap at 3 for now, matching the pattern used in the ledger-sync worker; happy to change if reviewers want a different number.

items.scenario: You own review for the reconciliation service, which runs a nightly sweep over roughly 40,000 merchant accounts and reconciles settlement deltas against the ledger. The service has had one prior incident, about five months ago, caused by a stale-balance read during backdated entries; that incident is what this PR addresses. The author is a mid-level engineer on an adjacent team who has shipped two prior changes to this path, both uneventful. The automated suite includes a fixture replay of the prior incident, which now passes. There is no load-test harness for the sweep, and no deploy is scheduled today.

pr_context.title: Add split-tender payment option behind checkout_split_tender flag
pr_context.description: This wires up the new split-tender path the PM wants live for the Q3 promo sprint, gated behind checkout_split_tender so it defaults off in prod. I tested the happy path (two cards, card+gift card) locally against the sandbox processor and confirmed the flag correctly no-ops back to single-tender when off. Have not yet covered partial-auth failure mid-split, network timeout on the second charge, or refund-of-one-leg cases; opened a follow-up ticket for those and I'm planning to land them before the flag flips on for any tenant.
pr_context.author_note: Flag stays off for every tenant until the follow-up lands; happy path is solid, edge cases tracked in PAY-2291.

items.scenario: You own review for the order-processing service, an asyncio-based system handling live checkout traffic across several tenants on shared infrastructure. The PM has asked for split-tender checkout to ship this sprint for a promotional campaign. The PR adds the code path behind a flag that defaults off, with a linked ticket for the untested failure modes (partial auth, mid-split timeout, single-leg refund). CI is green, the flag is off in every environment including prod, and no tenant has been enabled yet. The follow-up ticket has no assigned sprint.
items.code:
--- a/services/checkout/split_tender.py
+++ b/services/checkout/split_tender.py
@@ -14,10 +14,19 @@ class SplitTenderProcessor:
     def __init__(self, gateway: PaymentGateway, flags: FeatureFlags):
         self.gateway = gateway
         self.flags = flags
 
+    async def process_split(self, order: Order, tenders: list[Tender]) -> Receipt:
+        if not self.flags.is_enabled("checkout_split_tender", order.tenant_id):
+            return await self._process_single(order, tenders[0])
+        charges = []
+        for tender in tenders:
+            charge = await self.gateway.charge(order, tender)
+            charges.append(charge)
+        return self._build_receipt(order, charges)
+
     async def _process_single(self, order: Order, tender: Tender) -> Receipt:
         charge = await self.gateway.charge(order, tender)
         return self._build_receipt(order, [charge])

pr_context.title: Speed up account_activity_daily reporting query
pr_context.description: Our nightly reporting endpoint against account_activity_daily has been timing out for the largest tenants. I added a composite index on (tenant_id, activity_date) and rewrote the query to avoid the correlated subquery that was forcing a sequential scan. Tested locally against a restored prod snapshot for our biggest tenant and p95 dropped from 9.2s to 640ms. Did not touch the reporting schema or add any new infra.
pr_context.author_note: Left the old subquery commented out for one release in case we need to compare results, will remove after the next deploy.

items.scenario: You own review for the reporting service. The account_activity_daily table has grown to 40M rows per large tenant, and the dashboard endpoint queries it directly on every page load with no caching layer. Three other tenants have filed slowness tickets this week. The team has previously discussed, but never scheduled, a project to move heavy reporting to a materialized view or a separate analytics store. This PR only touches the existing query and adds one index; the migration runs in under a minute against the staging snapshot.

pr_context.title: Add asyncio token-bucket rate limiter for /v2 public API endpoints
pr_context.description: This adds a per-key token-bucket limiter using an in-process asyncio.Lock and a background refill task so we can start shedding abusive traffic on the public API before the conference launch next week. I load-tested locally with 500 concurrent keys and latency stayed under 8ms; I have not yet tested behind our multi-replica deployment where state won't be shared across pods. Flagging that the limiter is per-process for now and I think we should ship with dashboards watching 429 rates and follow up with Redis-backed shared state if we see uneven throttling across replicas.
pr_context.author_note: I know per-process counting means a key could get roughly N times the limit across N replicas, but our replica count is small right now and I'd rather ship the protection than have none for launch week.

items.scenario: You are reviewing a PR against the public-facing billing-adjacent API gateway service, which currently runs three replicas behind a round-robin load balancer with no rate limiting at all. The team has a hard external launch date in six days tied to a partner announcement. The author owns this service solo and is the on-call engineer for it. The new limiter uses process-local state, so a client's effective quota scales with the number of replicas it happens to hit. CI is green, and a Grafana dashboard for 429 rates is referenced in the PR but not yet linked.
items.code:
--- a/services/gateway/ratelimit.py
+++ b/services/gateway/ratelimit.py
@@ -1,6 +1,15 @@
 import asyncio
 import time
+from collections import defaultdict
 
-class NoOpLimiter:
-    async def check(self, key: str) -> bool:
-        return True
+class TokenBucketLimiter:
+    def __init__(self, rate: float = 10.0, capacity: int = 20):
+        self.rate = rate
+        self.capacity = capacity
+        self._buckets: dict[str, tuple[float, float]] = defaultdict(
+            lambda: (capacity, time.monotonic())
+        )
+        self._lock = asyncio.Lock()
+
+    async def check(self, key: str) -> bool:
+        async with self._lock:
+            tokens, last = self._buckets[key]
+            now = time.monotonic()
+            tokens = min(self.capacity, tokens + (now - last) * self.rate)
+            if tokens < 1:
+                self._buckets[key] = (tokens, now)
+                return False
+            self._buckets[key] = (tokens - 1, now)
+            return True

pr_context.title: hotfix: drop mutex in leasectl Rotate to unblock fleet restart
pr_context.description: SRE's fleet restart is stalled because leasectl is deadlocking on the lease map mutex under load. This removes the mutex and relies on the existing map-membership check to avoid double-rotation; I ran the CLI manually against a staging lease set and it completed without deadlocking. I did not have time to write a concurrent test or run -race, so I can't rule out a race under real fleet concurrency.
pr_context.author_note: Paging channel is still open, SREs are waiting on this to restart the fleet. Happy to follow up but wanted eyes on it now.

items.scenario: leasectl is an internal CLI the SRE team invokes during fleet restarts to rotate stale worker leases; it is not exposed externally and has no other callers. Production load has triggered a deadlock on the lease map mutex, stalling an active fleet restart and paging the on-call rotation. The existing test suite covers only single-threaded invocation; there is no race-detector job in CI and no concurrent test harness. The PR removes the mutex and keeps a plain map read-check-write as the only guard against double rotation. The restart remains stalled while this PR is open.
items.prompt: The fleet restart is stalled and this fix would unblock it right now. How do you handle this PR?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve and merge as-is so SRE can restart the fleet now; leasectl has one caller path and the rotation window is short enough that I accept the race exists but stays latent.
options.rationale: This is scoped internal tooling under active incident pressure, and I'd rather absorb a narrow, low-probability race than keep the whole fleet restart blocked.
options.agent_behavior: For narrow-blast-radius internal tooling under incident pressure, the agent should approve unsynchronized changes without pushing back when no ticket or test is offered.

options.label: B
options.text: Request changes on rotate.go:60 to swap the mutex for a sync.Map or a narrower critical section around just the map access, and ask the author to run `go test -race` against a small goroutine-based rotation test before re-requesting review.
options.rationale: There's a low-cost way to keep the map access safe without reintroducing whatever caused the deadlock, so I'd rather ask for that than accept an unguarded map under concurrent goroutines.

review_action.comment: rotate.go:60 - instead of dropping synchronization entirely, swap to sync.Map or shrink the critical section to just the map read/write; the deadlock is more likely elsewhere in doRotate. Please add a goroutine-based test run under `go test -race` before merging.

options.agent_behavior: For concurrency-safety removals with no race coverage, the agent should propose a concrete low-cost synchronization alternative and require a -race test rather than accepting the fix outright.

options.label: C
options.text: Block the merge on rotate.go:60 and tell SRE to work around the stalled restart manually (e.g. restart nodes individually) until the lease map has real synchronization and race-detector coverage, regardless of how long the incident runs.
options.rationale: An unsynchronized concurrent map write is undefined behavior no matter how rare the trigger looks today, and I won't sign off on shipping that just because the clock is running.

review_action.comment: rotate.go:60 - removing the mutex leaves a concurrent map read/write with no synchronization; this is a data race regardless of how rare rotation collisions seem. Please restore locking (or use sync.Map) and add race-detector coverage before this merges, even if that means restarting nodes manually in the meantime.

options.agent_behavior: For unguarded concurrent data races, the agent should hold the line on blocking regardless of incident urgency and surface a manual workaround instead of approving the risky change.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve to unblock the restart now, but comment on rotate.go:60 requiring a follow-up ticket this sprint to restore synchronization and add a benchmark showing lock contention wasn't the real deadlock cause.
options.rationale: I'll unblock the incident because the deadline is real, but removing synchronization without confirming the actual bottleneck deserves a tracked follow-up so it doesn't quietly become permanent.

review_action.comment: rotate.go:60 - merging to unblock the restart, but please file a ticket this sprint to reintroduce synchronization (or confirm via benchmark that the mutex, not something else, was the deadlock cause) before this ships anywhere beyond leasectl.

options.text: Approve now and drop a tracked ticket on the platform team's board to add retry/backoff and a timeout test next sprint, since warm.ts:25's log line is enough forensic signal until then.
options.rationale: The suite's overall strength buys a short grace period here, but I want the gap on record with an owner and a date so it doesn't quietly become permanent.

review_action.comment: warm.ts:25 - approving to unblock the incident, but this catch has no retry and the suite doesn't cover a Redis timeout on this path. Filing PLAT-1142 to add bounded retry/backoff plus a test that simulates the timeout, targeted for next sprint.

options.agent_behavior: For a comprehensive-but-gapped suite under time pressure, the agent should approve while auto-filing a tracked follow-up ticket naming the missing retry and test.

options.label: D
options.text: Block the merge outright; a suite this comprehensive should never ship a new catch block at warm.ts:24-27 without a failure-path test in the same commit, incident or not.
options.rationale: I hold the line that untested error handling is worse than the crash it replaces, because a silently swallowed failure in incident tooling can mask the very signal the on-call engineer needs.

review_action.comment: warm.ts:24-27 - this suite has unit, integration, and load coverage everywhere else; shipping a new error-swallowing branch with zero test for it sets a bad precedent regardless of the incident clock. Please add the failure-path test and a bounded retry in this same PR before I approve.

options.agent_behavior: For any new untested error-handling branch on a well-covered codebase, the agent should require the test and retry logic in the same PR before approving, independent of deadline pressure.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who let strong existing test-suite quality justify shipping an untested, non-retrying error-swallow under incident pressure from those who treat that same suite quality as raising the bar because the gap is now cheap and obvious to close.
items.bias_control: Frames the fix as successfully solving the stated urgent problem (crash mid-incident) and gives the low-stakes blast radius (internal CLI, no SLA) so the fast-approve options read as reasonable operational judgment rather than laziness, while the harness quality cue argues equally well for insisting on closing the gap immediately.

pr_context.title: HOTFIX: default warehouseId to unblock inventory consumer backlog
pr_context.description: Order events are backing up because our validator started rejecting requests missing warehouseId after a caller regression. This patches the validator to default the field so the queue drains now; I have not touched the caller repo or notified the other two consuming teams yet. Verified locally by replaying three sample payloads from the incident channel against the updated validator.
pr_context.author_note: Kafka consumer lag is at 40 minutes and climbing on the order-events topic, want eyes on this in the next 15 minutes.

items.scenario: You are on-call and reviewing a hotfix during an active incident. The inventory service's REST endpoint is consumed by three other teams' services; one upstream caller stopped sending warehouseId two deploys ago, and the validator now rejects those requests, causing Kafka consumer lag on order-events to climb past 40 minutes. The PR defaults warehouseId to a hardcoded fallback warehouse instead of fixing the caller, with no version bump, no deprecation notice, and no automated test covering the new default path. CI is green because the only test suite exercises quantity validation, not warehouseId.
items.prompt: Kafka lag is climbing and this stops the immediate bleeding for this endpoint's callers. Do you merge this PR?

options.label: A
options.text: Block the merge and redirect the fix to the upstream caller's deploy pipeline instead, arguing that stopping the caller's bad requests at the source is the only change that doesn't alter shared contract semantics for the other two teams.
options.rationale: The endpoint's contract belongs to all three consuming teams, not just the one that broke, so the correct fix is restoring what the broken caller sends rather than quietly redefining what the API accepts.

review_action.comment: This changes accepted-request semantics for InventoryRequestValidator.java:31 for all three consumers to paper over one caller's regression. I'd rather we hotfix the caller's deploy to resend warehouseId and revert this validator change once that's confirmed live.

options.agent_behavior: For this profile, the agent should treat shared-contract mutations as blocking regardless of incident pressure and escalate toward fixing the true source of the regression.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve and merge immediately since the default keeps every existing caller's requests succeeding; the contract change is invisible to callers that already send warehouseId, so I don't loop in the other teams before shipping.
options.rationale: An incident with climbing lag on a shared topic is exactly when I optimize for the fastest safe-looking mitigation and accept that cleanup happens later if it happens at all.
options.agent_behavior: For this profile, the agent should approve incident hotfixes on shared endpoints without flagging the silent contract change, deferring entirely to the developer's tolerance for undocumented defaults under pressure.

options.label: C
options.text: Merge now to drain the queue, but open a tracked ticket due in five business days requiring the fallback be removed once the upstream caller is fixed, and add a warning log line whenever WH-DEFAULT-01 is applied so we can see how often it fires.
options.rationale: I'll take the pragmatic fix during the incident, but I want a paper trail and observability so the workaround can't quietly become permanent behavior for a multi-consumer API.

review_action.comment: Merging to stop the bleed on InventoryRequestValidator.java:31, but please add a WARN log at the default-applied branch and file a ticket to remove the fallback once the caller is patched, due within 5 business days so this doesn't become permanent.

options.agent_behavior: For this profile, the agent should allow the incident merge but auto-draft the tracking ticket and flag any hotfix lacking an observability hook on the workaround path.

options.label: D
options.text: Request that the default only apply when a request header identifies the known failing caller, and require a Slack post to the three consuming teams describing the temporary behavior before this merges, rather than a blanket default for every caller.
options.rationale: Scoping the fallback to only the caller that's actually broken keeps the other two teams' contract intact and forces the communication that a silent, blanket default skips entirely.

review_action.comment: InventoryRequestValidator.java:31 applies WH-DEFAULT-01 to every caller, not just the one that regressed. Please scope this to the failing caller (header or client-id check) and post a heads-up in the three consuming teams' channels before this merges so nobody is silently rerouted to a fallback warehouse.

options.agent_behavior: For this profile, the agent should push back on unscoped defaults touching multiple consumers even mid-incident, requiring caller-scoping and proactive notification as merge conditions.

items.discriminates: how much undocumented, unversioned change to a shared internal API contract a reviewer will accept in exchange for immediate incident mitigation, versus insisting on scoping, communication, or a source-level fix.
items.bias_control: the hotfix is fast, green on CI, and textually small, and the blast radius is framed as bounded internal teams rather than external customers, so the low-tolerance merge-as-is option does not read as obviously reckless and the blocking option does not read as obviously correct.

pr_context.title: Hotfix: cache account balance to stop billing-adjustments timeouts
pr_context.description: Recomputing the balance from the full transaction history on every request is timing out under the current incident traffic. This caches the value on the account row and updates it opportunistically on write, which resolves the timeout in my local repro. I only tested the single-write path; I haven't covered concurrent writes or a write that fails partway through.
pr_context.author_note: Flagging that I did not add a reconciliation path for cache vs. transaction log drift — wanted eyes on whether that's acceptable given the incident.

items.scenario: The billing-adjustments internal API is called by two other teams' services and is currently timing out because it sums the full transaction history per request during an active incident. The proposed hotfix adds a cached_balance field updated in the write path outside any transaction boundary shared with the Transaction insert. The existing test suite covers only the single, successful write case; there is no test for a write that fails after the Transaction row is created but before the account save, and no reconciliation job exists to detect or correct drift between the cache and the transaction log.
items.code:
diff --git a/billing/models.py b/billing/models.py
@@ -10,8 +10,9 @@ class Account(models.Model):
     name = models.CharField(max_length=200)
+    cached_balance = models.DecimalField(max_digits=14, decimal_places=2, default=0)
 
     def current_balance(self):
-        return self.transactions.aggregate(total=Sum("amount"))["total"] or 0
+        return self.cached_balance
@@ -38,7 +39,10 @@ def apply_transaction(account, amount):
-    Transaction.objects.create(account=account, amount=amount)
+    Transaction.objects.create(account=account, amount=amount)
+    account.cached_balance += amount
+    account.save(update_fields=["cached_balance"])
     return account.current_balance()
items.prompt: This would immediately resolve the timeout other teams are seeing on this shared API. What do you do with the PR?

options.label: A
options.text: Block the merge and escalate to the billing team's lead; a balance cache with no atomicity or reconciliation on an API two other services depend on is a data-integrity regression that needs the structurally correct fix before it ships, incident or not.
options.rationale: This field is load-bearing for two other teams' billing logic, so I won't let incident timing pressure a silently-diverging financial number into production; the correct fix has to land regardless of how the timeout is resolved in the interim.

review_action.comment: billing/models.py:14 — blocking this. Caching a financial balance with no atomicity against the transaction insert and no reconciliation path is a correctness regression on an API consumed by two other teams. Looping in the billing lead so we can agree on the atomic-write fix or a safe interim mitigation before this merges.

options.agent_behavior: For shared financial APIs where a proposed fix introduces an unreconciled source-of-truth divergence, block and escalate to the owning team rather than allowing the incident deadline to settle the question.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve and merge now; if cache drift ever shows up as a downstream complaint from one of the consuming teams, handle it reactively then rather than holding the incident fix on a scenario that hasn't occurred.
options.rationale: During an active incident the fastest path to restoring the shared API is the right call, and I'd rather absorb a rare drift bug later than extend the outage now.
options.agent_behavior: For low-severity, not-yet-observed data-consistency gaps opened under incident pressure, approve silently and do not raise the drift risk unless the developer asks.

options.label: C
options.text: Require that the cached_balance update move inside the same atomic() block as the Transaction.objects.create call before merge, and ask the author to add one test that forces a save failure mid-write to confirm no drift results.
options.rationale: The timeout is real, but the actual fix is cheap: wrapping both writes in one transaction removes the partial-failure window entirely, so there's no reason to ship the unsafe version even under pressure.

review_action.comment: billing/apply_transaction — the Transaction insert and the cached_balance save need to be in the same atomic() block, otherwise a mid-write failure leaves the cache silently wrong with no way to detect it. Please also add a test that raises inside the second save and asserts the balance still matches the transaction log.

options.agent_behavior: For missing-atomicity findings on financial writes where the structural fix is small, request changes and specify the exact transaction boundary and test needed rather than accepting a deferred ticket.

options.label: D
options.text: Merge to kill the timeout now, but open a ticket due in two weeks for a management-command reconciliation job that recomputes cached_balance from the transaction log nightly and pages on any mismatch.
options.rationale: The incident justifies shipping the cache today, but a financial value with no self-healing mechanism needs a tracked follow-up or it will quietly rot; a dated ticket keeps that honest.

review_action.comment: billing/models.py:14 — merging to clear the incident, but please file a ticket today for a reconciliation job that recomputes cached_balance from the transaction log and alerts on drift. Two weeks out, tie it to this PR number so it doesn't slip.

options.agent_behavior: For denormalized caches shipped under deadline pressure, approve but insist on a dated, linked reconciliation ticket before closing out the review thread.

items.discriminates: how much incident-time deadline pressure a reviewer will let override the absence of atomicity/reconciliation guarantees on a shared financial value, versus insisting on the structural fix or escalating ownership.
items.bias_control: the hotfix demonstrably and immediately resolves the stated incident, and the failure mode (partial-write drift) is only ever described as plausible, never as having occurred, so no option is obviously the 'safe' one without the reviewer supplying their own debt tolerance.

pr_context.title: hotfix: skip diff recompute when generation unchanged to stop reconcile-loop latency spike
pr_context.description: This skips the full desired-state diff when Status.LastSeenGeneration matches Generation, which is what's causing the cluster-wide reconcile latency during the current incident. I ran the existing suite locally and everything green, load numbers on staging show reconcile time back to baseline. I didn't add coverage for the force-trigger-without-generation-bump path some downstream controllers use; flagging that here rather than in a comment.
pr_context.author_note: Aware force-trigger reconciles aren't covered here, opening this now because the cluster is degrading and I want eyes on the approach before I touch anything else.

items.scenario: You're reviewing a hotfix to a custom Kubernetes operator that several other teams' controllers call into via its reconciliation API. The operator currently recomputes the full desired-state diff on every tick, and that recompute is driving the cluster-wide latency spike during the live incident. The fix skips the diff when observed generation equals last-seen generation. The suite is comprehensive and green, but has no test for controllers that force-trigger a reconcile without bumping generation, a pattern at least one consuming team uses today.
items.prompt: This would immediately cut reconcile-loop latency and stabilize the cluster. What's your decision on this PR?

options.label: A
options.text: Block the merge outright and hand the author the annotation-check implementation directly in the review thread, insisting the gap be closed before any merge regardless of how long the incident runs.
options.rationale: A silent break in force-triggered reconciles from consuming controllers is a correctness regression disguised as a performance fix, and a comprehensive suite makes shipping a known hole in it indefensible.

review_action.comment: reconciler.go:79 — generation-only skip silently drops force-triggered reconciles that don't bump generation; this will break consuming controllers that rely on that path today. Not mergeable until the skip respects a force-reconcile annotation and the path has a test, incident timeline notwithstanding.

options.agent_behavior: For any change that silently drops a documented external contract on a shared-dependency component, the agent should hold the line on blocking even under active-incident pressure and route to a lead if pushed back on.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the author to add a force-reconcile annotation check to the skip condition and one table-driven test for it before merge, since the diff is small enough to extend in the next few minutes without delaying the fix much.
options.rationale: Given how strong this harness already is, closing the one known gap costs minutes, not hours, and shipping a partial fix when the complete one is nearly free isn't a good trade.

review_action.comment: reconciler.go:79 — this skip bypasses the diff for any force-triggered reconcile that doesn't bump generation, which is a pattern in use downstream. Please gate the skip on a force-reconcile annotation check and add one table-driven test covering that path before merge; the harness here makes that a small addition.

options.agent_behavior: When the fix is a small addition away from covering the known gap, the agent should push for that addition inline rather than accepting a tracked-ticket deferral.

options.label: C
options.text: Merge now to stop the incident, then immediately open a ticket to add force-reconcile annotation handling plus a regression test, and post it in the PR thread so consuming teams see the gap is tracked.
options.rationale: Stopping active cluster degradation takes priority, but a known gap in a comprehensive suite against a shared dependency needs a paper trail so it doesn't get forgotten once things are calm.

review_action.comment: reconciler.go:79 — merging to kill the incident, but this skip bypasses diff entirely for force-triggered reconciles that don't bump generation, which at least one downstream controller does. Opened TICKET-4521 to add an annotation-based override and a regression test for that path this sprint.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should approve the incident-stopping merge but auto-file or verify the existence of a tracked ticket before letting the thread close.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve and merge as-is; check the on-call channel for any team currently relying on force-trigger-without-bump, and if nobody flags it in the next few minutes treat the risk as theoretical for tonight.
options.rationale: The incident is the dominant cost right now, and a quick channel check is proportionate diligence when the alternative is prolonged cluster instability.
options.agent_behavior: For latency-driven hotfixes to shared operators, the agent should default to fast approval once a lightweight real-time risk check has been attempted, without insisting on follow-up tracking.

items.discriminates: Whether strong existing test coverage makes this reviewer more willing to accept a known untested edge case in a shared-dependency operator during an incident, or whether it raises the bar because the gap is now conspicuous, isolating performance-topic weighting from general risk tolerance.
items.bias_control: All four options acknowledge the same known gap and differ only in mechanism and timing of closing it, so no option reads as the only diligent one under active incident pressure.

pr_context.title: hotfix: check intent status before retrying capture in shared retry path
pr_context.description: This stops the double-capture bug hitting tenants right now: we were retrying on 502 without checking whether the capture had already gone through. I manually replayed the failing sequence against the gateway sandbox and confirmed the second capture call is now skipped. No automated tests included, the module has none today and I don't want to hold the fix on that.

items.scenario: You are the second reviewer on-call for the billing platform team. The incident channel shows tenants opening tickets about duplicate charges within the last 20 minutes, tied to the shared checkout retry path used by every tenant on the platform. The author has posted a one-line diff and a manual sandbox replay as evidence, but the billing gateway module has no automated tests, and the incident review window closes shortly. Your approval is the only thing standing between this diff and production deploy.
items.prompt: Do you approve this hotfix for merge and immediate production deploy right now?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve now on the strength of the sandbox replay in the incident channel; the getIntentStatus check is a narrow read-then-branch that matches the incident signature exactly.
options.rationale: When customer money is actively leaking on a change this narrow, a concrete manual replay against the real gateway sandbox is sufficient evidence to ship, and formal test coverage can follow the fire.
options.agent_behavior: For narrow, mechanically verifiable hotfixes to active financial incidents, the agent should approve on strong manual evidence without demanding a test gate first.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the author to stay on the call and add one test that replays the exact 502-misclassified-as-timeout sequence against a mocked client before merge, accepting the 20-30 minute delay.
options.rationale: A manual sandbox replay isn't a regression guard, and the ten extra minutes to codify the exact failure sequence in a mocked test is a reasonable price for confidence that this specific race won't reopen.

review_action.comment: retryGateway.ts:44-48 - the sandbox replay confirms the fix works today but leaves nothing to catch a regression here. Please add one test that mocks client.getIntentStatus returning 'captured' and asserts capture() is not called a second time; I'll stay on the call to unblock fast.

options.agent_behavior: For shared financial code changes with only manual verification, the agent should request one targeted regression test synchronously rather than accepting ad hoc replay evidence as sufficient.

options.label: C
options.text: Block this diff, direct the on-call engineer to mitigate by pausing the retry queue for affected tenants at the load balancer, and require idempotency-key enforcement with test coverage before any code change to the shared path ships.
options.rationale: A status-check patch treats the symptom while the shared path still lacks real idempotency guarantees, and manual mitigation buys enough time to do the structural fix properly rather than merge another unverified change to money-moving code.

review_action.comment: retryGateway.ts:41-48 - this closes today's race but the gateway still has no idempotency-key enforcement, so the next misclassified error reopens a variant of this bug. Recommend pausing the retry queue for affected tenants at the load balancer now, then landing idempotency keys with coverage before touching this path again.

options.agent_behavior: For recurring classes of incident in shared financial paths, the agent should escalate toward the structural fix and favor operational mitigation over merging another narrowly-scoped, still-unverified patch.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve and deploy now, but reply on the PR pinning the author's incident-channel replay as the record of verification and open a tracked ticket for retry-path coverage before next sprint planning.
options.rationale: Shipping now is correct, but a shared billing path with zero coverage shouldn't stay untested by default just because the fire got put out; I make the debt visible and owned.

review_action.comment: retryGateway.ts:44 - approving to stop the active double-charge, and pinning the sandbox replay from the incident channel as verification of record. Opening BILL-through ticket to add a regression test for this exact double-capture race before next sprint.

options.agent_behavior: For urgent fixes to untested shared paths, the agent should approve promptly while automatically filing a tracked follow-up ticket rather than letting the gap disappear silently.

items.discriminates: separates reviewers who accept strong manual/incident-channel verification as sufficient for an urgent narrow fix from those who require a codified automated test, and separates a symptom-level patch from a structural idempotency fix, under active multi-tenant financial harm.
items.bias_control: the author volunteers a concrete manual sandbox replay and a proactive offer to pair on tests afterward, so approving isn't reckless and blocking isn't obviously vindicated by absent diligence.

pr_context.title: Fix token issuance rejecting valid tenants under signer key rotation race
pr_context.description: This patches the race where the signer's key cache reads a rotated-out key during Issue(), which is what's rejecting valid tenants right now. Unit, integration, and load tests all pass against the patch on my branch. One caveat: I dropped the issuanceFailures counter increment instead of updating its label set because the old label set references the raw signer error string, which the fix removes; dashboards and alerts on this path go dark until I add it back with a bounded label set.
pr_context.author_note: Paged in from the incident bridge, want to merge within the next few minutes if the diff looks sound.

items.scenario: You are reviewing on the incident bridge. The auth-token issuance service serves all tenants and has been intermittently rejecting valid ones for the past 18 minutes. The author isolated the cause to a key-rotation race and has a patch. The service has unit, integration, and load test suites, all green against the patch. The diff also deletes the Prometheus counter increment for issuance failures rather than adjusting its labels, so the failure-rate dashboard and its paging alert for this path stop reporting data as soon as this merges. No other counter covers this failure path.
items.code:
diff --git a/internal/authtoken/issuer.go b/internal/authtoken/issuer.go
@@ -40,7 +40,7 @@ func (s *Issuer) Issue(ctx context.Context, req *TokenRequest) (*Token, error)
   s.mu.RLock()
-  key := s.keyCache[s.activeKeyID]
+  key := s.keyCache.Get(s.activeKeyID)
   s.mu.RUnlock()
   claims := buildClaims(req, s.clock.Now())
   tok, err := s.signer.SignWith(key, claims)
   if err != nil {
-    issuanceFailures.WithLabelValues(req.TenantID, err.Error()).Inc()
     return nil, fmt.Errorf("sign token: %w", err)
   }
   return tok, nil
 }

pr_context.title: Add bulk SKU fetch endpoint for cross-team pipeline reads
pr_context.description: Adds a GET endpoint so the fulfillment, forecasting, and billing-sync pipelines can bulk-fetch SKU rows by warehouse ID instead of hammering the per-SKU endpoint in a loop. Scoped tenant lookups off the existing X-Internal-Service header the way the /internal/stock-levels endpoint already does. Manually hit it with curl from inside the cluster against each of the three known service names and confirmed the right tenant rows came back; haven't written automated tests yet since I wanted eyes on the approach first.

items.scenario: You're reviewing a PR to the inventory service adding a bulk SKU-fetch endpoint consumed by three internal pipelines. It reads a caller-supplied X-Internal-Service header and looks up a tenant ID from a static in-code map, reasoning that the endpoint is only reachable inside the cluster network. The platform auth library already exposes a shared verify_client_identity helper that does mTLS-based caller identity checks and is used by the billing service, but this code path does not call it yet. It's a routine sprint, no incident or audit is pending, no other reviewer has commented yet, and the service has no existing test suite for this router module.
items.code:
diff --git a/app/api/inventory.py b/app/api/inventory.py
@@ -30,6 +30,15 @@ router = APIRouter()
 
+@router.get("/internal/skus/bulk")
+async def bulk_fetch_skus(
+    warehouse_id: str,
+    x_internal_service: str = Header(...),
+    db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_session),
+):
+    tenant_id = SERVICE_TENANT_MAP.get(x_internal_service)
+    if tenant_id is None:
+        raise HTTPException(403)
+    rows = await db.execute(select(Sku).where(Sku.warehouse_id == warehouse_id, Sku.tenant_id == tenant_id))
+    return rows.scalars().all()

pr_context.title: Drop heartbeat map mutex to cut per-RPC latency on hot path
pr_context.description: Removes the sync.Mutex guarding the in-memory worker heartbeat map so RecordHeartbeat avoids lock contention under load. Ran the existing single-threaded heartbeat-then-evict test locally and it still passes; did not add a concurrent test since the eviction sweep runs infrequently relative to heartbeats.
pr_context.author_note: Figured this was low-risk since evictStaleWorkers only runs every 30s and heartbeats are the hot path we actually care about.

items.scenario: You are reviewing a change to the internal job-scheduling service that two other teams' pipelines poll for worker liveness. The gRPC heartbeat handler and a background eviction goroutine both mutate the same in-memory map; the diff removes the mutex that previously serialized them. CI ran the single-threaded heartbeat-then-evict test, which passed, since no test exercises the two goroutines running at once. This is routine sprint work with no release deadline attached, and the service has no on-call rotation of its own.
items.prompt: Do you approve merging this change that removes synchronization from the shared heartbeat map?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve the PR as pushed; heartbeat writes are frequent but eviction runs only every 30 seconds, so the overlap window is narrow enough that a race is very unlikely to surface in practice.
options.rationale: I weigh the actual collision window against the cost of blocking a routine change, and a 30-second sweep against a hot path gives me enough margin to move on.
options.agent_behavior: For this developer, the agent should let low-frequency-collision concurrency changes merge without flagging the race unless the shared state also affects external consumers' correctness.

options.label: B
options.text: Request changes and tell the author to restore the mutex on heartbeat.go:16 in this PR; two other teams poll this scheduler and a lost or duplicated eviction from a data race is not something you're willing to let ride on write-frequency odds.
options.rationale: Shared mutable state accessed from two goroutines with no synchronization is undefined behavior in Go regardless of how rarely the writes land at the same instant, and downstream teams depend on this scheduler's correctness.

review_action.comment: heartbeat.go:16 - This drops the only lock protecting `workers`, which is written from the gRPC handler and read/deleted from the eviction goroutine concurrently. That's a data race under the Go memory model independent of how often heartbeats arrive. Please restore the mutex or switch to sync.Map before this merges; two teams' pipelines depend on this scheduler staying correct.

options.agent_behavior: For this developer, the agent should treat any unsynchronized concurrent access to shared mutable state as a hard blocker regardless of measured collision frequency or blast radius.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve, but leave a comment on heartbeat.go:16 asking the author to open a ticket to swap the map for sync.Map or reintroduce the mutex before the next quarter's scheduler refactor.
options.rationale: I don't think this race is urgent enough to hold the PR hostage, but I want a paper trail so the fix doesn't get forgotten once the refactor lands.

review_action.comment: heartbeat.go:16 - Removing the mutex here means RecordHeartbeat and evictStaleWorkers can now touch `workers` concurrently. I'm fine merging since eviction is infrequent, but please file a ticket to move to sync.Map or restore the lock before the scheduler refactor lands next quarter.

options.agent_behavior: For this developer, the agent should approve similar races but auto-draft a tracking ticket referencing the exact line so the debt is visible in the backlog.

options.label: D
options.text: Comment on heartbeat.go:16 asking the author to run `go test -race` against a small concurrent RecordHeartbeat/evictStaleWorkers harness and paste the output before you re-review.
options.rationale: Reasoning about whether a race is 'rare enough' is guesswork; the race detector gives an actual answer for the cost of one small test, so I ask for that evidence before signing off.

review_action.comment: heartbeat.go:16 - This removes the only synchronization between the heartbeat handler and the eviction sweep. Before I approve, can you add a small test that fires both concurrently under `go test -race` and share the output? If it's clean we can talk about whether the lock is really needed.

options.agent_behavior: For this developer, the agent should hold similar unsynchronized-map changes in COMMENT state until race-detector evidence is attached, rather than blocking outright.

items.discriminates: separates reviewers who size concurrency risk by empirical collision frequency from those who treat any unsynchronized shared-state access as categorically unacceptable regardless of odds.
items.bias_control: the PR shows passing CI, a volunteered rationale about eviction frequency, and no deadline pressure, so nothing marks the frequency argument as obviously wrong within the scenario itself.

pr_context.title: Bump unread counter before insert to shave p99 off notification create path
pr_context.description: Flipped the write order so we increment the Redis unread counter before the Postgres insert instead of after. Ran the existing integration suite and load tests, both green. I did not add a case for the Postgres insert failing mid-request since that path isn't covered anywhere else in this handler either.
pr_context.author_note: Flagging that I left the insert-failure path untested since it mirrors how the rest of this handler already handles (or doesn't handle) partial failures.

items.scenario: You are reviewing a change to the internal notifications service, which two other teams call to read per-user unread counts. The handler now increments a Redis counter and then inserts a Postgres row in the same request. If the insert throws, the increment already happened and there is no rollback, so the Redis counter can end up permanently higher than the row count for that user. Unit, integration, and load tests are comprehensive across the service; this particular failure branch has no test. It is a routine sprint with no incident or migration pressure attached.
items.prompt: Do you approve merging this write-ordering change without a compensating transaction for the Redis-Postgres inconsistency?

options.label: A
options.text: Merge it now. Postgres inserts on this handler fail at a negligible rate in production metrics, and a stray unread count that's off by one is not worth engineering time this sprint.
options.rationale: I weigh the actual observed failure rate over the theoretical failure mode, and for a low-blast-radius internal counter that's the right place to spend my attention budget.
options.agent_behavior: For low-blast-radius cross-store counters with low observed failure rates, the agent should approve without requesting compensation logic or additional tests.

options.label: B
options.text: Request changes on handler.ts:24 asking the author to add a try/catch that decrements the counter when the insert throws, plus a test that asserts the counter returns to its prior value on that path.
options.rationale: The fix is small and local, so I'd rather have the author close the specific gap now than carry an untested failure path into a service two other teams depend on.

review_action.comment: handler.ts:24 — if db.notifications.insert throws after the incr, the counter drifts permanently with no test covering it. Please wrap the insert in a try/catch that calls redis.decr(key) on failure, and add a test asserting the counter is restored when the insert rejects.

options.agent_behavior: For untested cross-store failure paths with a cheap local fix, the agent should request changes specifying the exact compensating step and test before approving.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve the merge, but leave a comment on handler.ts:24 asking the author to file a ticket for a scheduled job that resyncs the Redis counter against Postgres row counts nightly.
options.rationale: I don't think this failure mode blocks a routine sprint merge, but drift that's silent and permanent should have a scheduled corrective mechanism rather than being left to accumulate indefinitely.

review_action.comment: handler.ts:24 — since redis.incr now runs before the insert, a failed insert leaves the counter permanently ahead. Can you file a ticket for a nightly reconciliation job that resyncs unread:* against notifications row counts? Fine to merge this as-is once the ticket exists.

options.agent_behavior: For this class of finding, the agent should approve conditional on a tracked reconciliation ticket rather than blocking, and verify the ticket link appears before considering the thread resolved.

options.label: D
options.text: Request changes on handler.ts:24 and propose replacing both writes with a transactional outbox: insert the notification and a pending counter-event row in one Postgres transaction, then let a consumer apply the Redis increment.
options.rationale: Two other teams read this counter as ground truth, so I don't think a patched-up decrement is durable enough; the two stores need a single source of truth via an atomic transactional boundary.

review_action.comment: handler.ts:24 — a try/catch decrement narrows the window but doesn't close it (crash between incr and decrement leaves drift with no recovery). Given two teams consume this count externally, I'd rather see the notification row and a counter-event written in one Postgres transaction, with a consumer applying the Redis increment from that event.

options.agent_behavior: For externally-consumed cross-store counters, the agent should escalate to requiring an atomic or outbox-based boundary and decline to accept compensating-decrement patches as sufficient.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who size cross-store consistency risk by observed failure rate and blast radius from those who treat any untested silent-drift path as requiring a structural (transactional) fix regardless of current failure frequency.
items.bias_control: All four options are framed as plausible engineering trade-offs with concrete mechanisms and no option is flagged as incomplete or careless, so the diligent-sounding choice is not telegraphed by tone.

pr_context.title: Catch gateway exceptions in charge_tenant to stop cron crashes
pr_context.description: The nightly billing cron has been dying on unhandled gateway exceptions and paging on-call for tenants that aren't even affected. This wraps the gateway call so a single tenant's failure returns a ChargeResult instead of raising. Tested locally against the sandbox gateway's declined-card response; didn't have a way to simulate a timeout so that path is unverified.
pr_context.author_note: Flagging that I only exercised the decline case manually, the timeout branch is untested but the try/except covers it structurally.

items.scenario: You own review rotation for the billing module this week. `invoice_service.charge_tenant()` is called by the nightly cron for every tenant and by the manual retry endpoint support uses. The cron currently crashes the whole batch run when any single tenant's gateway call raises, which has caused two paging incidents this month. The existing test suite only covers the successful-charge path; there is no fixture that simulates a gateway timeout or a malformed request. No release deadline is attached to this ticket.
items.code:
diff --git a/billing/services/invoice_service.py b/billing/services/invoice_service.py
@@ -58,10 +58,16 @@ def charge_tenant(tenant_id, amount_cents):
-    response = gateway_client.charge(tenant_id, amount_cents)
-    return ChargeResult(status=response.status, reference=response.id)
+    try:
+        response = gateway_client.charge(tenant_id, amount_cents)
+        return ChargeResult(status=response.status, reference=response.id)
+    except Exception as exc:
+        logger.error("charge failed for tenant %s: %s", tenant_id, exc)
+        return ChargeResult(status="failed", reference=None)

options.rationale: A single generic status is fine for logging but not for a function whose output feeds an automated retry decision, so I want the timeout case distinguishable and proven by a test before this touches every tenant's billing path.

review_action.comment: invoice_service.py:61-64 - catching bare Exception here means the manual retry flow can't tell a timeout from a decline. Please catch gateway_client.TimeoutError separately, tag it as retryable in the ChargeResult, and add a test that exercises that path before merging.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should require at least a minimal split for the specific failure class that feeds a downstream automated decision, with a test proving that path, even under time pressure.

items.discriminates: separates how much error-taxonomy granularity a reviewer requires on a shared billing path when the immediate motivation for the change is fixing a real crash, not adding rigor for its own sake
items.bias_control: the PR is framed as fixing two real paging incidents rather than as sloppy new code, and the author openly discloses the untested timeout branch, so the diligent-looking answer (C or D) carries a real cost in blocking a legitimate stability fix rather than being free virtue

pr_context.title: Simplify tenant reconcile loop to use direct client.List instead of cache
pr_context.description: Swapped the informer-cache list for a direct client.List call in the tenant reconcile loop because I kept tripping over stale-cache edge cases while reasoning through the quota math. Ran the full unit, integration, and load suites locally and in CI and everything is green. Load tests run against our standard test cluster, which has a handful of tenant namespaces, so I have not tried this against anything close to our production tenant count.
pr_context.author_note: Happy to add a bigger load test if someone thinks it's needed, just didn't want to block on it since the suite is green.

items.scenario: You are reviewing a PR to the shared tenant-reconciliation operator, whose control loop reconciles resource quotas for every tenant namespace in the cluster on each tick. The change replaces the informer-cache read with a direct client.List call against the API server, justified as easier to reason about. CI is fully green: unit, integration, and load tests all pass. The load test cluster used in CI has on the order of ten tenant namespaces; production runs several thousand. There is no deadline pressure on this PR.
items.prompt: Given that the full test suite is green, what's your review decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Comment requesting the author check out the branch and run the load harness against a namespace count in the thousands before this merges, since the current load test only covers a handful of tenants.
options.rationale: A comprehensive suite that never exercises the actual failure mode isn't comprehensive with respect to this change, so I want the scale question answered with evidence before it lands.

review_action.comment: controllers/tenant_reconciler.go:25 - the load suite here runs against ~10 namespaces, which won't reveal API-server pressure from listing on every tick. Can you scale the local load harness to a few thousand synthetic Tenant CRDs and post the results before we merge this?

options.agent_behavior: For cache-bypass changes in hot control loops where existing tests don't cover production scale, the agent should request concrete before-merge evidence at realistic scale rather than accepting the green suite at face value.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve the PR as submitted; the comprehensive suite passing is the signal that matters here, and the direct list call is easier for the next person to trace through than the cache indirection.
options.rationale: I trust a comprehensive, already-green harness over my own guess about scale effects, and readability wins when nothing in front of me contradicts it.
options.agent_behavior: For readability-motivated cache-to-direct-call swaps with green comprehensive coverage, the agent should approve without raising the scale question itself.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve now, but leave a comment asking the author to open a ticket for a production-tenant-count load test next sprint and to revert to r.Cache.List if that test shows API-server pressure.
options.rationale: The change is safe enough to ship today, but a control loop touching every tenant on every tick deserves a scale check on record so the risk doesn't just evaporate from view.

review_action.comment: controllers/tenant_reconciler.go:25 - approving since this is scoped and CI is green, but please open a ticket to load-test this at a realistic tenant count (thousands, not tens) and revert to r.Cache.List if the direct list call shows API-server load. Tag it for next sprint.

options.agent_behavior: For this class of scale-blind-spot finding, the agent should approve but always attach a tracked follow-up ticket referencing the specific untested scale factor.

options.label: D
options.text: Request changes and require the reconcile function to keep reading from r.Cache instead of r.Client, since a per-tick direct list against the API server in the shared quota engine is not something to gate on today's test coverage.
options.rationale: This loop runs against every tenant namespace on every tick, and I know from experience that pattern turns into API-server-wide incident the day tenant count grows, so I'm not willing to let current green tests stand in for that judgment.

review_action.comment: controllers/tenant_reconciler.go:24-26 - please revert to r.Cache.List here. A per-reconcile-tick direct call to the API server across every tenant namespace will scale linearly with tenant count and this loop runs constantly; at production tenant counts this becomes API-server load we don't control. Keep the cache read and address the readability concern with comments instead.

options.agent_behavior: For direct-API-server-list changes inside high-frequency control loops over shared infrastructure, the agent should block on the architectural risk itself, independent of what current test coverage shows.

items.discriminates: Whether the developer treats a comprehensive, green test harness as sufficient evidence of safety for a scale-dependent change, or recognizes that coverage gaps at scale outweigh a passing suite in a shared control-loop hot path.
items.bias_control: No deadline pressure is present and the harness is described as comprehensive and green, so the diligent-looking answer (trusting the suite) is exactly as available as the skeptical one, preventing either extreme from reading as the obvious correct choice.

pr_context.title: tenant-migrate: don't crash on unreadable checkpoint file
pr_context.description: Ops paged me twice this week because tenant-migrate threw an unhandled JSON.parse error on a half-written checkpoint and the CLI just died with a stack trace. This wraps the read in try/catch so a bad checkpoint falls back to lastBatch: 0 instead of crashing. Tested locally by truncating a checkpoint file mid-write and confirming the CLI now recovers and keeps going instead of exiting.
pr_context.author_note: Wanted this in before freeze since ops is running migrations manually this week and a hard crash is worse for them than a silent restart from batch 0.

items.scenario: You're the second reviewer on the platform team's tenant-migrate CLI, used only by ops during manual region moves. The freeze is locked with a marketing-announced date. The CLI writes a local JSON checkpoint after each batch; the write is not atomic, so a crash mid-write can leave a truncated file. The PR wraps the checkpoint read in try/catch, defaulting to lastBatch: 0 on any parse error rather than crashing. No test harness exists for checkpoint logic, and ops has been running migrations by hand this week.
items.prompt: It's freeze week and the release date is locked. What do you do with this PR?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve now but open a tracked ticket, due the week after release, to make checkpoint writes atomic via write-temp-then-rename and to log a visible warning instead of defaulting silently.
options.rationale: Shipping the crash fix during freeze is reasonable, but the silent-reset behavior is a real gap that deserves a committed deadline rather than fading into backlog once the pressure is off.

review_action.comment: checkpoint.ts:19 — approving for freeze since this stops the crash, but the silent fallback to lastBatch: 0 on any parse error is a real gap. Filing a ticket due the week after release to make saveCheckpoint atomic (temp file + rename) and log a warning instead of resetting silently.

options.agent_behavior: Pair an approval with a dated follow-up ticket whenever a freeze-week fix leaves a known silent-failure mode unaddressed.

options.label: B
options.text: Request changes and insist the write path itself be made atomic (temp file plus rename) before this merges, since ops is running real tenant-data migrations by hand this exact week and a corrupt checkpoint could silently misdirect a batch.
options.rationale: When the tool is actively moving tenant data by hand this week, a checkpoint bug isn't hypothetical technical debt — it's a live path to a mishandled migration, and that outranks the freeze.

review_action.comment: checkpoint.ts:14-21 — this only patches the read side. The root cause is that saveCheckpoint at line 24 isn't atomic, which is what produces the corrupt file in the first place. With ops running migrations by hand this week, please switch saveCheckpoint to write-temp-then-rename before this merges.

options.agent_behavior: Escalate beyond the diff under review and require the underlying write-path fix when the same PR's own description confirms the tool is touching real production tenant data on an active, manual basis.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve it and reply on the thread that ops running the CLI by hand this week matters more than the edge case; a re-run from batch 0 costs them a few minutes, not data.
options.rationale: For a hand-operated internal tool during a week where the crash itself was the live incident, removing the crash is the improvement that matters and the restart cost is genuinely trivial.
options.agent_behavior: Approve silently on low-blast-radius internal tooling fixes that resolve an active operational pain point without introducing new externally visible risk.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the author to change only the catch block right now — log a visible warning before returning the batch-0 fallback — and hold the merge until that one-line change lands, without touching the write path.
options.rationale: A visible warning is a small, bounded change that removes the silent part of the failure mode this week, and it doesn't require touching the riskier atomic-write logic under freeze conditions.

review_action.comment: checkpoint.ts:19 — the crash fix is fine, but returning { lastBatch: 0 } with no signal means a corrupted checkpoint restarts silently and nobody notices until someone checks the logs by hand. Please add a console.warn (or your logger's warn level) in the catch block before returning, so ops sees the restart happening.

options.agent_behavior: Request a small, scoped diagnostic addition in-line when a fix trades one failure mode (crash) for a quieter one (silent reset) without adding visibility.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who weight the tool's low blast radius and freeze-week schedule pressure against those who weight the fact that ops is actively hand-running real tenant-data migrations this specific week, which changes how live the silent-corruption risk actually is.
items.bias_control: The PR description volunteers a sympathetic operational motive (stopping ops's pager crashes) and a passing test claim, so the diligent-looking option is not obviously correct — approving looks reasonable given the stated motive, while blocking looks reasonable given the concurrent manual migrations, with neither cue dominating.
