pr_context.title: ops-cli: add bulk_set_flag subcommand for weekend flag rollback
pr_context.description: Adds a subcommand so SREs can bulk-toggle feature flags by env/name during the release weekend without touching the DB console directly. Tested manually against staging with an exact flag name and confirmed the enabled column flips. Didn't get to a zero-match or concurrent-invocation test given the freeze timeline, calling that out here for visibility.
pr_context.author_note: Ran this against staging three times with exact flag names, all fine. Happy to follow up on edge cases after the weekend if folks want.

items.scenario: You're reviewing a change to ops_cli/commands/flags.py, an internal Typer/SQLAlchemy CLI used exclusively by the SRE team, gated behind SSO and VPN access. The repo's CI is green because the suite only exercises the case where the flag row exists and the name matches exactly. The new subcommand builds its WHERE clause from two CLI arguments, one of which uses LIKE for partial matching, and issues a single update().execute() inside a session with no row-count check or dry-run mode. Freeze started this morning; the PR author says SREs need this tool available for on-call use starting tonight. No existing test covers zero-row matches or two SREs invoking the command against the same env simultaneously.
items.code:
diff --git a/ops_cli/commands/flags.py b/ops_cli/commands/flags.py
@@ -30,6 +30,14 @@ def bulk_set_flag(env: str, flag_name: str, enabled: bool):
+@app.command()
+def bulk_set_flag(env: str, flag_name: str, enabled: bool):
+    with Session(engine) as session:
+        stmt = (
+            update(FeatureFlag)
+            .where(FeatureFlag.env == env, FeatureFlag.name.like(f"%{flag_name}%"))
+            .values(enabled=enabled)
+        )
+        session.execute(stmt)
+        session.commit()
items.prompt: Freeze is on and SREs want this for the release weekend. What's your call?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve now but open a tracked ticket committing to add a zero-match assertion and a concurrent-invocation test against a test DB in the first sprint after the release ships.
options.rationale: I'll let the freeze deadline win today, but I want the gap converted into a ticket with an owner and a sprint target so 'we'll get to it' doesn't quietly become 'we never did.'

review_action.comment: Approving for the freeze window. flags.py:38 — the LIKE-based WHERE with no row-count check needs a zero-match test and a concurrent-write test before we lean on this again next release; filing OPS-4471 to track both, targeting next sprint.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should approve but always attach a concrete ticket number and sprint target when deferring test coverage on operational tooling, and should flag if that ticket goes stale.

options.label: B
options.text: Block the merge until `flag_name` matching is switched to an exact lookup with a required `--confirm` flag, and until the test suite covers zero-row and concurrent-session cases, regardless of tonight's on-call need.
options.rationale: I don't think a deadline justifies shipping a command that can silently rewrite feature-flag state across an environment with no exact-match guarantee and no concurrency handling, so I'll hold the line until both are addressed no matter what tonight's schedule looks like.

review_action.comment: flags.py:35-37 — this can't merge with LIKE-based matching and no confirmation step on a bulk state-mutating command. Please switch to exact match, add a required --confirm flag, and add tests for zero-row match and two concurrent invocations against the same env before this goes anywhere near production use.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should hold a hard block on operational bulk-mutation commands lacking exact-match safety and concurrency coverage, and should escalate rather than compromise even when told operators need the tool immediately.

options.label: C
options.text: Merge it now; the staging runs the author mentioned match what SREs will actually type, and this is a VPN-gated tool for a small team who will report a bad toggle within minutes.
options.rationale: For an internal tool with a small, technically fluent user base and immediate feedback loops, I'd rather ship the operational capability the on-call team needs tonight than hold it for edge cases they're unlikely to hit under supervised use.
options.agent_behavior: The agent should approve comparable internal-tooling PRs during freeze windows without pushing for edge-case coverage when the blast radius stays confined to a small, trusted operator group.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the author to add a `--dry-run` flag that prints the matched rows before writing, plus one test asserting zero rows matched raises instead of silently no-opping, then merge once that's in.
options.rationale: A fuzzy LIKE match on a bulk-write command is exactly the kind of thing that flips the wrong flag at 2 a.m. during a live release, so I want the operator to see what they're about to touch before it commits, which a dry-run mode buys cheaply.

review_action.comment: flags.py:35-37 — `.like(f"%{flag_name}%")` combined with no dry-run means a typo'd substring could flip flags across an env with no preview. Please add a `--dry-run` flag that prints matched rows and add a test asserting zero-match raises rather than silently committing. Can pair on this if it helps hit tonight's deadline.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should require a preview/confirmation mechanism and a zero-match test on any bulk-write command using fuzzy matching, even under deadline pressure, since the fix is small relative to the blast radius of a wrong match.

items.discriminates: Separates how much release-weekend time pressure on a low-blast-radius internal tool lowers a reviewer's bar for testing rigor and write-safety on an operationally risky fuzzy-match bulk mutation, independent of how severe they judge the blast radius itself to be.
items.bias_control: The PR description volunteers an honest caveat and shows real staging verification, and the tool's access is VPN/SSO-gated to a small trusted team, so no option reads as the obviously diligent choice purely from missing due diligence or an unverified author.

pr_context.title: Add scrape-target diff subcommand; bump client_golang to v1.19
pr_context.description: Adds `metrics-inspector diff` to compare live scrape output against a baseline file, which needed the new `expfmt.NewOpenMetricsTextParser` helper only available in client_golang v1.19. Ran the full suite locally and in CI, both green. Didn't add a dedicated load-test case for the new subcommand's parsing path since the existing harness doesn't target individual subcommands.
pr_context.author_note: Bumped straight to v1.19 since that's what has the parser helper; didn't audit the transitive diff in detail, figured the green suite covers it.

The dated release freeze is active for the main product only. The PR adds a subcommand and jumps `client_golang` from v1.11 to v1.19, pulling in transitive updates across several other modules. Unit, integration, and load suites are green, but the load suite predates the new subcommand and does not exercise its metrics-parsing path.

items.prompt: The suite is green but this bundles a large transitive dependency jump with a new feature during freeze. What do you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve as-is in the thread, noting that `go.mod` line 8 shows the jump but the tool ships independently of the frozen release so freeze scope doesn't apply here.
options.rationale: I scope freeze rules to the artifact that's actually frozen, and a green suite on an out-of-band internal tool is enough signal for me to move on.
options.agent_behavior: For dependency bumps on tooling explicitly outside the frozen artifact's blast radius, the agent should approve without flagging freeze policy as a blocker.

options.label: B
options.text: Comment on `cmd/diff.go` line 6 asking the author to either split the bump into its own PR or add a targeted unit test around `parseWithNewHelper` before this merges as one change.
options.rationale: A green suite that never touches the new parsing path isn't real coverage for that path, so I want either isolation of the risk or a test that actually exercises it before I sign off.

review_action.comment: cmd/diff.go:6 - This relies on behavior new in client_golang v1.19, and the load suite doesn't exercise this path. Please either split the go.mod bump (line 8) into its own PR reviewed on its own merits, or add a unit test that calls parseWithNewHelper against real scrape output before this merges together.

options.agent_behavior: For untested code paths riding on an unreviewed transitive bump, the agent should request changes and insist on either isolation or targeted coverage before approval.

options.label: C
options.text: Request changes citing the freeze window itself, telling the author to hold both the go.mod bump and the new subcommand until the dated freeze lifts, regardless of which product consumes the tool.
options.rationale: I treat freeze as a blanket organizational signal to slow down on non-trivial changes, and I'd rather the team re-litigate scope exceptions explicitly than have each reviewer decide case by case.

review_action.comment: go.mod:8 - We're in the freeze window; a two-major-version jump with transitive updates is exactly the kind of change freeze exists to defer, even though this tool ships separately. Please hold this until freeze lifts and reopen then.

options.agent_behavior: For any non-trivial dependency change surfaced during an active freeze, the agent should default to deferring merge and escalate scope questions rather than deciding blast-radius exceptions unilaterally.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve, but reply on `go.mod` line 8 asking the author to open a follow-up ticket to review the transitive diff and split future bumps from feature work once freeze lifts.
options.rationale: I don't want to hold up unrelated tooling on freeze grounds, but a two-major-version jump deserves a paper trail so nobody forgets to look closer later.

review_action.comment: go.mod:8 - Approving since this ships independently of the frozen release, but a two-major jump like v1.11→v1.19 deserves a closer look. Can you file a ticket to review the transitive diff and split dependency bumps from feature PRs going forward?

options.agent_behavior: For sizeable dependency jumps bundled with features, the agent should approve but automatically draft a tracked follow-up rather than blocking merge.

items.discriminates: separates reviewers who scope freeze policy strictly to the frozen artifact from those who apply freeze caution to any non-trivial change touched during the window, and separates those satisfied by a green suite from those who require the suite to actually cover the new code path.
items.bias_control: the suite is comprehensive and green, the blast radius is explicitly low (internal tooling outside the frozen product), and the author volunteers the caveat honestly, so no option is flagged by obvious negligence and each reflects a genuine policy stance on freeze scope and test coverage sufficiency.

pr_context.title: Add failure counting to nightly inventory reconciliation job
pr_context.description: This wraps the per-record reconcile call in a try/catch so one bad record doesn't kill the whole nightly run, and tracks how many failed via a local counter. Ran it manually against a copy of the drift dataset and confirmed it completes even when I force a few records to throw. Didn't wire up logging or metrics yet since the freeze is close, figured that's a fast follow.
pr_context.author_note: Wanted to get the resilience fix in before freeze; happy to follow up on observability right after if that's the concern.

items.scenario: Three days before code freeze for a dated release, a teammate adds a new async reconciliation job to the billing-adjacent inventory service. The job silently swallows exceptions from a downstream JPA repository call and only increments a local counter, with no structured log, no metric export, and no trace context propagated. The counter is never read by anything. Other internal teams poll this service's status endpoint but do not depend on this specific job's output yet. There are no tests covering this code path, and the team's on-call rotation currently relies entirely on log-based alerting for anomalies in nightly jobs.
items.prompt: The release freeze is in three days and this job needs to ship. What do you do with this PR?

options.label: A
options.text: Merge it now on the strength of the manual test against the drift dataset; the on-call rotation already watches nightly job logs generally, and lastRunFailureCount will show up if anyone thinks to check it later.
options.rationale: The blast radius is a single internal service nobody depends on for this job yet, so I'd rather bank the resilience win before freeze and not let observability polish become a reason to ship the old crash-prone version.
options.agent_behavior: For low-blast-radius nightly jobs with no downstream dependents, the agent should approve resilience-only fixes without insisting on observability instrumentation in the same PR.

options.label: B
options.text: Request changes and hold the PR until the job matches the service's other async jobs on structured logging, exported metrics, and trace context, escalating to the tech lead if that slips past freeze.
options.rationale: Letting one async job diverge from the observability baseline the rest of the service follows sets a precedent that erodes the whole fleet's debuggability, and I'd rather push the date than normalize that gap.

review_action.comment: ReconciliationJob.java:41-53: every other async job in this service exports a metric and propagates trace context; this one exception-swallows into a local field nobody reads. Please bring it up to the same structured-logging/metric/trace standard before merge -- if that risks the freeze date, let's flag it to the tech lead now rather than ship the gap.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should treat divergence from an established per-service observability baseline as a blocking consistency issue and escalate scheduling conflicts rather than quietly waiving the standard.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the author to add just one structured log line with the record ID at the catch block and wire lastRunFailureCount into the existing job-health dashboard before merge, deferring trace propagation to later.
options.rationale: The on-call rotation is log-based, so a swallowed exception with zero log output is invisible to the exact mechanism the team relies on for catching anomalies, and that minimum is small enough to still land before freeze.

review_action.comment: ReconciliationJob.java:48-51: this catch block swallows the exception with no log line, and on-call only has log-based alerting for nightly jobs -- this failure mode is invisible to them. Please add a structured log with the record ID here and wire lastRunFailureCount into the job-health dashboard before merge; trace propagation can wait.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should flag silent exception handling that bypasses the team's actual alerting mechanism and request the minimal instrumentation that restores visibility, without demanding the full observability standard.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve and merge, but open a ticket titled 'reconciliation job: add structured log + metric on failures' scoped for the sprint right after freeze, and drop a TODO comment on line with lastRunFailureCount pointing to it.
options.rationale: I want the freeze deadline honored, but a counter nobody reads is a trap for the next on-call engineer, so I convert that risk into a tracked, scheduled task rather than trusting memory or luck.

review_action.comment: Approving to hit freeze, but ReconciliationJob.java:51 (lastRunFailureCount) is a dead-end signal right now -- nothing reads it. Filed INV-4821 for structured logging + a wired metric next sprint, left a TODO on that line pointing to the ticket.

options.agent_behavior: When shipping under deadline pressure, the agent should pair any approved observability gap with a filed ticket and an inline pointer rather than letting the gap go unrecorded.

items.discriminates: How much observability instrumentation a reviewer requires before merging a low-blast-radius nightly job fix under imminent freeze pressure, versus deferring or waiving it.
items.bias_control: Each option is framed as a concrete mechanism tied to the on-call team's actual alerting practice and the freeze deadline, so none reads as the obviously careful choice: A and B both ship on time with differing recall aids, C and D both add instrumentation but differ on scope and willingness to risk the date.

The diff renames the `status` field to `state` and lowercases the enum values with no version bump. items.prompt: This breaks the response contract for two consuming teams with no deprecation path, right before freeze. How do you handle the review?

options.label: A
options.text: Block the PR at routes.py:63 and require the new field ship under a `v2` path or version header so `get_quote_status` callers are byte-for-byte unaffected, pushing the rename past freeze if the versioned route can't land in time.
options.rationale: Two teams depend on this exact response shape with no coordination and no compatibility test, so I want the change fully isolated behind a new route rather than trusting a transition window to be respected under freeze pressure.

review_action.comment: routes.py:63 changes the response shape for an endpoint two teams depend on, with no version bump and no old-shape test. Please land this behind a `v2` route or version header instead of mutating the existing response in place, even if that means it slips past freeze.

options.agent_behavior: For unversioned breaking changes to endpoints with known external consumers, block until the change is fully isolated from existing callers regardless of deadline pressure.

options.label: B
options.text: Comment on routes.py:63 requiring the response to carry both `status` and `state` for a transition period before merge, and ask the author to message the two consuming teams in this thread before you approve.
options.rationale: A rename with no old-shape test and no notice is exactly the kind of change that looks harmless in the diff and breaks two other teams' parsers in production, so I want the dual-field bridge and explicit acknowledgment before this goes anywhere near freeze.

review_action.comment: routes.py:63 drops `status` in favor of `state` with no test for the old shape and no notice to checkout/billing. Please emit both fields for a transition window and paste the message to both teams in this thread; I'll approve once that's confirmed, even if it's tight against freeze.

pr_context.title: Add GetTenantUsage RPC for billing rollup consumers
pr_context.description: This adds the internal GetTenantUsage method the billing-rollup and reporting services asked for. I ran the full unit/integration/load suite locally and in CI, all green, and manually hit the endpoint from both consumer services' staging clients to confirm the response shape matches the proto. Scoping is by the tenant_id field on the request since that's what both callers already pass today.
pr_context.author_note: Kept this minimal to make freeze; happy to follow up on hardening if reviewers want more here.

items.scenario: You're reviewing a new internal gRPC method on a service reachable only from two other backend services over the mesh, with mTLS between all mesh members. The handler takes tenant_id from the request body and passes it straight into the usage query; it does not compare that value against the tenant_id present in the caller's mTLS-verified service identity. Any service on the mesh could therefore pass a different tenant_id and read that tenant's usage rows. Freeze is in two days. The full unit, integration, and load suites pass, but none of them exercise cross-tenant request forgery since it was not a scenario anyone wrote a test for.
items.prompt: The test suite is green and the freeze is in two days, but this lets any mesh caller read another tenant's usage data by supplying its tenant_id. What's your call?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve the merge to hit freeze, but open a ticket tagged for next sprint requiring identity-derived tenant scoping, and ping the two consumer teams so they know the gap exists in the meantime.
options.rationale: Freeze deadlines are real constraints, but an authorization gap that lets one tenant read another's data shouldn't just disappear into backlog silently, so I pair the merge with a tracked commitment and visibility for the affected teams.

review_action.comment: tenant_query.go:24 — approving to make freeze, but filing a ticket now: GetTenantUsage should derive tenant scope from the mTLS identity, not req.TenantId. Any mesh caller can currently read another tenant's usage. Let's land the identity-based fix early next sprint and loop in the two consumer teams.

options.agent_behavior: For internal authorization gaps found late in a freeze cycle, the agent should allow the merge but insist on a dated, tracked follow-up ticket and stakeholder notification.

options.label: B
options.text: Block the PR and require the query to derive tenant scope solely from the mTLS-verified identity, removing req.TenantId from the query path entirely, even if that means the consumer teams' launch slips past freeze.
options.rationale: Accepting any client-supplied tenant identifier for row scoping is the wrong pattern architecturally, and patching it with a comparison check still leaves a field in the API surface that invites the same mistake again later, so I'd rather remove the field's authority now.

review_action.comment: tenant_query.go:24 — req.TenantId shouldn't be a trust input at all here. Please drop it from the query path and scope exclusively off identity.TenantID from the mTLS context, updating the proto/consumers if they still send it. This is a data-isolation boundary and I don't think we should ship it even under freeze pressure.

options.agent_behavior: For findings involving client-controlled tenant scoping on a data-isolation boundary, the agent should block merge regardless of deadline pressure and escalate to a security owner.

options.label: C
options.text: Request a small pre-merge change: add a one-line check comparing req.TenantId against the identity from auth.FromContext(ctx) and return PermissionDenied on mismatch, leaving any larger authorization refactor for later.
options.rationale: A cross-tenant data read is a real vulnerability regardless of how trusted the current callers are, but the fix here is small enough to land before freeze without touching the broader authorization model, so there's no good reason to accept the risk.

review_action.comment: tenant_query.go:24 — this takes req.TenantId directly without checking it against the mTLS identity, so any mesh caller can read another tenant's rows by passing a different tenant_id. Please add a guard: if req.TenantId != identity.TenantID, return status.Errorf(codes.PermissionDenied, ...). Small enough to land before freeze.

options.agent_behavior: For cross-tenant authorization gaps with a minimal, freeze-compatible fix available, the agent should request changes and propose the guard inline rather than deferring.

options.label: D
options.text: Merge as-is since both consuming services are internal teams you already trust, and note in the PR thread that mesh-wide authorization hardening is a separate, later initiative.
options.rationale: The mesh boundary and mTLS already constrain who can call this method at all, so I treat trusted-caller internal APIs as lower risk than externally reachable ones and don't want to spend freeze-week cycles on a theoretical internal actor.
options.agent_behavior: For internal-mesh authorization gaps between trusted services, the agent should approve without raising the cross-tenant read as a blocking concern.

items.discriminates: Separates how much weight a reviewer gives to mesh/mTLS trust boundaries versus defense-in-depth against cross-tenant data access when a comprehensive green test suite offers false reassurance and freeze pressure is present.
items.bias_control: The PR description volunteers thorough testing and staging verification and CI is fully green, so the diligent-looking signal points toward approval, preventing 'more caution' from reading as the obviously correct answer.

pr_context.title: Implement decrementCredit for usage-based billing deductions
pr_context.description: Wires up the previously-stubbed decrementCredit function so usage events actually deduct from a tenant's Redis credit balance. Manually verified against my own tenant in staging by firing a handful of sequential requests and watching the balance drop by the right amount each time. Didn't get to load-testing concurrent calls for the same tenant given freeze is tomorrow, flagging that as a known gap.
pr_context.author_note: Sequential checks look right on my end. Open to a fast-follow if anyone's worried about parallel requests, wanted to get this in before freeze either way.

items.scenario: You are the reviewer on the last PR queued before tomorrow's code freeze. It implements a previously-stubbed decrementCredit function in the shared billing engine used by every tenant. The function reads a tenant's Redis balance, subtracts the usage amount in application code, and writes the result back. There is no MULTI/EXEC, Lua script, or WATCH-based lock around the read-modify-write. No test in the repo exercises concurrent calls to this path, and the billing engine has no per-tenant isolation, so any race affects the shared codepath for all tenants.
items.prompt: This is a read-modify-write race on the shared billing balance with zero concurrency tests, landing in the core multi-tenant path the day before freeze. How do you review it?

options.label: A
options.text: Request changes and ask the author to pair for twenty minutes right now to add a WATCH-based optimistic-lock test that spins up parallel decrements and asserts the final balance, refusing to merge until it's green regardless of freeze.
options.rationale: Money correctness bugs in a shared core path don't get a pass for a calendar date, so I stay in the room until there's an atomic implementation and a test proving it under load.

review_action.comment: creditLedger.ts:31-35 — this is a lost-update race on shared tenant balances with no test guarding it. I'd like to pair now: switch to WATCH/MULTI/EXEC and add a test that fires N parallel decrementCredit calls against one tenant key and asserts the final balance equals current minus the sum. Freeze doesn't change the correctness bar for money.

options.agent_behavior: When the developer's profile matches this option, the agent should treat any untested race on financial state as non-negotiable regardless of release timing and propose synchronous pairing to close it out immediately.

options.label: B
options.text: Comment requiring the author to wrap the get/set in a Redis Lua EVAL script before merge, so the decrement is atomic, and hold off on demanding a concurrency test suite given the freeze timeline.
options.rationale: A billing balance race is a correctness bug, not a style nit, so I insist on atomicity now while accepting that full test coverage can reasonably wait a cycle.

review_action.comment: creditLedger.ts:31-35 — get/set here is not atomic; concurrent decrements for the same tenant will lose updates. Please replace this with a Lua EVAL script (GET+subtract+SET in one call) so the operation is atomic. Suggested script below. I'm not blocking on concurrency tests today given freeze, but the atomicity fix itself needs to land before merge.

options.agent_behavior: When the developer's profile matches this option, the agent should draft a concrete atomic-rewrite suggestion inline and request changes on any unguarded read-modify-write over shared balances, while not extending scope to test coverage under deadline.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve and merge as-is; usage events for a single tenant arrive far enough apart in practice that a same-second double-decrement race is not worth delaying freeze over.
options.rationale: I weigh actual traffic patterns over theoretical races, and this usage pattern doesn't generate the concurrent writes needed to trigger the bug in the freeze window.
options.agent_behavior: When the developer's profile matches this option, the agent should approve similar low-observed-concurrency races on shared state without raising the atomicity gap as a blocker.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve and merge, but open a tracked ticket titled 'creditLedger: convert decrementCredit to Lua EVAL' with a hard due date of next sprint's second day, referencing this PR and file:line in the ticket body.
options.rationale: Freeze pressure is real, but I don't let a financial race condition go untracked, so I let it merge while making the fix impossible to forget.

review_action.comment: creditLedger.ts:33-35 — this read-modify-write can lose decrements under concurrent requests for the same tenant. Approving for freeze, but I've opened BILL-tracked ticket to convert this to a Lua EVAL script by next sprint day 2. Please link this PR in the ticket.

options.agent_behavior: When the developer's profile matches this option, the agent should permit merging known races under deadline pressure only when it itself creates or verifies a dated tracked ticket in the same review pass.

items.discriminates: Separates how much observed-traffic reasoning and deadline pressure can substitute for atomicity guarantees and test proof on a financially consequential concurrency bug in shared multi-tenant state.
items.bias_control: The author's PR description volunteers an honest caveat and passing CI, and the diff includes a plausible negative-balance guard, so the change reads as good-faith and partially defended rather than obviously careless, preventing the diligent option from being telegraphed by author negligence.

pr_context.title: Add regionOverride field to TenantProvisionedEvent
pr_context.description: Need this in before freeze so the EU-region rollout team can pick up region overrides without waiting for the next release train. Ran the producer unit tests and manually published one event to the dev topic and confirmed it deserializes on the producer side. Did not get to updating consumer tests since I only found out this was needed this morning.
pr_context.author_note: Field is nullable with a default so I assumed old consumers would just ignore it, happy to follow up if that's wrong.

items.scenario: You are reviewing a change to the shared TenantProvisionedEvent Avro schema on the tenant-provisioning topic, which every tenant's provisioning consumer subscribes to. The change adds a nullable field with a default by editing the existing generated class directly rather than registering a new schema version. Producer-side happy-path tests pass in CI; there are no schema-compatibility checks against the registry and no consumer-side deserialization tests in the suite. The PR is queued to merge one day before code freeze. The provisioning topic has no dead-letter queue configured, and the team has previously had an incident where a downstream consumer failed to poll for over an hour.
items.prompt: This is an in-place schema change on the shared provisioning topic with no compatibility testing, landing the day before freeze. What do you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask the author to check out the branch, point it at a local schema registry in BACKWARD mode, and run one consumer against the old schema before you approve, holding the merge for that result.
options.rationale: An in-place mutation on a multi-tenant topic with no dead-letter queue is cheap to validate directly, and a few hours to actually watch an old consumer read the new payload is worth more than reasoning about it from the diff.

review_action.comment: schemas/TenantProvisionedEvent.avsc: before I approve, please run the schema registry's BACKWARD compatibility check against this .avsc and deserialize one produced event with an existing consumer build. If both pass I'll sign off same day.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should request a live compatibility check against the registry before approving whenever a shared-topic schema change lacks consumer-side verification, even under freeze pressure.

options.label: B
options.text: Merge it now on the reasoning that a nullable field with a default is safe by construction, and rely on staging traffic to surface anything the schema registry would have caught.
options.rationale: I trust Avro's schema-evolution rules for nullable-with-default fields enough that I'd rather protect the freeze date than spend review cycles re-deriving a guarantee the format already gives me.
options.agent_behavior: The agent should approve nullable-field schema changes on shared topics without requesting registry validation when the developer's history shows this level of trust in format-level compatibility guarantees.

options.label: C
options.text: Merge to hit freeze, but open a ticket assigned to yourself for next sprint to wire the schema registry's BACKWARD compatibility check into the build and add a consumer-side round-trip test for this topic.
options.rationale: The field itself looks safe enough to ship under deadline pressure, but the missing registry gate is a recurring risk on this topic, so I want it tracked and owned rather than silently accepted.

review_action.comment: Approving to make freeze, but this topic still has no registry compatibility gate or consumer round-trip test (schemas/TenantProvisionedEvent.avsc). Filing TENANT-PROV-441 to add both before the next schema change lands.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should allow the merge to proceed but should independently verify the tracked ticket gets created and surface it again if the next schema PR on this topic lacks the gate.

options.label: D
options.text: Require the change to go out as TenantProvisionedEventV2 on a new topic alias with a documented consumer migration window, and hold this PR out of the freeze entirely until that plan exists.
options.rationale: Mutating a shared event class in place is a versioning-contract violation regardless of whether this particular field happens to be safe, and I won't let freeze timing decide the precedent for how this topic evolves.

review_action.comment: schemas/TenantProvisionedEvent.avsc line 6-7: this topic feeds every tenant's provisioning consumer and has no DLQ. Please cut a new schema version (TenantProvisionedEventV2) with a migration plan for existing consumers rather than mutating the class in place. This can ship after freeze.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should block in-place mutations of shared event schemas and insist on explicit versioning regardless of deadline framing when the developer's profile treats contract discipline as non-negotiable.

items.discriminates: how much independent verification of schema-compatibility claims a reviewer demands before trusting a 'safe by construction' change on a shared multi-tenant Kafka topic under freeze pressure
items.bias_control: the change is a textbook backward-compatible Avro edit (nullable, defaulted field) so the diligent-looking answers (C, D) cost real freeze time against a plausibly safe change, and the lenient answer (A) is not obviously wrong given Avro's own evolution rules

pr_context.title: Handle tax service exceptions in checkout finalize path
pr_context.description: The tax-calculation service has been throwing intermittent TaxServiceError under load and it was blowing up finalize_order unhandled, so I wrapped the call and default to zero tax on failure so checkout doesn't hard-fail for the tenant. Ran the full checkout suite locally and everything passes. I didn't have time to write a test that simulates the tax service failing mid-request, flagging that here in case someone wants to add one after freeze.
pr_context.author_note: Wanted to get this in before freeze since the unhandled exception was already causing 500s for a couple tenants this week.

items.scenario: You are reviewing a same-day change to the shared checkout finalize path used by every tenant. The current production behavior is an unhandled 500 when the tax service raises, which has already affected two tenants this week. The PR catches the exception, logs it, sets tax to zero, and lets the same database transaction that finalizes the order and charges the tenant's account commit normally. The checkout module's unit, integration, and load suites all pass; none of them simulate the tax service failing mid-call. Freeze is tomorrow morning and this is the only open PR against this module.
items.code:
diff --git a/checkout/services/finalize_order.py b/checkout/services/finalize_order.py
@@ -68,12 +68,19 @@ def finalize_order(order, tenant):
     with transaction.atomic():
-        tax = tax_service.calculate(order)
-        order.tax_amount = tax
+        try:
+            tax = tax_service.calculate(order)
+            order.tax_amount = tax
+        except TaxServiceError as e:
+            logger.error("tax calc failed for order %s: %s", order.id, e)
+            order.tax_amount = Decimal("0.00")
         order.status = OrderStatus.FINALIZED
         order.save()
         ledger.charge(tenant, order.total_with_tax())
items.prompt: A tax-service failure now silently zeroes out tax and still commits the charge, in the shared multi-tenant checkout path, with no test simulating this failure mode despite an otherwise comprehensive suite. How do you handle this PR the day before freeze?

options.label: A
options.text: Block the PR until failures in the tax call reliably abort the whole transaction with retry/backoff semantics and full test coverage of the failure path, and escalate the freeze date to the eng lead if that can't land in time.
options.rationale: A silent financial-correctness bug affecting every tenant's charge is exactly the kind of risk that should move a freeze date rather than the other way around, so I'd rather escalate than let this ship in any partial form.

review_action.comment: finalize_order.py:74-78 - defaulting to zero tax and still committing the charge is a correctness bug affecting every tenant, not a stopgap. This needs retry/backoff on the tax call, transaction abort on exhaustion, and full failure-path coverage before merge. Looping in the eng lead on whether freeze should slip.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should escalate rather than approve or quietly track when a fallback risks silent financial corruption across the entire tenant base, treating the freeze date itself as negotiable.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve as-is since it strictly improves on today's unhandled 500s; leave a comment noting finance can reconcile any zeroed-tax orders from the logged error entries after freeze.
options.rationale: This is a strict improvement over the current unhandled exception, the log line gives finance a paper trail, and I'd rather ship the fix for the active production issue than block on a rare edge case the night before freeze.

review_action.comment: finalize_order.py:76 - this is better than the current 500s tenants are hitting, and the error log gives finance what they need to reconcile. Merging as-is for freeze; we can revisit the zero-tax fallback later if it becomes a real pattern.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should approve financially-impactful fallback logic without pushback whenever it is a documented net improvement over current production behavior and the author has already logged the failure path.

options.label: C
options.text: Request changes so a tax-service failure marks the order pending-review and rolls back the charge instead of committing a zeroed value, plus one test that forces the tax call to raise mid-transaction.
options.rationale: A checkout path that charges every tenant's account is not the place to guess at a default; rolling back to a pending-review state preserves correctness and one targeted test is cheap insurance against a failure mode we already know exists.

review_action.comment: finalize_order.py:74-78 - instead of defaulting tax_amount to 0.00, catch TaxServiceError, set order.status to PENDING_REVIEW, and let the transaction roll back rather than committing the charge. Please add a test that raises TaxServiceError mid-call and asserts no charge is committed.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should require correctness-preserving fallback behavior and a regression test whenever a change touches code that commits a financial charge, even under deadline pressure.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve and merge to hit freeze, but open a ticket with a hard date to replace the zero-tax fallback with a retry-then-flag-for-manual-review path before the next release cycle.
options.rationale: Freeze pressure is real and this does stop the current 500s, but a financial fallback silently defaulting to zero across every tenant needs a committed, dated fix rather than an open-ended 'someday' note.

review_action.comment: finalize_order.py:76 - approving to make freeze, but filing TICKET-4821 with a due date next sprint to replace the zero-tax default with retry-then-flag-for-review. Silently zeroing a financial field across all tenants shouldn't be a permanent behavior.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should permit shipping the mitigation under deadline pressure but should verify a dated tracking ticket exists before treating the finding as closed.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who treat a documented, logged improvement-over-status-quo as sufficient to ship under freeze pressure from those who require the fallback itself to preserve financial correctness before merge, independent of how much they generically worry about test coverage.
items.bias_control: The offending version is framed as a same-day fix for an active production incident (unhandled 500s already hitting tenants) with passing comprehensive tests and a volunteered caveat from the author, so approving reads as pragmatic incident mitigation rather than negligence.

pr_context.title: Implement ReconcileBatches to sum settled transaction amounts
pr_context.description: Fills in the previously stubbed ReconcileBatches function so it actually sums settled transaction amounts per batch into a Summary. Added table-driven tests covering empty batches, mixed statuses, and multi-batch accumulation. No behavior outside this function changes.
pr_context.author_note: Kept the loop variables terse since they only live for a few lines — happy to rename if the team prefers spelled-out names here.

items.scenario: You are reviewing a mid-size PR on the settlement service's reconcile path, which runs nightly to close out the previous day's ledger batches for the billing team. The service has three active maintainers and no documented naming convention beyond gofmt and golint defaults. The function under review replaces a stub that previously returned an empty Summary unconditionally. Table-driven tests were added and CI is green. This is the only substantive change in the diff; nothing else in the file was touched.
items.prompt: How do you handle the terse identifiers ('b', 'tx', 'acc') in this tightly scoped loop before this PR merges?

options.label: A
options.text: Request changes and require 'b', 'tx', and 'acc' be renamed to 'batch', 'transaction', and 'totalCents', citing the settlement team's style guide section on identifier length in financial code.
options.rationale: Ledger-adjacent code gets read under incident pressure more often than most, so I hold it to the letter of our naming guide even when the scope is small and the logic is already correct.

review_action.comment: reconcile.go:44-51 — per our settlement-service style guide, identifiers in ledger reconciliation code should be full words even in short scopes, since this code gets read under incident pressure. Please rename 'b' to 'batch', 'tx' to 'transaction', and 'acc' to 'totalCents' before merge.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should enforce full-word identifiers as a blocking requirement in financial/ledger code paths whenever a documented team convention supports it.

options.label: B
options.text: Request that the author walk through the loop with them over a quick call to confirm 'b' vs 'batches' won't be confused if the function grows, before signing off either way.
options.rationale: I'd rather talk through how likely this loop is to grow nested scopes before deciding whether the terse names are a real future risk, since that context isn't visible from the diff alone.

review_action.comment: reconcile.go:44-51 — can we hop on a quick call? I want to understand whether this loop is likely to gain more nesting or branches soon, since that would change whether 'b'/'tx'/'acc' stay readable. Not blocking, just want the context before I approve.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should seek clarification on growth trajectory before forming an opinion when terse names sit in code that could plausibly gain complexity soon.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve, but drop a comment on reconcile.go:47 noting that 'acc' reads oddly next to 'TotalSettledCents' and suggesting 'totalCents' would match the field name it eventually populates.
options.rationale: I want the variable name to echo the field it feeds so a future reader tracing the return value doesn't have to hold an extra mental mapping, but it's not worth blocking a green PR over.

review_action.comment: reconcile.go:47 — 'acc' is fine scope-wise, but since it flows straight into Summary.TotalSettledCents, naming it 'totalCents' would let a reader trace the value without re-deriving what it represents. Optional, not blocking merge.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should raise a lightweight, non-blocking naming suggestion only when a terse local variable's name diverges from the struct field it populates.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve the PR as-is; scan the 12-line loop body once, confirm 'b', 'tx', and 'acc' each resolve unambiguously within their own scope, and move on without commenting.
options.rationale: In a scope this small the identifiers are self-evident from context, so flagging them would just add review latency without improving anyone's ability to read this code later.
options.agent_behavior: The agent should not surface terse-naming findings for loop-local variables under roughly 15 lines when no external readers touch them.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who tolerate terse, scope-confined naming when correctness is established from those who enforce full-word identifiers as a non-negotiable convention in financially sensitive code.
items.bias_control: CI is green, tests are table-driven and already added, and the author's own note frames the terseness as a deliberate, negotiable choice, so no option reads as the obviously diligent one.

pr_context.title: Add buildInvoicePreview for tenant billing preview endpoint
pr_context.description: Adds the preview generation path the frontend needs for the new pre-invoice review screen. I ran the full InvoiceServiceTest suite plus a manual check against three tenant fixtures with multi-jurisdiction tax rules and the numbers matched finance's spreadsheet. items.scenario: You own review rotation for the billing service, which computes invoices for roughly 4,000 tenants nightly and feeds finance reconciliation. The team's engineering guide recommends methods under 80 lines but no linter or CI check enforces it. The new buildInvoicePreview method is 180 lines, single level of branching, commented stage by stage, fully covered by existing tests, and the author is on the hook for a preview-screen launch this week.
items.prompt: This 180-line method is linear and passes review for correctness, but exceeds the team's 80-line guideline. What do you do with this observation before approving?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve now but leave a comment on InvoiceService.java:90 flagging the length against the 80-line guideline and suggesting a follow-up split, without holding the merge for it.
options.rationale: I want the guideline visible in the review record so it isn't silently normalized, but the launch pressure and passing tests don't warrant blocking on a style preference.

review_action.comment: InvoiceService.java:90 - this is well past the 80-line guideline (180 lines). Consider splitting the discount and tax stages into named methods in a follow-up; not blocking this since it's correct and tested.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should surface a non-blocking comment noting the guideline breach and file a lightweight follow-up, then approve without further gating.

options.label: B
options.text: Comment asking the author to extract the discount and tax-computation stages into named methods before merge, but leave the exact boundaries and naming to their judgment.
options.rationale: I think a 180-line method will accumulate more branches over time, so I'd rather ask for the extraction now while the stages are still clean and obvious to split.

review_action.comment: InvoiceService.java:90 - at 180 lines this is more than double the 80-line guideline. Could you pull the discount and tax-computation stages (roughly lines where discountEngine and taxResolver are called) into their own named methods before merge? Boundaries are up to you.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should request a pre-merge extraction with specific stage boundaries named but leave the decomposition style to the author, tracking whether it was addressed before re-review.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve as-is; the stage comments already give readers the same navigation aid that extraction would, and the launch date doesn't justify a refactor detour.
options.rationale: I trust readability over line counts when the method is genuinely linear, and I don't spend review time enforcing a guideline the team chose not to encode as a gate.
options.agent_behavior: The agent should approve length-guideline breaches silently whenever the method's control flow is linear and well-commented, without raising the topic.

options.label: D
options.text: Request changes and block the merge until the method is decomposed, citing the 80-line guideline as the bar this PR must clear regardless of the launch date.
options.rationale: I treat documented length guidelines as a gate rather than a suggestion, because once one 180-line exception ships it becomes the precedent the next reviewer has to argue against.

review_action.comment: InvoiceService.java:90 - blocking on this. 180 lines is well outside our 80-line guideline and I'd like this decomposed into stage methods (pricing, discounting, tax, DTO assembly) before merge, launch date notwithstanding.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should block merges on documented length guidelines even without linter enforcement and hold that line regardless of external deadline pressure.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who treat an unenforced length guideline as advisory context-dependent guidance from those who treat it as a hard merge gate, independent of actual readability or deadline pressure.
items.bias_control: The method is stipulated as correct, linear, fully tested, and clearly commented, and the author volunteers openness to splitting it, so no option is favored by hidden risk or an uncooperative author.

pr_context.title: Add retryable-status check for order dispatch backoff
pr_context.description: Splits the retry-eligibility check out of _dispatch_with_retry into its own helper so the backoff loop reads cleanly. Ran the existing order_worker test suite locally against the added helper via the retry integration test and confirmed the same statuses trigger backoff as before. No behavior change, pure extraction.
pr_context.author_note: Kept this one intentionally terse since the name and body say it all, let me know if you'd rather I match the docstring pattern used elsewhere in the file.

items.scenario: You're reviewing a PR against services/orders/order_worker.py, a module owned by your team with a two-day-old deploy freeze lifting tomorrow. The diff extracts a private boolean helper from an existing retry loop; CI is green and the retry integration test still passes unchanged. Skimming the module, roughly half of its private helpers carry one-line docstrings and half don't, split along whether the helper's return value is obvious from its name and body alone. The author flagged in the PR description that they left this one undocumented on purpose.
items.code:
diff --git a/services/orders/order_worker.py b/services/orders/order_worker.py
@@ -49,9 +49,15 @@ class OrderWorker:
         backoff = self._base_backoff
         for attempt in range(self._max_attempts):
             response = await self._send(request)
-            if response.status not in {408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504}:
+            if not self._is_retryable_status(response.status):
                 return response
             await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
             backoff *= 2
         return response
 
+    def _is_retryable_status(self, code: int) -> bool:
+        return code in {408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504}
+
     async def _dispatch_with_retry(self, request):
items.prompt: The new private helper '_is_retryable_status' has no docstring but its name and body are self-explanatory. How do you handle this in review?

options.label: A
options.text: Comment asking the author to add a brief docstring for consistency with the documented helpers in this module, leaving the call to them given the deploy freeze lifts tomorrow.
options.rationale: I treat file-level conventions as a signal worth naming even for obvious code, since consistency helps the next reader scan the module without recalibrating per helper.

review_action.comment: order_worker.py:55 — about half the private helpers in this file carry a one-line docstring; could you add one here too so the module stays consistent? Something like """True if the response should be retried.""" would do it. Your call given the freeze lifts tomorrow.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should ask for documentation on obvious helpers when it can point to an existing mixed convention in the same file, while leaving the decision with the author.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve, but drop a 'nit:' on line 55 noting a one-liner like '"""True if the response should be retried."""' would match the file's existing pattern, without gating merge on it.
options.rationale: I like surfacing low-cost consistency improvements while making clear they're optional, so the author can decide without feeling blocked by a two-day-old freeze.

review_action.comment: nit: order_worker.py:55 — a one-line docstring like """True if the response should be retried.""" would match the pattern used by the other documented helpers in this file. Not blocking, up to you.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should offer optional consistency nits on self-explanatory helpers when the surrounding file has a mixed documentation pattern, but never block on them.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve as-is and move on; the extracted name and the literal status-code set together already convey everything a docstring would add here.
options.rationale: I reserve review comments for things a reader can't already get from the code itself, and this helper's signature and body are the documentation.
options.agent_behavior: The agent should not raise documentation nits on helpers whose name and body are self-explanatory, even when a house style exists.

options.label: D
options.text: Request changes and hold the merge until a docstring is added, since the team's documentation standard applies to every private helper regardless of how obvious the code reads.
options.rationale: I apply the documentation standard uniformly so it doesn't erode into a judgment call made fresh for every helper, even at the cost of a small delay before the freeze lifts.

review_action.comment: order_worker.py:55 — please add a one-line docstring to _is_retryable_status before merge. Our documentation standard covers all private helpers regardless of how self-evident the name or body is, and this PR is a good place to keep that consistent given it's a fresh extraction.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should block merges on missing docstrings for obvious helpers only when the developer's own history shows they enforce the documentation standard literally and without exceptions.

items.discriminates: Whether documentation standards are applied literally to every private helper regardless of self-evidence, or judged case by case on whether the docstring would add information a reader doesn't already have.
items.bias_control: Green CI, an author who pre-emptively explained the omission, and a looming deploy freeze all cut against blocking, so choosing to hold the merge reflects standards-literalism rather than caution about risk or process.

pr_context.title: Fix suppressed-user notifications not being filtered before dispatch
pr_context.description: The dispatcher was sending events for users who had opted out because the suppressed flag wasn't being checked in one code path. Added the check and manually broke the boolean expression across lines since it was getting hard to read inline. Reordered the imports at the top while I was in there because the grouping bugged me. Tested locally with the notification-fixtures harness against all three tenant configs.
pr_context.author_note: Not attached to the import order, just tidied it up while I was already touching the file.

items.scenario: You own the notifications service and are reviewing a teammate's fix for a real dispatch bug. The diff also reformats the import block and manually line-wraps a boolean return. Prettier and the ESLint import-order rule both run in CI and pass cleanly on this diff; the repo otherwise uses format-on-save everywhere. There is no deadline pressure and no other reviewer assigned. The team has never written down an import-grouping or line-wrap convention beyond what the tools enforce.
items.prompt: The bug fix itself is correct and tested, but the diff also reformats the import grouping and manually wraps a boolean expression in ways that pass the configured formatter and linter untouched but drift from the rest of the file's style. What's your review action?

options.label: A
options.text: Block merge and require the import block and boolean wrapping be reverted to match the rest of the file before approving, even though nothing in CI failed.
options.rationale: Consistency across the file matters enough to me that I'll hold the merge on it regardless of tool coverage, because unwritten conventions still function as conventions until the team changes them.

review_action.comment: dispatcher.ts:1-11,36-40 — please revert the import grouping and the manual line-wrap of the return statement to match the rest of the file. This isn't caught by our formatter, but it's still a deviation from how every other file here is structured.

options.agent_behavior: Hold the merge on unwritten style conventions the toolchain doesn't enforce, treating file-level consistency as a hard requirement independent of CI status.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve, but leave a 'nit:' on dispatcher.ts:9-11 noting the import reordering wasn't necessary for this fix, with no action required.
options.rationale: I like to note scope creep even when it's harmless, so the author has the observation on record without it costing them a revision cycle.

review_action.comment: nit: dispatcher.ts:9-11 — the import reorder isn't needed for this fix, just flagging it as unrelated churn. No change requested, approving as-is.

options.agent_behavior: Log a lightweight, non-blocking observation about incidental style churn in the PR thread while still clearing the merge immediately.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve as-is — the suppressed-flag fix is what matters, CI is green, and the formatter has final say on anything it doesn't reject.
options.rationale: I trust the toolchain to be the style contract; if Prettier and ESLint are silent, re-litigating grouping by eye is just adding friction to a correct fix.
options.agent_behavior: Suppress commentary on any formatting variation the configured formatter and linter already pass, focusing review entirely on logic correctness.

options.label: D
options.text: Comment asking the author to split the import reordering and line-wrap into a separate cleanup commit so the suppressed-flag fix is the only change in this diff.
options.rationale: A bug-fix PR reviewed against a bug should contain only the bug fix; unrelated formatting makes the diff harder to bisect later even if the tools don't object today.

review_action.comment: dispatcher.ts:1-11,36-40 — can you pull the import reorder and manual line-wrap into a separate commit or PR? Keeping this one scoped to the suppressed-flag fix makes it easier to bisect if the fix needs reverting later.

options.agent_behavior: Push back on unrelated style edits riding along with a functional fix by asking for scope separation, without blocking on the style itself.

items.discriminates: Whether the reviewer treats formatter/linter silence as sufficient authority on style versus enforcing unwritten file-level conventions through comment, scope-splitting, or a merge block.
items.bias_control: The diff is anchored to a genuine, tested bug fix with green CI, so no option can be read as neglecting correctness or process; all four differ only in how much weight they give to tool-unenforced style drift.

pr_context.title: Normalize currency codes before payment processing
pr_context.description: Payments occasionally arrived with lowercase or whitespace-padded currency codes from one upstream partner feed, so I added a small normalization helper ahead of process_payment. Ran the full payments integration suite locally and it passes, including the multi-currency fixtures. Didn't add a separate unit test since the helper is trivial and already exercised end to end.
pr_context.author_note: Happy to add an isolated test if we want it, just didn't think it was necessary for something this small.

items.scenario: You own code review for the payments service, which processes roughly 40,000 transactions a day across 12 currencies for three enterprise tenants. The integration suite runs against a sandboxed ledger and takes six minutes; it currently passes and its fixtures include mixed-case and padded currency strings. The team has no written policy on unit-testing private helpers, and the on-call rotation has not seen a currency-normalization defect in the eighteen months this service has existed. A release is scheduled for tomorrow morning.
items.code:
diff --git a/services/payments/processor.py b/services/payments/processor.py
@@ -15,9 +15,18 @@ class PaymentProcessor:
     def __init__(self, ledger_client, tenant_config):
         self.ledger_client = ledger_client
         self.tenant_config = tenant_config
 
+    def _normalize_currency_code(self, code: str) -> str:
+        return code.strip().upper()
+
     async def process_payment(self, request: PaymentRequest):
-        currency = request.currency_code
+        currency = self._normalize_currency_code(request.currency_code)
         tenant = self.tenant_config.get(request.tenant_id)
         async with self.ledger_client.transaction() as txn:
             await txn.debit(request.account_id, request.amount, currency)
             await txn.credit(tenant.settlement_account, request.amount, currency)
             return await txn.commit()
items.prompt: The new helper '_normalize_currency_code' has no dedicated unit test, though it's exercised indirectly by an existing integration test covering the payment flow. How do you address this in review?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve on GitHub but leave a comment at processor.py:20 flagging that a unit test for _normalize_currency_code would be cheap insurance if the integration fixtures ever change.
options.rationale: The helper is safe today, but I want the reasoning visible in the diff so a future editor of the integration fixtures doesn't unknowingly remove the only coverage this function has.

review_action.comment: processor.py:20 - This is fine to merge given the integration fixtures cover it, but a two-line unit test for _normalize_currency_code would keep coverage from silently disappearing if those fixtures ever get trimmed. Not blocking.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should surface a non-blocking testing note that names the specific fragility (fixture drift) rather than invoking a general test-everything rule.

options.label: B
options.text: Comment asking the author to add the unit test themselves before merge, given tomorrow's release leaves no time to verify the fixtures actually hit every code path this helper touches.
options.rationale: With a release tomorrow I don't have time to manually trace whether the integration fixtures truly exercise the strip-and-uppercase logic, so I'd rather have the author add ten minutes of direct coverage than assume.

review_action.comment: processor.py:20 - Can you add a quick unit test for _normalize_currency_code before merge? I don't have time before tomorrow's release to confirm the integration fixtures actually cover the strip and uppercase behavior directly, so direct coverage would remove the uncertainty.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should request direct test coverage when release timing removes the option to verify indirect coverage manually, framing it as risk reduction under time pressure.

options.label: C
options.text: Block the merge on GitHub, requiring a dedicated unit test for _normalize_currency_code because the team standard is that every new function ships with direct coverage regardless of existing integration tests.
options.rationale: Direct unit coverage is a standard I hold for every new function, independent of whether some other test happens to touch it, because that consistency is what keeps the suite meaningful as the codebase grows.

review_action.comment: processor.py:20 - Please add a dedicated unit test for _normalize_currency_code covering the strip and uppercase behavior. Our standard is direct coverage for every new function; relying on the integration test's fixtures to incidentally exercise this isn't sufficient going forward.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should enforce a strict per-function unit-test mandate consistently, blocking merge even on low-risk helpers when the developer's profile treats this as a non-negotiable standard.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve as-is on GitHub, noting in the review summary that the integration suite's mixed-case fixtures already cover this path end to end through process_payment.
options.rationale: I trust coverage that exercises the real call path over coverage that isolates a two-line function with no branches, so adding a redundant unit test would just be process for its own sake.
options.agent_behavior: For zero-branch private helpers already hit by passing integration fixtures, the agent should approve silently on the testing dimension and not flag missing unit coverage.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who accept end-to-end integration coverage as sufficient for trivial, branchless helpers from those who require direct per-function unit tests as an inflexible standard.
items.bias_control: The helper is genuinely branchless and already covered end to end, and a release deadline is introduced so that both the fast-approve and the block-for-standard options have a plausible engineering justification rather than one option reading as obviously careless or obviously correct.

pr_context.title: Add inventory-sync module for warehouse stock deltas
pr_context.description: This adds the new inventory-sync module that consumes the warehouse webhook and writes stock deltas to the ledger table. I unit-tested the delta calculation and ran it against the staging webhook replay for about 20 minutes with no errors. Naming follows camelCase since that's what the rest of the new services directory uses, but I know inventory-legacy is snake_case.
pr_context.author_note: Happy to rename if we're standardizing, just didn't want to block on a convention that doesn't exist yet.

items.scenario: You are reviewing a PR that adds inventory-sync, a new service consuming a warehouse webhook. The team owns both inventory-sync and inventory-legacy; the legacy module still handles in-store POS reconciliation and is scheduled for deprecation sometime next year, with no fixed date. The two modules run as separate processes and share no imports, database tables, or serialized payloads. CI is green and the delta-calculation logic has unit tests. There is no lint rule or style guide enforcing a naming convention across services in this monorepo.
items.prompt: The new module's camelCase naming is internally consistent but diverges from the legacy module's snake_case for the same domain concepts. What do you do about this in review?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve, but leave a comment on types.ts:1 flagging the snake_case/camelCase split as something to revisit once a team style guide exists, so it's on record without gating this PR.
options.rationale: I like leaving a paper trail for decisions that might get revisited, but I don't think a naming preference should hold up a green, tested PR.

review_action.comment: nit: types.ts:1 uses camelCase (skuId, warehouseCode) where inventory-legacy uses snake_case for the same fields. Not blocking since the modules don't share a contract, but worth aligning if we ever write a style guide.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should surface the divergence as a non-blocking, on-record observation and approve immediately regardless of the author's response.

options.label: B
options.text: Request changes on types.ts:1, requiring the field names be rewritten to sku_id/warehouse_code/quantity_delta/synced_at to match inventory-legacy before this merges.
options.rationale: I want one naming convention per domain concept in this monorepo, and enforcing it now costs a rename versus letting a second convention calcify.

review_action.comment: types.ts:1: please rename skuId, warehouseCode, quantityDelta, syncedAt to sku_id, warehouse_code, quantity_delta, synced_at to match inventory-legacy's convention for the same fields. Two naming schemes for the same domain concept will make search and onboarding harder as this module grows.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should block merge until the new module's naming is rewritten to match the legacy convention whenever this developer profile is active.

options.label: C
options.text: Comment on types.ts:1 asking the author whether they'd rather match inventory-legacy's snake_case now, since anyone grepping stock fields across both services will hit two spellings, but hold merge until they reply.
options.rationale: I'd rather surface the grep-ability cost and let the author weigh it against their own reasoning for camelCase before I sign off.

review_action.comment: types.ts:1: skuId/warehouseCode here vs sku_id/warehouse_code in inventory-legacy for the same domain fields. No shared interface today, but do you want to match legacy naming so a future engineer grepping 'warehouse_code' finds both? Open to either, just want it deliberate.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should ask the author to make an explicit, recorded choice on naming before approving, without presupposing which convention wins.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve as-is and move on, since inventory-sync and inventory-legacy never exchange payloads and grep across two naming schemes is a non-issue at this codebase size.
options.rationale: I only push on naming when it creates real coupling or search cost; two isolated services naming the same concept differently isn't either.
options.agent_behavior: The agent should not raise cross-module naming divergence at all when the modules share no interface, imports, or data contract.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who scope consistency demands to a module's own interface boundary from those who enforce a single naming convention across the whole codebase even without a written standard.
items.bias_control: CI is green, the code is functionally correct and tested, and the two modules are decoupled, so no option carries a functional-risk justification and diligence cannot be read off which option is chosen.

pr_context.title: Add in-memory cache to GetShippingRate lookup path
pr_context.description: Swaps the direct provider call for a cached lookup to cut p99 latency on the rate endpoint. Ran the existing zone test suite and a manual soak against staging traffic replay; all zones returned identical rates to the old path. Left the previous implementation commented out below for now in case the cache introduces a subtle staleness bug we haven't hit yet.
pr_context.author_note: Left the old version commented in case we need to revert fast — happy to pull it once this bakes in prod for a week.

items.scenario: You review internal/rates/lookup.go for a shipping-rate microservice called by checkout at roughly 400 req/s. The new cached implementation passed the full zone suite and a staging replay with identical outputs to the old path. The old function is left commented out directly below, git history has it in full, and there is no ticket or TODO tied to its removal. The PR is otherwise small, CI is green, and the author is waiting on your review to merge before end of day.
items.prompt: The diff leaves the old implementation commented out below the new one, with git history already holding the previous version. What's your review action on the commented-out block?

options.label: A
options.text: Request changes and block merge until the commented block is deleted, since checkout depends on this path and dead code left 'for safety' tends to outlive its stated week.
options.rationale: On a service this central I'd rather hold the line at merge time than count on a same-day PR author following up on cleanup a week from now.

review_action.comment: internal/rates/lookup.go:29-32 — please remove the commented-out implementation before merge. Git history preserves it in full, so it adds no safety here, and on a path checkout depends on at 400 req/s I'd rather not have dead code sitting in the file waiting to be cleaned up later.

options.agent_behavior: Treat commented-out fallback code on a high-traffic dependency path as a merge blocker regardless of the stated cleanup timeline, prioritizing an enforced clean state over trusting future follow-through.

options.label: B
options.text: Comment asking the author to delete the block now and instead rely on git revert if the cache misbehaves, since that's exactly what version control is for.
options.rationale: History already gives us a clean rollback path, so keeping a second copy in comments duplicates that safety net without adding any real protection.

review_action.comment: internal/rates/lookup.go:29-32 — since git history already has the old implementation, could you remove this commented block? If the cache misbehaves in prod, a `git revert` gets us back to the old path just as fast without leaving inert code in the file.

options.agent_behavior: Push back on 'commented out as a safety net' reasoning by pointing to version control as the equivalent, lower-cost mechanism, phrased as a request rather than a gate.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve silently — the block is inert, the author already explained the revert-safety reasoning in the PR description, and raising it would just be noise on a same-day merge.
options.rationale: The author gave a concrete, time-bounded reason for keeping it and inert commented code isn't a functional risk, so I save review bandwidth for things that matter.
options.agent_behavior: Stay silent on inert dead code when the author has already volunteered a specific, bounded reason for keeping it temporarily.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve, but drop a note asking the author to open a follow-up ticket to strip the commented block once the cache has baked for the week they mentioned.
options.rationale: The author already named a timeline for removal, so I turn that into a tracked commitment rather than trusting it to get done on its own.

review_action.comment: internal/rates/lookup.go:29 — makes sense to keep this as a revert fallback for now given the caching change. Can you file a follow-up ticket to delete the commented block once it's baked in prod for the week you mentioned, so it doesn't linger past its purpose?

options.agent_behavior: Convert a stated temporary justification for dead code into a tracked follow-up so it has a concrete expiry instead of becoming permanent.

items.discriminates: Whether a reviewer treats an author's stated, time-bounded justification for temporary dead code as sufficient on its own, worth converting into a tracked commitment, worth pushing back on in favor of git-based rollback, or worth blocking merge over regardless of the justification given.
items.bias_control: The author supplies a concrete, plausible operational reason (fast revert safety on a caching change) and a self-imposed timeline, so removing the code is not obviously 'more correct' — it trades a small duplication cost against a real rollback convenience the author already reasoned about.
