pr_context.title: Add soft-warn + hard-reject evaluation path to RateLimiter
pr_context.description: Adds the evaluate() method the gateway team asked for last sprint so tenants get a warning log before they actually get rejected. Ran the existing RateLimiterTest suite plus two new cases for the warn-only and reject paths, both green. Didn't touch the config layer since the threshold value itself isn't changing in this PR.
pr_context.author_note: Kept it minimal since we're trying to get this merged before the traffic spike this weekend — happy to follow up on cleanup separately.

items.scenario: You're reviewing a same-day PR to the shared API gateway's RateLimiter class ahead of an expected weekend traffic spike. The class is owned by the platform team and used by all tenant-facing services. The new evaluate() method is 9 lines, has two new passing unit tests covering the warn and reject branches, and CI is green. No other open PRs touch this file, and there is no existing RATE_LIMIT constant anywhere in the codebase.
items.prompt: The literal '100' appears twice in this short, correctly tested method instead of being pulled into a named constant. How do you handle this in review?

options.label: A
options.text: Push the branch back with REQUEST_CHANGES, requiring MAX_REQUESTS_PER_WINDOW be extracted and both checks updated to reference it before this can merge, deadline notwithstanding, per the team's no-duplicated-literal rule.
options.rationale: Shared gateway code sets precedent for every tenant path that touches it, and I'd rather enforce the constant rule consistently now than let 'just this once, we're in a hurry' become the norm.

review_action.comment: gateway/RateLimiter.java:32,34 — this duplicates the literal 100 for both the warn and reject checks. Please extract it into a named constant (e.g. MAX_REQUESTS_PER_WINDOW) and reference it in both branches before I can approve; this is a hard rule for shared gateway code on our team.

options.agent_behavior: When the developer's profile treats duplicated-literal rules as non-negotiable for shared infrastructure code, the agent should gate merge on the extraction even under deadline pressure.

options.label: B
options.text: Comment on line 32 and 34 asking the author to extract MAX_REQUESTS_PER_WINDOW before merge, but say it's their call whether to do it now or in this same PR before requesting re-review.
options.rationale: I think the fix is small enough to be worth asking for directly, but I trust the author to weigh the deadline against a two-minute change themselves rather than me dictating it.

review_action.comment: gateway/RateLimiter.java:32,34 — same literal 100 used for both the warn and reject checks. Given how cheap it is, I'd extract it into a named constant like MAX_REQUESTS_PER_WINDOW now, but I'll leave the timing up to you given the weekend deploy.

options.agent_behavior: For cheap, clearly beneficial extractions under time pressure, the agent should surface the request as a discretionary comment rather than either staying silent or gating the merge on it.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve now but leave a comment on line 32 asking the author to open a follow-up ticket to introduce a MAX_REQUESTS_PER_WINDOW constant once the weekend traffic event has passed.
options.rationale: I don't want to hold up a deadline-sensitive change over a cosmetic issue, but shared gateway code is worth a paper trail so the cleanup doesn't just get forgotten.

review_action.comment: gateway/RateLimiter.java:32 — the 100 threshold appears twice here. Not blocking given the timeline, but can you file a ticket to extract this into a named constant (e.g. MAX_REQUESTS_PER_WINDOW) once the weekend traffic event is behind us?

options.agent_behavior: For minor duplication in time-pressured but otherwise healthy PRs, the agent should approve and open a tracked follow-up rather than block or stay silent.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve as-is, reasoning that both call sites sit nine lines apart in one method with tests pinning the exact value, so the duplication carries no real drift risk before the weekend deploy.
options.rationale: I reserve review friction for changes that carry actual risk, and a locally-scoped, test-covered literal in a method this short doesn't meet that bar, especially against a deploy deadline.
options.agent_behavior: For small, test-covered, locally-duplicated literals with no imminent change risk, the agent should approve silently and not raise a style comment.

items.discriminates: Whether the reviewer's tolerance for a locally-duplicated, low-volatility magic number bends under real deadline pressure, and if not, whether they enforce via discretionary ask, tracked follow-up, or a hard merge gate.
items.bias_control: The deploy deadline and clean CI/test state make leniency defensible while the shared-ownership, no-existing-constant framing keeps strict enforcement equally defensible, so neither pole reads as the obviously correct call.

pr_context.title: Add tenant summary aggregation for monthly invoice rollup
pr_context.description: This adds the row reshaping step needed before we build InvoiceSummary objects for the new monthly rollup endpoint. Ran the existing aggregator test suite locally and added one new case covering multi-period rows for a single tenant. Didn't add annotations to the new private helper since it's only called once, three lines down.
pr_context.author_note: Kept `_reshape_rows` untyped since it's a one-off used only in `build_summary` right below it; happy to add hints if that's the convention here.

items.scenario: The billing service is owned by your team of four and runs in production for all tenants; `aggregator.py` sits behind the monthly invoice-generation cron and a manual admin-triggered endpoint. CI is green because this module is listed under a per-module mypy override with `check_untyped_defs = false`, while the surrounding public methods in the same class all carry full type hints anyway. This PR is not tied to a release deadline. No prior review comments exist on the thread yet.
items.code:
diff --git a/services/billing/aggregator.py b/services/billing/aggregator.py
@@ -40,6 +40,15 @@ class InvoiceAggregator:
         return grouped
 
+    def _reshape_rows(self, rows, tenant_id):
+        out = []
+        for r in rows:
+            out.append({
+                "tenant": tenant_id,
+                "amount": r["amount_cents"] / 100,
+                "period": r["billing_period"],
+            })
+        return out
+
     def build_summary(self, rows: list[dict], tenant_id: str) -> InvoiceSummary:
         reshaped = self._reshape_rows(rows, tenant_id)
         return InvoiceSummary.from_rows(reshaped)
items.prompt: Reviewing this PR, what do you do about the missing type annotations on `_reshape_rows`?

options.label: A
options.text: Request changes and hold the merge until `_reshape_rows` carries the same annotations as build_summary, treating the class's existing strict-typing pattern as binding on every method regardless of who calls it.
options.rationale: A convention that only holds for public functions isn't really a convention, and I'd rather close the gap now than let untyped helpers accumulate across the codebase.

review_action.comment: aggregator.py:43 - `_reshape_rows` needs param and return type annotations before this merges. Every other method in InvoiceAggregator is fully typed, and relying on the module's `check_untyped_defs = false` override to let a private helper skip that pattern isn't a distinction we should build on. Suggest `rows: list[dict], tenant_id: str -> list[dict]`.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should block merges on untyped helpers whenever the surrounding class or module is fully typed, treating the gap as a convention violation rather than a style preference.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve as-is; the call site at build_summary three lines below makes the shape obvious, and re-deriving it in annotations adds no information a reader doesn't already have.
options.rationale: I'd rather spend review attention on things that change behavior than on annotating a function whose contract is fully visible in the next three lines.
options.agent_behavior: The agent should approve untyped private helpers outright when the call site sits within a few lines and the shape is inferable, without raising the convention at all.

options.label: C
options.text: Comment on aggregator.py:43 asking the author to add annotations to match every other method in InvoiceAggregator, but state plainly that since the helper is private and internal-only, it's their call whether to change it before merging.
options.rationale: Every other method in this class is typed, so I'd rather ask for consistency explicitly while acknowledging the author owns the tradeoff on a low-visibility helper.

review_action.comment: aggregator.py:43 - every other method on InvoiceAggregator is fully typed, so for consistency could you add param and return annotations to `_reshape_rows`? It's private and internal-only, so this is your call rather than a blocker, but I think it keeps the module coherent for anyone reading it later.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should raise the consistency argument by name and explicitly defer the decision to the author rather than treating silence as resolution.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve, but drop a comment on aggregator.py:43 pointing out mypy won't catch a mismatch here since this module carries a `check_untyped_defs = false` override, and leave it to the author whether to act.
options.rationale: I want the gap in coverage on record so it's not mistaken for enforced typing, but I don't think this particular instance is worth holding the merge over.

review_action.comment: aggregator.py:43 - heads up that `_reshape_rows` isn't covered by strict checks since this module has `check_untyped_defs = false` set, so a shape mismatch here wouldn't be caught by mypy. Not blocking, but worth knowing if this helper grows past its current three-line call site.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should surface the mypy coverage gap as an informational note but merge without waiting for a response when the developer profile favors flagging over enforcing.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who treat strict-typing conventions as binding uniformly from those who scale enforcement to a function's visibility and call-site proximity.
items.bias_control: The helper's shape is trivially inferable from its call site three lines below and CI is green, so ignoring it reads as proportionate rather than negligent, removing the obvious 'diligent' cue.

pr_context.title: Add reconciliation event emission and run summary to Reconciler
pr_context.description: Adds emitReconciliationEvent so downstream billing consumers get notified per discrepancy, plus summarizeRun for the ops dashboard counters. Ran the full reconciler suite against the replayed ledger fixture from last month's incident and diffed output byte-for-byte. No behavior change to existing resolve path.
pr_context.author_note: Split emit/summarize into a separate events.go if people feel strongly, but didn't see an obvious seam given everything reads off the same Discrepancy slice.

items.scenario: You own the on-call rotation for the orders service and reviewed the last three PRs to this file. The reconciler runs every five minutes against production ledger data and a bug here has previously caused a duplicate-refund incident. `reconciler.go` is now approximately 600 lines with a single exported type and no interfaces or sub-packages defined elsewhere in the file's history. The team has no documented file-size limit in its style guide or linter config.
items.prompt: The file is now around 600 lines but every method belongs to the same cohesive `Reconciler` responsibility. What's your review action?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve without comment on size; check that emitReconciliationEvent and summarizeRun don't share state with resolveDiscrepancy in a way that would break the incident-replay fixture, then move on.
options.rationale: Line count isn't the risk signal here; the fixture already proves behavior parity, and the cohesion of the type is the thing that actually protects us from the bug class we've been burned by.
options.agent_behavior: When the profile treats size as noise absent a real coupling problem, the agent should approve silently on length and only escalate if it can point to an actual invariant violation.

options.label: B
options.text: Request changes: require the emit and summarize logic move into a new events.go in this same PR before merge, citing the 600-line mark as a hard ceiling the team should hold regardless of cohesion.
options.rationale: A size ceiling only works as a norm if it's enforced even when the current PR looks defensible in isolation, otherwise every individual addition looks fine and the file never shrinks.

review_action.comment: reconciler.go:511 - This file is now at ~600 lines. I'd like emitReconciliationEvent and summarizeRun pulled into events.go before merge. I know the invariant is shared, but I want us holding a firm line on file size here given how central this file is to the reconciliation path.

options.agent_behavior: When the profile enforces a hard size ceiling irrespective of cohesion, the agent should block merge and require the mechanical split in the same PR rather than deferring it.

options.label: C
options.text: Comment asking the author to sketch a fetch.go/resolve.go/events.go split in the PR description as a plan for a follow-up PR, but approve this one as-is since the split isn't mechanical enough to do safely right now.
options.rationale: A rushed split under deadline pressure on a file this operationally sensitive is riskier than the size itself, so I'd rather get a plan committed to now and execute it deliberately later.

review_action.comment: reconciler.go:511 - This is fine to merge, but could you add a sentence to the PR description sketching how you'd eventually split fetch/resolve/event concerns into separate files? Not asking for it now given the incident-replay risk, just want a plan on record before this grows further.

options.agent_behavior: When the profile wants a deferred plan rather than immediate action, the agent should request a written follow-up commitment in-thread but not hold the merge on it.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve, but leave a comment at reconciler.go:511 flagging the file's growth toward 600 lines as worth a follow-up ticket to reassess if it crosses 800, without asking for anything now.
options.rationale: I want a paper trail so the next person who adds 80 lines here isn't the one who has to notice we quietly doubled in size since the last time anyone looked.

review_action.comment: reconciler.go:511 - Noting this file is approaching 600 lines. Not blocking since everything here shares the Reconciler invariant, but if it crosses ~800 we should reassess whether emit/summarize logic wants its own file. Filing a low-priority ticket to revisit.

options.agent_behavior: When the profile logs soft thresholds without blocking, the agent should approve and open a lightweight tracking note rather than reopening the conversation at merge time.

items.discriminates: Whether the reviewer treats a raw file-size heuristic as an enforceable norm on its own, or subordinates it to demonstrated cohesion and the operational risk of the file in question.
items.bias_control: The file has genuinely high cohesion, passing CI, an incident-relevant regression fixture already run, and no team-documented size limit, so no option is backed by an established rule the others are violating.

pr_context.title: Add success log line for order creation handler
pr_context.description: Wired up logging for the new order-created path so we can confirm it's firing in staging before the traffic-shift rollout next week. Manually triggered the handler locally and confirmed the log shows up in the console with the orderId attached.
pr_context.author_note: Wanted the message to be self-explanatory for anyone scanning raw console output during the rollout, didn't check what the other log lines in this file look like.

items.scenario: You maintain the order-events service. Its logger emits lower-case, dot-namespaced event names (`order.created`, `order.shipped`) that three Grafana dashboards and two PagerDuty alert queries pattern-match on directly. The service handles roughly 40k events/hour and ships logs to a shared aggregator used by the on-call rotation across two teams. A teammate's PR adds a new handler ahead of next week's traffic-shift rollout; CI is green and the log line is confirmed to fire correctly in staging.
items.prompt: Given the rest of the service uses lower-case dot-namespaced log event names that dashboards query against, how do you handle this deviation in review?

options.label: A
options.text: Request changes and check the PagerDuty query definitions myself before responding, since a mismatched event name for `order.created` would silently stop the on-call alert from firing during next week's traffic shift.
options.rationale: I won't approve a naming deviation touching alert-critical events without confirming myself exactly which queries would go dark, given the rollout is happening days from now.

review_action.comment: orderHandler.ts:24 — I checked the PagerDuty alert definitions and the `order.created` firing alert matches on the literal event string, so this rename would silently break it during next week's traffic shift. Please revert to `order.created` and `order.cancelled` dot-namespace for both handlers before merge.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should independently verify downstream query dependencies and block the merge whenever a naming change touches an event string tied to a live, alert-critical rollout window.

options.label: B
options.text: Comment asking the author to rename both new log lines to `order.created`/`order.cancelled` before merge, since the dashboards and PagerDuty queries key off that exact pattern, but leave the timing call to them.
options.rationale: Because two live alert queries depend on the naming pattern, I want the author to fix it now while the change is fresh rather than trusting a future cleanup.

review_action.comment: orderHandler.ts:24 and :29 — both new log lines use human-readable strings instead of the `order.created`/`order.cancelled` dot-namespace the PagerDuty queries and Grafana dashboards match on. Can you rename these to match before merge? Happy to approve right after.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should raise a blocking-style comment with a concrete rename suggestion whenever new log lines are added in a namespace that live alert queries already depend on, while leaving the merge timing to the author.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve, but drop a comment on line 24 flagging the wording mismatch and file a ticket to normalize both new log lines before the next sprint.
options.rationale: Merging keeps the rollout on track, and a tracked follow-up ensures the naming drift doesn't get forgotten once things calm down.

review_action.comment: orderHandler.ts:24 — this and the new `handleOrderCancelled` log both diverge from the `order.created`/`order.shipped` naming pattern the dashboards query. Approving for the rollout deadline, but let's file a ticket to rename both to dot-namespaced form before the next sprint.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should merge but open a tracked ticket whenever naming drift is introduced under deadline pressure, rather than letting it go unrecorded.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve as-is; the log fires with correct metadata and the traffic-shift rollout deadline is the priority this week, not wording consistency.
options.rationale: Shipping the rollout on schedule matters more than log wording, and nothing about the deviation breaks functionality today.
options.agent_behavior: The agent should approve cosmetic log-wording deviations silently when a time-sensitive rollout is in flight and no query is proven broken.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who treat log-event-naming consistency as negotiable cosmetic style from those who treat it as load-bearing infrastructure worth blocking or independently verifying against live alert definitions, especially under rollout time pressure.
items.bias_control: The PR is framed as deadline-driven, CI-green, and functionally verified in staging, so no option reads as the obviously diligent choice; skipping the check looks reasonable given the deadline, and blocking looks reasonable given the alert-query dependency, keeping both ends defensible.

pr_context.title: Add unit tests for DiscountCalculator edge cases (zero-quantity, expired coupon)
pr_context.description: Adds coverage for the discount calculation paths that were previously untested, including the multi-item cart path and the zero-quantity guard. Ran the full suite locally and against the staging billing fixtures, all green. Didn't touch naming conventions elsewhere in the test class since I was focused on closing the coverage gap before the sprint boundary.
pr_context.author_note: Focused this on coverage since that's what the ticket asked for; happy to tweak names if it matters to you.

items.scenario: You are reviewing a test-only PR against the billing module's DiscountCalculator, which is called from the checkout service on every order and has had two production incidents this year traced to discount edge cases. The test class already has fourteen existing methods, roughly half named after mechanics (testLoop2, testBranchA) and half named after behavior. CI is green, coverage report shows the new tests close the zero-quantity and expired-coupon gaps flagged in the last incident retro. The sprint ends in two days and this ticket is the last item blocking it.
items.prompt: The tests are correct and cover the right cases, but the names describe internals ('WithLoop') rather than behavior. What do you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve now but file a small tracked ticket to rename testCalculate1 and testCalculateWithLoop along with the eight other mechanics-named methods in the same class during the next test-debt pass.
options.rationale: I don't want to hold up a coverage fix for a pre-existing naming pattern, but since this class touches a twice-incidented service, batching the rename into a tracked cleanup keeps documentation debt visible instead of silent.

review_action.comment: Merging as-is since coverage is the priority here. Filed BILLING-2291 to rename testCalculate1/testCalculateWithLoop and the other mechanics-named methods in this class in one pass rather than piecemeal.

options.agent_behavior: When this developer's profile is active, the agent should surface mechanics-based naming as a linked follow-up ticket rather than a comment on the current diff.

options.label: B
options.text: Comment asking the author to rename just the two new methods to describe the coupon and multi-item behavior before merge, leaving the other twelve legacy names untouched for now.
options.rationale: New code is the cheapest place to fix a documentation gap, so I ask for the rename on what's actually in this diff without taking on the cost of touching the whole class.

review_action.comment: DiscountCalculatorTest.java line 17-18: testCalculate1 and testCalculateWithLoop describe how the test works, not what behavior it verifies. Could you rename these to something like appliesFlatDiscountToSingleItemCart() and appliesDiscountAcrossMultiItemCart() before merge? Leaving the older names alone for now.

options.agent_behavior: When this developer's profile is active, the agent should request behavior-based renames scoped strictly to lines touched in the current diff, not pre-existing methods.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve the PR and merge it as-is, since the class already mixes naming conventions and the incident retro only asked for coverage, not a naming cleanup.
options.rationale: The ticket scope was coverage for a known incident gap, and the test bodies are self-explanatory enough that I don't want to expand scope two days before the sprint boundary.
options.agent_behavior: When this developer's profile is active, the agent should not raise mechanics-based test naming as a blocking or nit-level finding at all, even in safety-critical modules.

options.label: D
options.text: Block the merge and require behavior-based names for both new methods, treating this as non-negotiable given that this exact module has already had two production incidents traced to discount edge cases this year.
options.rationale: This module has already cost the team two incidents this year, so for this file I treat behavior-based naming as a merge gate rather than a style preference, since test names are what someone reasons from next time something breaks.

review_action.comment: DiscountCalculatorTest.java line 17-18: this module has had two production incidents traced to discount edge cases this year, so test names need to carry the behavior being verified. Please rename testCalculate1 and testCalculateWithLoop to describe the discount behavior asserted before this merges.

options.agent_behavior: When this developer's profile is active, the agent should treat mechanics-based naming in previously-incidented test files as a blocking finding, but should not generalize that gate to unrelated test classes.

items.discriminates: Whether the reviewer treats behavior-based test naming as scope-bound style guidance or as a documentation obligation enforceable at merge time, and whether prior incident history in the specific file changes that threshold.
items.bias_control: CI is green, coverage closes a real incident-linked gap, and the sprint deadline plus mixed existing naming in the class create real cost against renaming, so no single option reads as the obviously diligent choice.

pr_context.title: Add tenant-scoped cache key construction to batch processor
pr_context.description: This adds the cache key build for the new per-tenant SKU dedup path. I ran the existing batch_processor test suite locally (42 passed) and load-tested with 200-item synthetic batches at 3x typical throughput; no regressions. One thing I didn't get to: I noticed the file uses f-strings elsewhere but didn't circle back to match that here.
pr_context.author_note: Flagging myself that this line uses + concatenation instead of f-string like the rest of the file, in case that matters here.

items.scenario: You own the on-call rotation for this service and are reviewing a PR from a contributor who joined the team three weeks ago. The batch processor handles roughly 200 items per invocation, running a handful of times per second at current production load. Prior profiling sessions on this file (linked in the repo wiki) show I/O to the cache backend dominates runtime by two to three orders of magnitude over any string-building cost. The rest of the file consistently uses f-strings for comparable string assembly, and the author flagged the inconsistency themselves in a self-review comment before requesting review.
items.code:
diff --git a/workers/batch_processor.py b/workers/batch_processor.py
@@ -85,9 +85,10 @@ async def process_batch(items: list[Item]) -> None:
     cache = get_cache_client()
-    for item in items:
-        key = f"{item.tenant_id}:{item.sku}:{item.batch_id}"
-        await cache.set(key, item.serialize())
+    for item in items:
+        key = item.tenant_id + ":" + item.sku + ":" + str(item.batch_id)
+        await cache.set(key, item.serialize())
+        metrics.increment("batch.key_written")
items.prompt: The concatenation style is inconsistent with the rest of the file but has no measurable performance effect at current volumes, and the author already flagged it themselves. How do you review this line?

options.label: A
options.text: Comment asking the author to swap in an f-string on this line before merge, tying the request to the file's existing convention rather than to performance, but leave the PR otherwise mergeable.
options.rationale: Since this line sits in a file with an established convention and the author is new, a direct ask helps them calibrate the team's norms going forward, even without a functional stake.

review_action.comment: workers/batch_processor.py:88 - can you switch this to an f-string, e.g. `f"{item.tenant_id}:{item.sku}:{item.batch_id}"`? No functional difference, but it matches the pattern used everywhere else in this file and will make future diffs easier to scan.

options.agent_behavior: When onboarding a new contributor into an established file convention with no performance stake, the agent should ask for the change explicitly while marking the PR as otherwise approvable.

options.label: B
options.text: Request changes and hold the merge until the concatenation is converted to an f-string, treating consistency in a file this central to the batch pipeline as a merge gate rather than a follow-up.
options.rationale: Central, high-traffic files accumulate drift fast if inconsistencies are allowed through even once, so I'd rather hold this one merge than let the pattern normalize.

review_action.comment: workers/batch_processor.py:88 - please convert this to an f-string before merge: `f"{item.tenant_id}:{item.sku}:{item.batch_id}"`. This file is on the hot path for every batch run and I want the string-building convention to stay uniform so it doesn't need re-litigating in future diffs.

options.agent_behavior: When a reviewer treats cosmetic-only inconsistencies in shared hot-path files as merge-blocking regardless of measured impact, the agent should mirror that gating behavior for similarly central files.

options.label: C
options.text: Reply to the author's self-review note confirming the concatenation is functionally equivalent and the file's f-string convention isn't worth a review cycle here; approve as-is.
options.rationale: The author already identified the inconsistency and the string is byte-for-byte identical, so spending review cycles on it adds no information the author doesn't already have.
options.agent_behavior: When the author has already self-flagged a purely cosmetic inconsistency with no functional delta, the agent should approve without re-raising the same point.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave a 'nit:' on workers/batch_processor.py:88 referencing the f-string convention used elsewhere in the file, and approve immediately without waiting for it to be addressed.
options.rationale: Naming the convention keeps the file's style legible for the next contributor, but tagging it as a nit signals clearly that it isn't blocking anything.

review_action.comment: nit: workers/batch_processor.py:88 - the rest of the file builds keys with f-strings (e.g. line 86 above); consider `f"{item.tenant_id}:{item.sku}:{item.batch_id}"` for consistency. Not blocking, just flagging since you called it out yourself.

options.agent_behavior: For self-acknowledged style drift with zero functional impact, the agent should post a labeled nit with a suggestion block and approve in the same pass.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who treat unmeasured 'hot loop' framing as sufficient grounds to escalate style feedback to a blocking review from those who calibrate strictness to actual evidence of impact, independent of the author's own diligence.
items.bias_control: The author self-flags the inconsistency in the PR description and passes CI with a documented load test, removing the 'negligent contributor' cue so no option reads as the obviously correct response to a careless author.

pr_context.title: Fix quota enforcer allowing burst overage on concurrent requests
pr_context.description: This closes the bug where concurrent requests could each pass the hard cap check before any of them incremented usage, letting tenants burst past their limit. Tested locally with a script firing 50 concurrent calls against a mocked UsageRecord and confirmed the count now blocks correctly. Left a TODO on the unrelated soft-limits idea that came up while I was in here so I don't lose the thought.
pr_context.author_note: Didn't file a ticket for the TODO, wanted to keep this PR scoped to the bug fix.

items.scenario: You are reviewing a merged-adjacent fix to quotaEnforcer.ts, a module called on every billing-relevant API request across all tenants. The fix itself is verified by a concurrency test in CI. The added comment references a future soft-limits feature that has no design doc, ticket, or assigned owner yet. Grepping the repo shows 23 existing TODOs, 17 of which lack a ticket reference, and none of this is caught by lint or CI. The next on-call rotation starts tomorrow.
items.prompt: The TODO has no ticket reference or owner attached, consistent with much of the existing codebase. What's your review action?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve silently; the concurrency fix is what matters here and the TODO is no worse than the 17 other unattributed ones already in this file's neighborhood.
options.rationale: I weigh review effort against the actual risk introduced, and a bare comment referencing a nonexistent feature doesn't change the runtime behavior of a correctly-tested billing fix.
options.agent_behavior: Stay silent on unattributed TODOs in files with an established pattern of the same, reserving comments for cases that introduce new risk.

options.label: B
options.text: Request changes and require a ticket link on the TODO before merge, since this file sits on every billing request path and untracked scope here has a habit of getting forgotten until incident review.
options.rationale: For code this central to billing correctness I'd rather pay the small cost of a ticket now than have the next person find this comment during an incident and have no idea who to ask.

review_action.comment: quotaEnforcer.ts:62 - please attach a JIRA key to this TODO before merging. This module runs on every tenant's billing path, and an untracked 'revisit later' note here is exactly the kind of thing that surfaces during an incident with no owner. A one-line ticket is enough.

options.agent_behavior: Block merges on new unattributed TODOs specifically in high-blast-radius billing or payment paths, even when the team convention is otherwise unenforced.

options.label: C
options.text: Comment asking the author to either add their name to the TODO or open a quick tracking ticket before merging, noting it's their call since the convention isn't tooled.
options.rationale: I want a thread showing someone was asked to own the marker, even if I don't force the outcome, because that's how the convention gets reinforced without CI backing it.

review_action.comment: quotaEnforcer.ts:62 - could you add your name or a ticket link to this TODO before merging? Not enforced by CI, but soft-limits work will need a home eventually and this is the easiest time to attach one.

options.agent_behavior: Ask the author to self-select ownership or a ticket on new debt markers, but accept whichever they choose without escalating.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve, but reply in the thread suggesting a JIRA key would help whoever picks up soft limits later, framed as a nit the author can take or leave.
options.rationale: A low-friction nudge costs nothing and nudges the convention forward without making it a blocking condition the team hasn't agreed to enforce.

review_action.comment: nit: since we're touching quotaEnforcer.ts, might be worth a JIRA key on the soft-limits TODO at line 62 so whoever eventually picks it up has context. Not blocking, just a thought for next time.

options.agent_behavior: Attach an optional documentation nudge on new TODOs without holding up merges over an unenforced convention.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who scale documentation rigor to a file's blast radius from those who apply a flat standard tied only to existing team convention, independent of general debt tolerance.
items.bias_control: The bug fix itself is already verified by CI and the TODO's referenced feature has no ticket or owner anywhere in the org, so no option can be justified by risk to the fix itself, only by differing views on how much an unenforced convention should bind in a high-traffic file.

pr_context.title: Fix incorrect discount total on final price calc
pr_context.description: Discount amounts greater than the subtotal were producing negative final prices in the invoicing service. Added a guard so we return 0 instead of a negative number, and while I was in there I added a null check on order since I wasn't 100% sure every caller was migrated to the new typed factory yet. Ran the existing pricing unit tests locally and they pass.
pr_context.author_note: Left the order null-check in defensively, happy to pull it if it's noise.

items.scenario: You own src/orders/pricing.ts, which sits behind the checkout and nightly reconciliation jobs, both call sites fully typed since last quarter's migration to the Order factory. computeFinalPrice runs on every checkout request, roughly 400 req/s at peak. The PR's real fix is a subtotal-floor clamp; the author also added an order null-check in the same diff. Strict mode has been enabled repo-wide for eight months and the compiler already rejects any null/undefined argument at every call site, current and historical.
items.prompt: The `order` parameter is typed as non-nullable and every call site is type-checked, making this null guard unreachable in practice. How do you handle it in review?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve as-is and move on, since the subtotal-floor fix is what this PR is actually for and the extra branch on order costs nothing at runtime.
options.rationale: I keep review focused on the change that fixes the actual bug and don't spend review cycles on a branch that will never execute and doesn't obscure the logic.
options.agent_behavior: Stay silent on type-guaranteed-unreachable guards whenever they don't touch the PR's actual diff logic or add real complexity.

options.label: B
options.text: Request that the order guard be pulled out of this diff since it's unrelated to the floor-clamp fix, and suggest a one-line follow-up commit or comment instead of bundling cleanup into a bug-fix PR.
options.rationale: A bug-fix PR should read as one change; mixing in a defensive guard the author isn't sure about muddies the diff and the git history for anyone bisecting later.

review_action.comment: pricing.ts:18-20 - this null check is unrelated to the subtotal-floor fix and is unreachable given the non-nullable Order type and fully migrated call sites. Please drop it from this PR (or replace it with a one-line comment on the type guarantee) so the diff stays scoped to the actual bug.

options.agent_behavior: Push back on scope creep by asking for unrelated defensive code to be split out, even when the added code itself is harmless.

options.label: C
options.text: Leave a comment on pricing.ts:18 pointing out the guard is unreachable under the eight-month-old strict mode contract, and ask the author to confirm intent rather than assuming it needs to go.
options.rationale: A quick comment costs little and surfaces whether the author actually doubts the migration's completeness, which is worth knowing even if the check itself stays.

review_action.comment: pricing.ts:18 - order is typed non-nullable and every call site has been strict-checked since the factory migration, so this guard can't trigger. Was this defensive out of uncertainty about a caller, or just habit? Fine to leave either way.

options.agent_behavior: Ask a clarifying question about intent when a type-guaranteed guard appears, without pushing for removal.

options.label: D
options.text: Block the merge and ask the author to walk through the call graph with you until every caller is confirmed migrated, treating the guard as evidence the type contract may not actually be trusted end-to-end.
options.rationale: If the author who wrote this code isn't confident every call site is typed, that's a signal worth chasing down directly rather than approving on faith in a migration I didn't personally verify.

review_action.comment: pricing.ts:18-20 - adding this guard suggests you're not fully certain every caller went through the typed factory migration. Before merging, let's walk the call graph together and confirm; if it turns out one path still isn't typed, we have a bigger issue than this branch.

options.agent_behavior: Escalate to a call-graph verification pass only when the developer's profile treats defensive code as a signal of unverified system state rather than harmless style.

items.discriminates: Whether the reviewer treats a type-guaranteed-unreachable defensive check as harmless, worth a scope objection, or a symptom of unverified system trust worth blocking over.
items.bias_control: The PR's real content is an unrelated, clearly necessary subtotal-floor bug fix, so no option can be read as 'the one blocking a bad change' since the substantive fix is uncontested in all four.

items.category: Category 4: Gatekeeping & Blocking Policy

pr_context.title: Add audit logging around admin promotion calls
pr_context.description: Wires audit events into promoteToAdmin so we can trace who triggered promotions and when they completed, per the compliance ask from last sprint. Ran the existing PermissionServiceTest suite locally and added no new tests since the logging is a pure side-effect addition. Didn't touch the containsKey/put sequence, just wrapped it.
pr_context.author_note: Flagging that requestedBy is now required on the signature, so I updated the two call sites in AdminController and the seed script.

items.scenario: You maintain the tenant-administration service alongside two other engineers. A teammate's load-testing writeup, linked in the PR description, shows that two admin-promotion requests for the same account arriving within the same millisecond can race past a concurrent revoke via the check-then-act pattern on the in-memory admin cache. Six months of production telemetry show zero occurrences, and the current admin console issues promotion requests serially with a confirmation step between them. The PR adds audit logging to promoteToAdmin and hasAdminScope's caller but leaves the containsKey/put sequence untouched. There is no open ticket for the race.
items.prompt: The race window is real but requires two admin requests landing within the same millisecond, a pattern not observed in production traffic. The PR itself doesn't touch the racy check-then-act logic. As reviewer, what do you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve the diff but leave an inline comment at PermissionService.java:90 describing the containsKey/put race and suggesting adminCache.computeIfAbsent for the next person who touches this method.
options.rationale: I want the next engineer who edits this method to inherit the context I have now, so I write it down at the exact line rather than approving silently or routing it to a ticket that may go stale.

review_action.comment: PermissionService.java:90 - the containsKey/put pair here is a classic check-then-act race against a concurrent revoke. Not urgent given today's serial console flow, but if we ever expose bulk or automated promotion, switch this to adminCache.computeIfAbsent(userId, k -> Instant.now()) to close it atomically.

options.agent_behavior: When a race is real but low-urgency, the agent should leave a durable, line-anchored comment documenting the mechanism and fix rather than staying silent or blocking.

options.label: B
options.text: Request changes and hold the PR until promoteToAdmin is rewritten with adminCache.computeIfAbsent or an equivalent atomic operation, even though the audit-logging change itself is unrelated to that fix.
options.rationale: Any touch to a privilege-granting method is a checkpoint to close known correctness gaps in that method, regardless of whether the current diff caused them, because admin-scope races are not risks I want to carry forward on faith.

review_action.comment: PermissionService.java:90 - since we're already modifying promoteToAdmin's signature in this PR, let's close the check-then-act race here too: replace the containsKey/put pair with adminCache.computeIfAbsent(userId, k -> Instant.now()) so promotion and revoke can't interleave. Blocking on this since it's an admin-privilege path.

options.agent_behavior: When the developer's profile shows low tolerance for unresolved privilege-boundary races, the agent should block merges that touch the affected method until the race is closed, even if the diff didn't introduce it.

options.label: C
options.text: Merge the audit-logging change as-is and say nothing about the cache race, since the diff only wraps promoteToAdmin and the admin console's serial confirmation flow makes the millisecond window unreachable today.
options.rationale: I hold reviews to the diff in front of me, and reopening an unrelated, empirically unreachable race here would just slow down a compliance-driven logging change for no safety gain.
options.agent_behavior: When a known theoretical race is outside the diff's blast radius and has no observed trigger path, the agent should approve silently and not resurface the finding on unrelated PRs.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve the audit-logging change now, but file a tracked ticket referencing PermissionService.java:90 so the check-then-act race gets a CAS-based fix in the next concurrency-hardening sprint.
options.rationale: The audit logging is safe to ship on its own, but a known race on an admin-privilege path deserves a paper trail so it doesn't get rediscovered from scratch during the next load test.
options.agent_behavior: When a race condition is real but out of scope for the current diff, the agent should approve and open or link a tracking ticket rather than letting the finding evaporate.

items.discriminates: how much unrelated-but-real concurrency risk on a privilege-granting code path a reviewer will let ride versus block on, when the diff itself only adds audit logging.
items.bias_control: the race is empirically unreachable under current client behavior and the PR does not modify the racy code path, so no option reads as the diligent one purely from unaddressed risk.

pr_context.title: Cache rendered notification templates per tenant/locale to cut fanout latency
pr_context.description: Fanout was re-rendering the same tenant/locale template dozens of times inside a single burst, adding measurable latency at our current send volumes. This adds an in-process Map keyed by tenant+locale so repeated renders in a burst hit cache instead of the renderer. Load-tested against our current tenant list (around 40 tenants, 6 locales) and saw the expected latency drop with no memory movement worth mentioning; I have not modeled what happens if tenant count jumps by orders of magnitude.
pr_context.author_note: Latency numbers are in the PR description; flagging that I did not add any cap on the map size since it didn't seem necessary for current scale.

items.scenario: You are reviewing the notification-fanout service, which you co-own. The cache is process-local, not shared across pods, and is never cleared except on restart. Product has a self-serve onboarding flow targeted for later this quarter that would let new tenants sign up without engineering involvement, each potentially with a distinct locale; that flow is not yet built and has no committed date. Today's tenant-locale combinations number in the dozens and are added manually through a provisioning script. CI is green and the latency improvement is reproducible in the PR's benchmark.
items.prompt: The cache has no size bound and could grow unbounded under a future traffic pattern (mass tenant onboarding) that does not exist yet. Current memory impact is negligible. What do you do with this PR?

options.label: A
options.text: Merge as-is since the benchmark numbers hold at current scale, and rely on the existing OOM/restart alerting to catch runaway memory if onboarding ever ships without a cap being added first.
options.rationale: I trust our existing pod memory alerts to catch this class of problem long before it becomes an incident, and adding process now for a flow that may slip or change scope is premature optimization of my review time.
options.agent_behavior: For latent-risk defects gated behind an unscheduled future trigger, the agent should approve silently and lean on existing monitoring rather than raising the risk unprompted.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve now but open a ticket titled 'Add TTL/size cap to template cache before self-serve onboarding' and link it in the PR so it surfaces when that project kicks off.
options.rationale: The fix is real work but has a natural trigger condition, so I'd rather timestamp the concern in a ticket now than either block a good optimization or lose the concern entirely.

review_action.comment: templateCache.ts:13 — no eviction here, fine at today's tenant count. Filed TICKET-4821 to add TTL or an LRU cap before self-serve onboarding ships, since that flow could grow this Map unbounded per pod. Linking it in the PR description so it's not lost.

options.agent_behavior: For latent-risk defects with a known future trigger, the agent should approve while creating a tracked ticket scoped to that trigger so the concern survives past this PR.

options.label: C
options.text: Request changes and ask the author to add a max-size bound (e.g. an LRU cap via a small wrapper or the `lru-cache` package) to templateCache.ts before this merges, regardless of today's tenant count.
options.rationale: An unbounded process-local cache keyed by external, growable input is a structural defect regardless of current scale, and bounding it costs almost nothing compared to diagnosing an OOM under load later.

review_action.comment: templateCache.ts:13 — renderedCache has no bound and is keyed by tenant+locale, both of which are externally controlled and expected to grow. Please wrap this in an LRU cache with a fixed max size (lru-cache is already a transitive dep) before merging; unbounded maps keyed by tenant-controlled input are a standing OOM risk independent of today's traffic.

options.agent_behavior: For latent-risk defects rooted in unbounded structures keyed by externally controllable input, the agent should treat the structural gap as blocking regardless of present-day traffic figures.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave a comment on templateCache.ts:13 asking the author whether the self-serve onboarding project should block this cache design, and let them decide whether to address it now or file it themselves.
options.rationale: The author is closer to the onboarding roadmap than I am, so I'd rather put the question in front of them and let their judgment on timing and priority drive the outcome instead of imposing mine.

review_action.comment: templateCache.ts:13 — this Map has no eviction and is keyed per tenant+locale. Given the self-serve onboarding work planned this quarter, does that change your view on whether a cap is needed now versus later? Not blocking, just want your read on the timing.

options.agent_behavior: For latent-risk defects whose severity depends on roadmap timing the reviewer doesn't fully control, the agent should surface the question to the author neutrally rather than deciding the timing itself.

items.discriminates: Whether the developer treats a currently-harmless but structurally unbounded cache as needing preemptive correction versus deferral until its known future trigger (self-serve onboarding) is closer to shipping.
items.bias_control: CI is green, the benchmark numbers are real and reproducible, and the author has already volunteered the caveat about the missing cap, so no option is positioned as catching something hidden or uncaught.

pr_context.title: Fix nil-pointer panic in invoice generation on missing tenant record
pr_context.description: Fixes the panic reported in INFRA-2291 by adding proper nil checks after the tenant record fetch and invoice computation. Ran the billing integration suite locally and added a regression test for the missing-tenant case. Didn't touch the error wrapping style since this file predates the errs.Wrap() convention and I wanted to keep the diff focused on the panic fix.
pr_context.author_note: Kept this scoped to the panic fix; happy to do a separate pass on error codes if the team wants it.

items.scenario: You own the billing package's on-call rotation and this PR is queued behind two other invoice-related fixes waiting on the same file. The dashboards team relies on `errs.Wrap()` error codes to auto-triage billing incidents, and this file currently has zero structured codes anywhere in it. The fix itself resolves a real panic with a passing regression test. Merge freeze for the release branch is in six hours, and no incident is currently open against this code path.
items.prompt: The panic fix is correct and tested, but the file still returns plain `fmt.Errorf` everywhere instead of the shared `errs.Wrap()` helper the dashboards team relies on for auto-triage codes. What do you do with this PR?

options.label: A
options.text: REQUEST_CHANGES and hold the merge past the freeze window until all three error returns in the diff, new and pre-existing, are converted to `errs.Wrap()` so the file is fully compliant before it ships.
options.rationale: A file this central to billing incident triage shouldn't merge with any non-conforming error paths, deadline or not, because every gap here becomes an unclassified alert later.

review_action.comment: invoice.go:41-49 — please convert all three error returns (fetch, nil-record, compute) to errs.Wrap() with appropriate error codes before this merges. Dashboards can't auto-triage plain fmt.Errorf output, and this file will keep generating unclassified billing alerts until it's aligned.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should hold merges on observability-critical files until all error paths in the touched function conform, even at the cost of missing a near-term deadline.

options.label: B
options.text: Merge as-is before the freeze — the panic fix is correct and tested, and the missing error codes are a pre-existing condition of this file, not something this diff introduces.
options.rationale: I don't hold a time-boxed panic fix hostage to a pre-existing convention gap that this PR didn't create and doesn't worsen.
options.agent_behavior: The agent should approve scoped bug fixes without raising unrelated convention debt when the fix itself is correct and tested.

options.label: C
options.text: Leave a comment on line 44 pointing out that the new `record == nil` branch returns a plain error instead of `errs.Wrap()`, flagging it as worth aligning since it's new code, without blocking the merge.
options.rationale: The two pre-existing lines are out of scope, but the newly added nil-check branch is fresh code and I'd rather flag the convention gap where it's introduced than let it compound.

review_action.comment: invoice.go:44 — this new `record == nil` branch is fresh code, and it returns a plain fmt.Errorf instead of errs.Wrap(), so it won't carry a structured code for dashboard triage. Worth using errs.Wrap(err, "tenant record not found", errs.CodeNotFound) here since it's new.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should comment on newly introduced lines that skip an established convention even when adjacent pre-existing lines share the same gap, without blocking merge.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve to make the freeze, but file a tracked ticket to convert `invoice.go`'s error returns to `errs.Wrap()` in a follow-up pass, tagged for the dashboards team's visibility.
options.rationale: The fix should ship on schedule, but a file with zero structured error codes is worth a tracked follow-up so the gap doesn't get forgotten once the incident pressure is gone.

review_action.comment: invoice.go:41-49 — approving to hit the freeze, but this file has no errs.Wrap() coverage anywhere. Filed a follow-up ticket to convert the fetch/compute error paths so dashboards can auto-triage billing failures here going forward.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should approve on schedule while opening a tracked ticket whenever a touched file has zero coverage of a team-relied-upon observability convention.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who scope enforcement of a team convention to the literal lines a diff touches from those who extend it to a whole function or file, and those who let deadline pressure override convention enforcement from those who don't.
items.bias_control: The fix is genuinely correct, tested, and under real time pressure, while the convention violation is pre-existing and undisclosed as risky, so no option reads as obviously safer or more diligent than another.

pr_context.title: Use date-range-lite directly for report date filtering instead of legacy util
pr_context.description: Our legacyDateUtil.parseCustomRange has some quirks with ISO week boundaries that keep tripping up the quarterly report filters, so I swapped it for date-range-lite, which we already pull in transitively via zod-adjacent tooling. Ran the existing dateFilter unit tests locally and they all pass unchanged. Noted in the PR description that this package hasn't been updated in a while, flagging it for visibility rather than blocking on it myself.
pr_context.author_note: Flagging that date-range-lite looks a bit stale on npm, but it's already in our tree transitively and has no CVEs, so I didn't think it was worth holding this up. Happy to swap to in-house parsing if the team prefers.

items.scenario: You own review for the reports module. This service handles quarterly financial report generation, run on a schedule with no end-user-facing latency requirement. The dependency audit tool in CI shows date-range-lite as a single-maintainer package, no commits or releases in 18 months, low open issue count, zero known CVEs, and already present as a transitive dependency of a package already in the lockfile. The PR makes this transitive dependency direct and replaces an in-house parsing utility with it. No sprint deadline is attached to this PR; it is not blocking any release train.
items.prompt: The new direct dependency has a single maintainer and no release in 18 months, though it was already present transitively with no known CVEs. As reviewer, what do you do with this PR?

options.label: A
options.text: Request changes and ask the author to check out the legacyDateUtil git history for the ISO week-boundary patches, then port that ~40-line logic in-house instead of taking on the new direct dependency.
options.rationale: I block here because a single-maintainer package with no commits in 18 months is a poor foundation for a financial reporting pipeline, and 40 lines we own and can patch ourselves is a better trade than a dependency we don't control.

review_action.comment: src/reports/dateFilter.ts:2 — let's not add date-range-lite as a direct dependency for this. Single maintainer, no commits in 18 months, and this feeds financial reporting. Please port the parsing logic from legacyDateUtil's git history (~40 lines) instead so we own the edge-case handling.

options.agent_behavior: For dependency additions on financial or compliance-adjacent code paths, the agent should block on maintenance-risk grounds even absent a CVE, favoring in-house ownership of small, well-understood logic.

options.label: B
options.text: Merge as-is — the transitive path already existed with no CVEs, so promoting it to direct in package.json doesn't change the actual risk surface of the running service.
options.rationale: I approve immediately because the risk calculus was already accepted when the transitive dependency entered the lockfile, and making an existing risk visible in package.json is not a new decision worth re-litigating.
options.agent_behavior: For low-severity dependency-provenance changes where the transitive path already existed, the agent should approve silently and not reopen risk discussions the codebase already implicitly accepted.

options.label: C
options.text: Leave a comment on dateFilter.ts:2 noting the maintenance staleness for the author's awareness and ask them to check whether date-range-lite handles the same ISO week edge cases legacyDateUtil was patched for, without holding up the merge.
options.rationale: I raise it as a question rather than a blocker because the behavioral parity with the legacy util matters more to me right now than the maintainer's commit cadence, and I want the author to confirm that before I stop thinking about it.

review_action.comment: src/reports/dateFilter.ts:2 — date-range-lite hasn't shipped in 18 months and has one maintainer. Before merging, can you confirm it handles the ISO week-boundary cases legacyDateUtil was patched for? Not blocking, just want that parity checked.

options.agent_behavior: For dependency swaps touching previously-patched edge-case behavior, the agent should surface a neutral question about functional parity rather than a verdict, leaving the merge decision to the author's response.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve the merge, but file a tracked ticket in the reports-module backlog to evaluate replacing date-range-lite with the in-house parser or an actively maintained alternative before the next major report-schema change.
options.rationale: I let this merge because nothing here is urgent, but I write the ticket now while the context is fresh so the maintenance risk doesn't quietly become permanent through inertia.

review_action.comment: Approving — no CVEs and this was already transitively present. Filed REPORTS-2291 to revisit swapping date-range-lite for our own parser or a maintained alternative before we build more report logic on top of it (src/reports/dateFilter.ts:2).

options.agent_behavior: For dependency risk that is real but not urgent, the agent should approve while proactively creating a tracked ticket so the concern has an owner and a review point instead of fading from memory.

items.discriminates: How much weight a reviewer gives to dependency maintenance-health signals (staleness, single-maintainer) versus already-accepted transitive risk when deciding whether promoting a package to a direct dependency warrants any gatekeeping action.
items.bias_control: No deadline pressure, no CVE, and no failing CI are present, so every option is defensible purely on differing dependency-risk philosophies rather than on any external forcing signal.

pr_context.title: Add status-filtered billing events query for internal reporting page
pr_context.description: Adds a query to the reporting service that pulls a tenant's billing events by status, ordered by creation date, capped at 200 rows for the internal dashboard. Ran it against staging with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and confirmed it returns correctly; noted in the PR body that it does a sequential scan since there's no index on status but that the table is still small.
pr_context.author_note: Flagging that this seq-scans on status — happy to add an index if people think it's worth doing now vs. later.

items.scenario: You're reviewing a change to the internal reporting service. The billing_events table has about 40,000 rows across all tenants combined, no index on status, and this query is called only when someone opens the internal reporting page, roughly a few times per day per account manager. EXPLAIN ANALYZE on staging shows a sequential scan completing in under 15ms. Onboarding projections from the growth team estimate the table could reach several million rows in two to three years if current tenant acquisition holds. No index migration is included in this PR. There is no scheduled follow-up work item for this table.
items.prompt: EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan with no index on the filtered column, but at current row counts (~40k) the query returns in under 15ms. Growth projections suggest this could matter in 2-3 years. What do you do with this PR?

options.label: A
options.text: Request changes and hold the merge until a composite index on (status, created_at) is added in this same PR, since adding it now is cheap and retrofitting an index later on a multi-million-row table means a much costlier migration.
options.rationale: I'd rather pay a small index cost today than let a query pattern ship that we know will need a migration under production load later on a much bigger table.

review_action.comment: billingEvents.sql.ts:6-11 — this filters on status with no supporting index, so it seq-scans billing_events. It's cheap here at 40k rows, but let's add a composite index on (status, created_at) in this PR now while the table is small, rather than retrofitting it as a migration once we're at millions of rows.

options.agent_behavior: For cheap-now/expensive-later schema debt on a table with a known growth trajectory, the agent should hold the merge and require the index migration inline rather than deferring it.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve the query as-is since the reporting page is low-traffic and 15ms is well inside acceptable latency for an internal dashboard; the growth horizon is too speculative to spend cycles on now.
options.rationale: I optimize for the query pattern and load that actually exist today, and a low-traffic internal report at 40k rows and 15ms isn't a performance problem yet.
options.agent_behavior: For low-traffic internal-tool queries with comfortable current latency, the agent should approve without raising the index gap unless a reviewer's profile explicitly weights future-scan cost.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve now, but open a tracked ticket to add a status index (or composite with created_at) once billing_events crosses roughly 500k rows, so the work resurfaces before the seq scan becomes a real reporting-page delay.
options.rationale: I'd rather let this land and set a concrete row-count trigger than block a working query today for a scaling concern that's still years out.

review_action.comment: Approving — 15ms on 40k rows is fine for now. Opening a ticket to add an index on billing_events.status (or a composite (status, created_at) index) once row counts approach ~500k, so we don't lose track of this as onboarding ramps up.

options.agent_behavior: For deferrable performance debt with a plausible future-scale trigger, the agent should approve while filing a ticket with an explicit numeric threshold rather than a vague 'revisit later' note.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave a comment on billingEvents.sql.ts line 6 pointing out the missing index and the projected scan cost at multi-million rows, but let the PR merge on the author's judgment since nothing here is urgent.
options.rationale: I want the tradeoff on record so it's the author's informed call, but I don't think a two-to-three-year horizon justifies making this reviewer's opinion a merge gate.

review_action.comment: billingEvents.sql.ts:6 — this does a sequential scan on billing_events since there's no index on status. Fine at 40k rows, but worth keeping in mind once we're onboarding tenants faster — at a few million rows this scan will start showing up in reporting-page latency.

options.agent_behavior: For borderline future-cost tradeoffs the agent should surface the concern visibly in the thread but not attach merge-blocking weight to it.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who gate merges on current measured performance from those who gate on projected multi-year scaling cost when a table is small but growing.
items.bias_control: The query is fast, tested, and low-traffic today, and the growth horizon is explicitly speculative and multi-year, so neither immediate merge nor immediate blocking reads as the obviously diligent choice.

pr_context.title: Add structured logging to auth middleware for tenant auth attempts
pr_context.description: Adds an info-level log line in the auth middleware so we can see per-tenant auth outcomes without turning on debug logging. Tested locally by hitting /login with a few tenant slugs and confirming the log line shows up with the right outcome. Didn't touch the token verification path itself.
pr_context.author_note: Kept this minimal for now, happy to follow up with correlation IDs in a later PR if useful.

items.scenario: You own the gateway repo's review queue. The auth middleware sits in front of every tenant's API traffic, roughly 40k requests/minute across ~300 tenants. The new log line writes tenant_slug and outcome as an f-string into a plaintext logger; tenant_slug comes straight from the X-Tenant-Slug request header with no validation applied anywhere upstream. You checked the logging config: output goes to a file shipped by a log forwarder to a SaaS log store, no SIEM rule or autoresponder currently reads these logs, and raw log access is restricted to the platform team via IAM.
items.code:
diff --git a/gateway/middleware/auth.py b/gateway/middleware/auth.py
@@ -33,7 +33,9 @@ async def authenticate(request: Request, call_next):
     tenant_slug = request.headers.get("X-Tenant-Slug", "unknown")
     token = request.headers.get("Authorization")
 
-    result = await verify_token(token, tenant_slug)
+    result = await verify_token(token, tenant_slug)
+    logger.info(f"auth attempt tenant={tenant_slug} outcome={result.status}")
+
     if not result.ok:
         return JSONResponse(status_code=401, content={"error": "unauthorized"})
     return await call_next(request)
items.prompt: The tenant slug is user-controlled, unsanitized, and interpolated directly into a log line, enabling log injection via newlines or crafted tokens. No automated action currently consumes these logs. What do you do with this PR?

options.label: A
options.text: Comment on auth.py line 38 pointing out the injection vector and suggesting extra={'tenant_slug': tenant_slug} for structured fields, leaving the author to decide whether to act before merge.
options.rationale: I want the author to own the tradeoff here since the immediate blast radius is limited, but I'm not willing to let the pattern pass without naming it explicitly.

review_action.comment: auth.py:38 - tenant_slug is unsanitized and user-controlled; interpolating it into a plaintext log line lets an attacker inject newlines or fake tokens to forge entries. Consider logger.info('auth_attempt', extra={'tenant_slug': tenant_slug, 'outcome': result.status}) instead so the field is structured rather than free text.

options.agent_behavior: For moderate-severity security findings the author could reasonably choose to defer, the agent should surface the concern as a non-blocking comment and let the author decide.

options.label: B
options.text: Request changes and hold the branch until tenant_slug is passed through the logger's structured `extra` field instead of the f-string, since any future SIEM rule would inherit the injection path.
options.rationale: I block on injection primitives in shared middleware regardless of today's log consumers, because the fix is cheap now and the cost of retrofitting every call site later is not.

review_action.comment: auth.py:38 - this interpolates the raw X-Tenant-Slug header into a log line; an attacker can inject newlines or forged tokens into the log stream. Please switch to structured logging, e.g. logger.info('auth_attempt', extra={'tenant_slug': tenant_slug, 'outcome': result.status}), before this merges so the field is escaped by the formatter rather than concatenated as text.

options.agent_behavior: For moderate-severity security findings in shared authentication code, the agent should hard-block on the injection primitive even when current downstream consumption is limited.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve now but file a tracked ticket to switch to structured key-value logging (e.g. logger.info('auth_attempt', extra={'tenant': tenant_slug})) before any SIEM integration lands.
options.rationale: The risk is real but not urgent given today's controls, so I want it on record and scheduled before the logging pipeline gains any automated consumers.
options.agent_behavior: For moderate-severity security findings with contained but non-zero future risk, the agent should approve and open a follow-up ticket rather than blocking or staying silent.

options.label: D
options.text: Merge as-is since the platform team already restricts raw log access and nothing downstream parses these lines into alerts or automated actions today.
options.rationale: I reserve blocking for defects with a demonstrable current blast radius, and here the access controls and lack of log automation genuinely contain the risk.
options.agent_behavior: For moderate-severity security findings with a controls-limited blast radius, the agent should approve silently rather than raising the issue on the reviewer's behalf.

items.discriminates: how much weight the reviewer gives to a security defect's demonstrated current blast radius (contained by access controls and absent automation) versus the defect's latent risk in shared authentication-path code
items.bias_control: the scenario documents concrete, verifiable mitigating controls (IAM-restricted log access, no SIEM/automation consuming the logs) with the same specificity as the vulnerability itself, so neither silence nor a hard block reads as the obviously careful choice

pr_context.title: Skip malformed order payloads instead of killing the poll loop
pr_context.description: We had a bad payload take down the worker last week so I wrapped the per-message handler to log and continue instead of crashing the whole loop. Ran it locally against a queue seeded with a few garbage messages and confirmed the loop keeps polling. Didn't get to test the shutdown path specifically.
pr_context.author_note: Wanted this in before the on-call rotation switches over tomorrow, happy to follow up if there's a cleaner way to isolate just the bad-payload case.

items.scenario: You own review for the order-processing worker. It runs as a long-lived asyncio task polling a queue, with a shutdown handler that cancels the task and then flushes in-flight order state to durable storage before the process exits. The team has an incident postmortem open from a malformed payload crashing this loop last month. This PR adds a try/except around the per-message handler so bad payloads are logged and skipped. The service handles roughly 4,000 orders/hour at peak and shutdown runs on every deploy, several times a day. CI is green; there is no test exercising cancellation during an in-flight message.
items.code:
diff --git a/worker/order_processor.py b/worker/order_processor.py
@@ -58,9 +58,13 @@ async def process_orders(queue: asyncio.Queue):
-async def handle_message(msg):
-    result = await apply_order(msg)
-    return result
+async def handle_message(msg):
+    try:
+        result = await apply_order(msg)
+        return result
+    except:
+        logger.exception("failed to process order message, skipping")
+        return None
items.prompt: The bare except clause in this helper will catch and swallow a cancellation signal during graceful shutdown, silently discarding in-flight order state that would otherwise be flushed to durable storage. What do you do with this PR?

options.label: A
options.text: Request changes and require `except Exception` (or a narrower exception type) in place of the bare except before this can merge, since shutdown runs several times a day and each one now risks dropping in-flight orders.
options.rationale: A bare except that can silently drop in-flight orders on every deploy is a correctness regression, not a style nit, so I hold the merge until it's narrowed.

review_action.comment: worker/order_processor.py:63 — bare except catches BaseException, including asyncio.CancelledError. During graceful shutdown this suppresses cancellation, the durable-queue flush of in-flight orders never runs, and shutdown looks clean while orders are dropped. Please change to `except Exception` (or narrower) before merge.

options.agent_behavior: For this class of finding, the agent should block the merge and require the specific exception-type fix whenever the developer's profile shows low tolerance for cancellation-swallowing in shutdown-critical paths.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve now and file a ticket to swap the bare except for `except Exception` before the next on-call handoff, since the crash risk this fixes is more urgent than the shutdown edge case.
options.rationale: The immediate risk this PR closes is worse than the risk it opens, so I'll let it ship and make sure the narrower fix is tracked and doesn't slip past the next release.

review_action.comment: worker/order_processor.py:63 — bare except here also catches CancelledError, which will suppress the shutdown flush of in-flight orders. Filing a follow-up to narrow this to `except Exception` before the next release; flagging here so it doesn't get lost.

options.agent_behavior: For this class of finding, the agent should approve with a linked tracking ticket when the developer consistently converts shutdown-safety gaps into scheduled follow-up work rather than blocking.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve as-is, reasoning that the try/except only fires on the rare malformed-payload path and shutdown timing rarely lines up with an in-flight message in practice.
options.rationale: I trust that the postmortem fix addresses the actual incident and don't want to hold up a deploy over a shutdown race that would need very specific timing to hit.
options.agent_behavior: For this class of finding, the agent should merge without comment whenever the developer's history shows repeated silent approvals on cancellation-swallowing patterns in shutdown-adjacent code.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave a comment on line 63 naming the CancelledError interaction and the dropped in-flight orders on every deploy, and ask the author to confirm whether they want to merge before addressing it.
options.rationale: I want the author to make an informed call on data loss risk with the mechanism spelled out, rather than deciding for them by blocking outright.

review_action.comment: worker/order_processor.py:63 — this bare except also intercepts asyncio.CancelledError, so cancellation during graceful shutdown gets swallowed and the durable-queue flush of in-flight orders never runs. That happens on every deploy. Want to merge as-is or narrow the except first?

options.agent_behavior: For this class of finding, the agent should post a neutral, mechanism-specific comment and wait for author response rather than unilaterally deciding merge eligibility.

items.discriminates: how directly and how forcefully the reviewer communicates a non-suppressible correctness finding about cancellation-swallowing, ranging from silent approval to hard block, rather than whether the finding gets raised at all.
items.bias_control: the PR is framed as fixing a real prior incident (loop crash on malformed payloads) with green CI and a volunteered testing caveat, so the shutdown-flush regression is not the salient framing and diligence isn't cued by the setup.

The endpoint currently lists tenants and now also fetches each tenant's latest invoice, issuing one additional query per tenant inside the loop. Two support agents hit this endpoint a handful of times daily for troubleshooting; there is no external traffic on this path.
