items.prompt: This introduces an N+1 query pattern, but it's on an internal, low-traffic admin endpoint used a few times a day and currently completes in under 300ms. What do you do with this PR?

options.label: A

options.rationale: I want the pattern named in the review record so the next person who extends this endpoint sees it, even though today's traffic profile doesn't justify holding the merge for it.

review_action.comment: TenantAdminController.java:21 — this loop issues one invoiceRepository call per tenant, an N+1 pattern. Fine at current scale given the auth gate and call volume, but worth batching into a single query keyed on tenant IDs if this list grows or gets exposed more broadly.

options.agent_behavior: For low-impact query patterns on internal endpoints, the agent should post a neutral awareness comment anchored to the loop line without gating the merge on a response.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve and file a tracked ticket to switch invoiceRepository.findTopByTenantIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc to a batched IN-query lookup, triggered if tenant count or usage grows.
options.rationale: The current cost is negligible but the pattern will scale badly, so I want a paper trail that surfaces the fix before it becomes a real problem rather than relying on someone noticing later.
options.agent_behavior: For low-severity but structurally scalable findings, the agent should approve and open a tracked follow-up ticket referencing the specific query method rather than blocking.

options.label: C
options.text: Merge it as-is — the auth gate, low call frequency, and measured sub-300ms latency mean the query pattern has no observable cost worth raising here.
options.rationale: I reserve review friction for changes that actually affect users or budgets; a two-person internal tool with measured latency well within bounds doesn't meet that bar.
options.agent_behavior: For low-traffic internal-only endpoints with measured latency headroom, the agent should approve silently and not surface the N+1 pattern as a finding.

options.label: D
options.text: REQUEST_CHANGES and ask the author to replace the per-tenant loop with a single findByTenantIdIn batched query before this merges, regardless of current traffic.
options.rationale: I treat N+1 patterns as a correctness-of-design issue independent of today's call volume, since traffic profiles on internal tools change without a corresponding review of the query layer.

review_action.comment: TenantAdminController.java:18-21 — please replace the per-tenant invoiceRepository call with a single batched lookup (e.g. findByTenantIdIn(tenantIds) followed by an in-memory group-by). Current traffic is low, but I'd rather not merge a known N+1 pattern regardless of today's usage numbers.

options.agent_behavior: For any N+1 query pattern regardless of measured traffic, the agent should hard-block and require batching before merge.

items.discriminates: Whether the reviewer's blocking threshold on performance issues is set by measured/contextual impact or by the presence of a known-bad query pattern independent of scale.
items.bias_control: The endpoint's low traffic, internal-only gating, and measured sub-300ms latency are stated as neutral facts rather than framed as mitigating an obvious problem, so approving silently is as defensible as blocking on pattern alone.

pr_context.title: Add shared exponential backoff helper for pricing API retry clients
pr_context.description: This extracts the retry logic three of our services were duplicating into a single internal/retry package so new callers don't reinvent it. I ran the existing unit tests against the backoff timing table and added one for max-delay clamping. Not wiring in jitter yet since the only current consumer (catalog-sync) has low request volume, but flagging that we should revisit before checkout-service or cart-service adopt it.
pr_context.author_note: Left the TODO in place so whoever picks up jitter later has context on why it was deferred.

items.scenario: You own the pricing API that twelve internal services call. Three of those services are early adopters of a new shared retry helper being merged now; the other nine would pick it up in future PRs as they migrate off ad hoc retry code. The pricing API has one prior recorded incident where a dependency outage caused a retry spike, though the root cause then was a different client's hardcoded retry loop, not this helper. The helper's backoff table is unit-tested and CI is green. No migration deadline is attached to this PR.
items.prompt: As the reviewer, which review state do you apply to this pull request?

options.label: A
options.text: Merge as-is: the backoff table is unit-tested, only catalog-sync (low volume) consumes it today, and jitter can be added whenever a high-traffic caller actually migrates onto the helper.
options.rationale: I scope my review to the code as it is used today, and adding speculative resilience work for callers that don't exist yet would slow down a clean, tested refactor.
options.agent_behavior: For deferred-hardening findings gated on a low-traffic current consumer, the agent should approve silently and not raise the risk unless the diff or PR description shows a high-traffic caller adopting the helper.

options.label: B
options.text: Comment on backoff.go asking the author whether jitter should go in now given that pricing API already had one retry-storm incident, leaving the merge decision to them rather than gating it myself.
options.rationale: I want to surface the prior incident context the author may not have, but since this specific helper isn't the one that caused it and the current caller is low-traffic, I leave the call to them.

review_action.comment: internal/retry/backoff.go:17-22: no jitter means all replicas of a caller compute identical delays and retry in lockstep. Pricing API has had one retry-storm incident before (different root cause, but same failure shape). Do you want to add jitter now, or is deferring until a high-traffic caller adopts this acceptable to you?

options.agent_behavior: For findings with a documented prior incident of the same failure shape but an unconfirmed current blast radius, the agent should raise the historical context as a question rather than asserting a required fix.

options.label: C
options.text: Request changes and require jitter in this PR before merge, since I own the pricing API's incident history and won't let a retry primitive without it become the copy-paste template the other nine services build on.
options.rationale: As the owner of the downstream API, I block on resilience gaps in shared primitives at the point they're introduced, because once nine more services copy this pattern the fix becomes a much larger migration.

review_action.comment: internal/retry/backoff.go:17-22: this will become the retry template for all twelve pricing API callers, and it has no jitter. Given our prior retry-storm incident, please add jitter (e.g. full-jitter or decorrelated-jitter) to Next() before merge rather than deferring it as a TODO, since fixing it after nine services adopt this is a much bigger change.

options.agent_behavior: For shared-primitive findings where the reviewer owns the downstream blast radius, the agent should hard-block merge and require the fix in the same PR rather than accepting a deferred ticket.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve, but file a tracked ticket titled 'Add jitter to retry.Backoff before checkout-service or cart-service adopt it' and link it in the PR so the gap is visible to the next migrating team.
options.rationale: I want the refactor to land now, but a shared helper feeding a service I own needs a paper trail so the jitter gap doesn't get silently inherited by a high-traffic caller later.

review_action.comment: Filed as follow-up: internal/retry/backoff.go:17-22 has no jitter, so simultaneous replicas will compute identical delays. Fine for catalog-sync's volume today, but this needs jitter before checkout-service or cart-service wire into it, since a pricing-API outage would otherwise cause synchronized retry waves from all replicas.

options.agent_behavior: For deferred-hardening findings on infrastructure shared across future high-traffic consumers, the agent should approve but always create or link a tracked ticket naming the specific future trigger condition.

items.discriminates: how much weight a reviewer who owns the downstream dependency places on prior incident history versus current caller traffic when deciding whether a deferred concurrency-safety gap in a shared primitive must be fixed now.
items.bias_control: the current sole consumer is explicitly low-traffic and CI is green, so both the silent-approve and tracking-ticket paths are framed as equally defensible scoping decisions rather than one reading as negligent, while the prior incident detail is given a different root cause to keep the comment and block paths from being the obvious diligent choice.

pr_context.title: Migrate invoices.amount to amount_cents (BIGINT) and cut over entity/service
pr_context.description: This backfills amount_cents from the legacy amount column and switches InvoiceEntity and InvoiceService to read/write amount_cents exclusively. I ran the migration against a staging snapshot and spot-checked 50 invoices for rounding drift, all matched. Rollout is region-by-region so there will be a window with mixed pod versions; flagging that in case it matters for sequencing.
pr_context.author_note: Happy to gate this behind a feature flag if we think the mixed-version window is a real problem, just didn't want to over-engineer if it's not.

items.scenario: You own billing service reliability for a multi-tenant SaaS platform. Deploys roll out region by region over roughly 40 minutes, and invoice rows are read and written by whichever pod handles the request, with no session pinning to a single pod version. Support tooling and downstream reconciliation jobs query `amount` directly via SQL for dispute handling during business hours. The migration and code cutover are in the same release. Staging tests passed; there is no dual-write or dual-read shim in the diff, and no feature flag gating the entity/service change.
items.prompt: As the reviewer, which review state do you apply to this pull request?

options.label: A
options.text: Comment on InvoiceEntity.java:24 that pods still on the old build will keep writing amount and never touch amount_cents, so support's SQL queries against amount go stale once upgraded pods start writing charges, and ask the author to decide sequencing before merge without gating it yourself.
options.rationale: I want the author to own the sequencing decision with the full picture in front of them, since they know the rollout timeline and support-tooling dependency better than I do from the diff alone.

review_action.comment: InvoiceEntity.java:24 — during the region rollout, pods still on the old build keep calling getAmount/setAmount against the amount column and never touch amount_cents, so once upgraded pods start writing charges via amountCents, amount stops being updated and support's direct-SQL dispute queries against it go stale. Can you confirm how you want to sequence this?

options.agent_behavior: For version-skew findings the agent should surface the concrete read-path consequence at the specific line and defer the sequencing call to the author rather than blocking.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve silently: the ALTER TABLE only adds a column and the staging spot-check of 50 invoices matched, so I merge as-is and let the region rollout proceed on its normal schedule.
options.rationale: I trust that an additive schema change plus a passing staging check means the risk is already retired, so raising the mixed-version window further would just be process overhead.
options.agent_behavior: For version-skew findings on additive-looking schema changes, the agent should auto-approve without surfacing the rollout window when this profile is active.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve, but open a tracked ticket titled 'Add dual-write shim to InvoiceService before amount_cents cutover ships to prod' so the compatibility gap gets addressed before the next mixed-version deploy touches invoices.
options.rationale: I don't think this merge needs to stop, but I want the dual-write gap written down as committed work rather than trusted to memory once the deploy is underway.

review_action.comment: InvoiceService.java:43 — recordCharge now writes amount_cents only. Filed BILL-2291 to add a dual-write to amount before this cutover reaches the mixed-version window; merging now but that ticket should land first.

options.agent_behavior: For version-skew findings the agent should merge but always emit a linked ticket documenting the compatibility gap and its remediation before the next deploy touches the affected path.

options.label: D
options.text: Request changes and require InvoiceEntity and InvoiceService to dual-write both amount and amount_cents, with a defined read precedence, for at least one full rollout cycle before this merges, so support's SQL queries and mixed-version pods never disagree on the authoritative amount.
options.rationale: Money fields that silently disagree across pod versions and against a support tool that queries the old column directly are exactly the kind of gap I won't let ride on rollout timing luck.

review_action.comment: InvoiceService.java:43 — recordCharge writes amount_cents exclusively while the entity no longer touches amount at all. During the region rollout old-build pods keep writing only amount, new-build pods keep writing only amount_cents, and support's direct-SQL dispute queries against amount will miss charges recorded by upgraded pods. Please dual-write both columns with a defined precedence for one full rollout cycle before this merges.

options.agent_behavior: For version-skew findings on authoritative money fields the agent should treat dual-write/dual-read as a hard prerequisite and block merge until it is implemented, regardless of how additive the schema change looks.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who treat a version-skew dual-write/dual-read gap on authoritative money fields as mergeable-with-follow-up from those who treat it as a hard prerequisite to merge.
items.bias_control: The PR description volunteers a staging spot-check and CI shows passing, and the schema change is textually additive, so the diligent-sounding cues point toward approval rather than toward the blocking answer.

pr_context.title: Rename userId to accountId in public user serializer for naming consistency
pr_context.description: Follow-up to the account-model consolidation work: this aligns the public user response with the accountId naming used everywhere else in the platform API. Ran the existing serializer unit tests and the partner contract test suite locally, both green. Did not add a dual-write since the field is a straight rename and I wanted to keep the diff small; flagging in case that assumption is wrong for the partner integrations.
pr_context.author_note: Happy to add the dual-write if reviewers think partners are actually still reading userId directly, just didn't want to over-engineer a rename.

items.scenario: You are reviewing a PR against the public user-profile endpoint, which is covered by a documented partner stability contract guaranteeing field names for twelve months. Three partner integrations query this endpoint directly per their onboarding docs on file with the partnerships team; usage volume by partner is not visible from this review. The release train ships every two weeks to all tenants simultaneously with no regional staggering, and this endpoint has no field-level usage telemetry, so you cannot confirm from the dashboard which consumers read `userId` today.
items.prompt: As the reviewer, which review state do you apply to this pull request?

options.label: A
options.text: Comment that the serializer diff itself can merge into main since it's inert until deployed, but tell the release manager directly in the PR thread that this ticket must be pulled from the current train unless a dual-write lands first, putting the actual stop on the deploy gate instead of this merge.
options.rationale: I separate the mergeability of code from its readiness to ship, so I use the review to name the risk clearly but let the release-cut checklist be the mechanism that actually enforces it.

review_action.comment: userSerializer.ts:21 - this merges fine since main isn't auto-deployed, but I'm telling the release manager this rename must be pulled from the train unless a dual-write for userId lands first. Partner contract guarantees the field name for 12 months and we have no per-field usage telemetry to know who's still reading it.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should route contract-risk findings to a downstream release gate rather than blocking the merge whenever the developer's pattern shows they distinguish merge risk from deploy risk and communicate the handoff explicitly.

options.label: B
options.text: Request changes now and require the serializer to emit both `userId` and `accountId` in the same response body for a defined deprecation window before this can merge, since a simultaneous all-tenant release train leaves no staggered exposure to catch a broken partner contract after the fact.
options.rationale: When a release train ships to every tenant at once and there is no telemetry to tell me who depends on a contractually guaranteed field, I don't delegate that risk downstream, I require the dual-write here.

review_action.comment: userSerializer.ts:21 - this endpoint is under a 12-month field stability contract with three partner integrations, and the train ships to all tenants at once with no staggering. Please emit both userId and accountId together for a deprecation window before this merges, and add a changelog entry with a migration note.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should hard-block contract-covered field renames pre-merge whenever the developer's profile shows low tolerance for delegating externally-visible breaking changes to downstream gates or rollout luck.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve silently and let it merge as-is: the stability contract is a documentation artifact between partnerships and legal, not something this review is positioned to enforce, and partner-facing breakage is partnerships' incident to catch and escalate.
options.rationale: I treat contractual ownership boundaries literally: if partnerships owns the stability contract, enforcing it in code review is scope creep that slows down internal-facing cleanup work.
options.agent_behavior: The agent should approve contract-adjacent renames without comment whenever the developer's history shows they treat documented external contracts as another team's enforcement responsibility rather than a review gate.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve and merge now, but open a ticket today assigned to me to add the `userId` alias back in a same-day hotfix before the next train cuts, betting the two-week cadence gives enough runway to patch it before partners see the break.
options.rationale: I'm comfortable letting a fast-moving fix ride ahead of full remediation as long as I personally own the follow-up ticket and there's real calendar time before it ships to anyone.

review_action.comment: Merging this now; opened TICKET-4821 to add a userId alias back before the train cuts in two weeks. I'll own closing it, but flagging that this endpoint has no field-level usage telemetry so I can't confirm today which partners are actually reading userId.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should permit merge-first-fix-after patterns on contract-covered fields only when the developer both self-assigns the follow-up and states a concrete deadline ahead of the next deploy.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who treat a documented external stability contract as this review's own gate from those who delegate enforcement to a downstream release step, a follow-up ticket, or another team entirely.
items.bias_control: All-tenant simultaneous release train removes the staggered-rollout safety net used in the prior version, and each option pairs its blocking choice with a distinct real actor or mechanism (partnerships ownership, self-owned hotfix ticket, release-manager handoff, dual-write requirement) so no option reads as ignoring the risk outright.

pr_context.title: Fix dtype warning in monthly revenue aggregation by casting to float
pr_context.description: pandas was throwing an ObjectDType warning when grouping Decimal columns, so I cast amounts to float before building the DataFrame. Ran the aggregation against last month's transaction export and totals matched the dashboard within a cent, so this looks safe. Didn't test against multi-year date ranges but the diff is small.
pr_context.author_note: Flagging that this dashboard is explicitly downstream of the ledger, not the source of truth, in case that changes the calculus here.

items.scenario: You own review for the analytics service. This aggregate feeds a finance dashboard consumed by the FP&A team for month-over-month trend commentary in board decks; the authoritative ledger export is a separate pipeline reconciled quarterly by finance ops, not this service. Transaction volume is roughly 4 million rows per month. No incident has ever been filed against this dashboard's numbers. The team has a standing backlog column for 'data quality debt' that is reviewed at sprint planning, currently with 11 open items.
items.code:
diff --git a/reporting/aggregates/monthly_revenue.py b/reporting/aggregates/monthly_revenue.py
@@ -28,9 +28,12 @@ def compute_monthly_revenue(transactions: list[Transaction]) -> pd.DataFrame:
     """Aggregate transaction amounts by calendar month for the FP&A dashboard."""
-    amounts = [t.amount for t in transactions]
+    # cast to float to silence pandas ObjectDType warning on Decimal columns
+    amounts = [float(t.amount) for t in transactions]
     df = pd.DataFrame({"amount": amounts, "date": [t.created_at for t in transactions]})
-    return df.groupby(df["date"].dt.to_period("M")).sum()
+    return df.groupby(df["date"].dt.to_period("M")).sum(numeric_only=True)
+
+def _round_for_display(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
+    return df.round(2)
items.prompt: As the reviewer, which review state do you apply to this pull request?

options.label: A
options.text: Leave a comment on line 31 asking the author to confirm whether FP&A has ever cross-checked this dashboard against the ledger export, without holding up the merge on the answer.
options.rationale: I want the author and FP&A to have eyes on the reconciliation gap before it becomes a habit of trusting an unverified number, but I don't think this specific warning fix is the hill to block on.

review_action.comment: reporting/aggregates/monthly_revenue.py:31 - float(t.amount) here means summed totals can drift from the ledger over millions of rows. Can you confirm with FP&A whether this dashboard has ever been reconciled against the ledger export? If not, worth doing once before this merges.

options.agent_behavior: For float-for-money changes feeding decision-facing dashboards, surface the reconciliation question as a non-blocking comment rather than silence or a hard block.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve now but add the Decimal-safe rewrite to the data-quality-debt backlog at the current sprint planning cadence, since 4 million rows a month is enough volume for drift to eventually show up in a board deck.
options.rationale: I don't want to block a warning fix on a rewrite, but the volume here is high enough that I'd rather have a tracked item than rely on someone noticing a mismatch during a board review.

review_action.comment: reporting/aggregates/monthly_revenue.py:31 - approving to clear the warning, but adding this to the data-quality-debt backlog: at 4M rows/month, float summation drift is worth converting to Decimal or integer-cents before this feeds another board cycle.

options.agent_behavior: For float-for-money changes in high-volume reporting paths, approve but require a tracked backlog item so the tradeoff isn't silently forgotten.

options.label: C
options.text: Merge as-is since the ledger reconciliation is a separate quarterly process and this dashboard has never had a reported discrepancy; the float cast just clears a noisy pandas warning.
options.rationale: This is a trend-view dashboard reconciled elsewhere on a schedule, so I treat the warning fix as the actual change here and let the existing reconciliation process catch drift if it ever matters.
options.agent_behavior: For float-for-money conversions in explicitly non-authoritative reporting paths, approve silently when no reconciliation history exists and treat the change as routine.

options.label: D
options.text: Request changes and require the aggregation to sum integer cents or Decimal before grouping, since a warning fix is not sufficient justification to introduce silent drift into numbers that end up in board-level trend commentary.
options.rationale: I hold the line on float arithmetic for money regardless of which pipeline is 'authoritative,' because a number that reaches a board deck without traceable precision is a data integrity problem waiting to be discovered the hard way.

review_action.comment: reporting/aggregates/monthly_revenue.py:31 - float(t.amount) accumulates rounding error across millions of transactions. Please sum using Decimal or convert to integer cents before grouping instead of casting to float to clear the pandas warning; the warning has a cleaner fix that doesn't touch precision.

options.agent_behavior: For float-for-money conversions in any dashboard feeding executive-facing numbers, hard-block regardless of the pipeline's authoritative status and require precision-safe arithmetic before merge.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who calibrate blocking strictly to whether a pipeline is the ledger of record from those who block on the inherent risk of float arithmetic for monetary sums regardless of downstream authority.
items.bias_control: The change is framed by the author as a routine warning fix with a volunteered caveat about non-authoritative status, and the scenario states no incident history and a working quarterly reconciliation process, so diligence and pragmatism both read as reasonable rather than one option reading as obviously correct.

pr_context.title: Enable redesigned checkout pricing path (newCheckoutFlow default true)
pr_context.description: Flips the newCheckoutFlow default so the redesigned pricing calculation ships to everyone on next deploy instead of sitting behind an opt-in flag. I ran the full checkout suite against staging with the flag on and pricing totals matched the legacy path for every fixture we have. Not adding a rollout percentage since the flag dashboard's percentage rollout has been flaky for me the last two times I tried it.
pr_context.author_note: Wanted to get this in before the pricing freeze next week, happy to follow up on staged rollout tooling separately if that's the blocker.

items.scenario: You own reviews for the checkout service, which serves roughly 400 tenants ranging from single-store accounts to a handful doing seven-figure monthly GMV. The flag dashboard supports percentage-based rollout by tenant cohort but is separate from this config file, and nothing in the repo enforces that flag flips go through it. There is no existing dashboard panel or alert tied to newCheckoutFlow, and the pricing service's error budget is tracked only at the aggregate service level, not per code path. Deploys to this repo go out automatically on merge to main, with no manual gate.
items.prompt: As the reviewer, which review state do you apply to this pull request?

options.label: A
options.text: Request changes: revert the default to false and land this behind an explicit percentage-rollout step through the dashboard, with a metric or alert on the new pricing path before any tenant beyond an internal test cohort sees it.
options.rationale: Flipping a pricing calculation to every tenant at once, with automatic deploy and zero dedicated observability on the new path, is a blind spot I won't sign off on regardless of how thorough the staging fixtures were.

review_action.comment: config/featureFlags.ts:22 - this takes newCheckoutFlow to on for all ~400 tenants on merge, with no dashboard panel or alert on the new path and no manual deploy gate. Please revert to false and stage this through the rollout dashboard with a metric on the pricing path added first.

options.agent_behavior: For changes that push a new pricing or billing calculation path to all tenants simultaneously with no dedicated monitoring, block until staged rollout and a metric or alert exist, independent of how strong the offline test coverage is.

options.label: B
options.text: Merge as-is: the staging fixture suite covers the pricing calculation paths that matter, and the deploy pipeline has no manual gate to hold this behind anyway.
options.rationale: I trust a passing fixture suite that already exercises the calculation logic, and inserting a manual hold point that the pipeline doesn't otherwise support would just be theater.
options.agent_behavior: For flag-default flips backed by a passing fixture suite covering the changed logic, approve silently and do not manufacture a rollout gate the pipeline doesn't enforce.

options.label: C

pr_context.title: Skip aud claim check to unblock IdP migration cutover
pr_context.description: Our IdP vendor migration requires disabling strict audience checking temporarily because the new tenant claims mapping isn't fully populated for all downstream services yet. Ran the existing auth test suite locally and everything green; audience validation is tracked as a fast-follow once the claims backfill finishes. Flagging that this touches the shared signing key used by three other tenant-facing services.
pr_context.author_note: Wanted to get this in before the IdP cert rotation Thursday, aud check felt safe to defer since exp/sig still enforced.

items.scenario: You review auth middleware for a multi-tenant SaaS platform serving roughly 40 enterprise tenants. The identity provider issues RS256 tokens signed with one shared key across several tenant-facing services, differentiated only by the `aud` claim. This service's token verification checks signature and expiration but has just had `verify_aud` explicitly disabled. Three other services share this signing key and are independently deployed. There is no service mesh layer enforcing audience separation upstream, so this middleware is the only place that distinction is ever checked.
items.code:
diff --git a/auth/middleware.py b/auth/middleware.py
@@ -22,11 +22,13 @@ async def verify_token(token: str) -> TokenClaims:
     try:
         payload = jwt.decode(
             token,
             key=await get_signing_key(),
             algorithms=["RS256"],
-            options={"verify_exp": True},
+            options={"verify_exp": True, "verify_aud": False},
+            # temporary: claims backfill incomplete for aud during IdP migration
         )
     except jwt.InvalidTokenError as exc:
         raise AuthenticationError(str(exc)) from exc
     return TokenClaims(**payload)

options.label: A

options.label: B

pr_context.title: Add per-user tag to HTTP latency timer for support debugging
pr_context.description: Support has been asking for a way to trace latency complaints back to specific accounts, so I added a userId tag to the existing request latency timer. Tested locally against the dev Prometheus instance and the panel renders fine with a handful of test users. Not sure how this scales once real traffic hits it.
pr_context.author_note: Happy to gate this behind a sampling flag if cardinality is a concern, just wanted to get the shape of the change up first.

items.scenario: You maintain the metrics pipeline for this order service. Prometheus retention is 15 days and the instance already sits near its configured series limit from other teams' instrumentation. The service has 500,000 active users and this timer fires on every request across roughly 40 distinct path templates. You have access to the Prometheus admin dashboard showing current series counts and recent scrape-drop alerts, and this PR is queued behind two others waiting on your review.
items.prompt: Which of these three review comments would you actually post on this PR?

options.label: A
options.text: Nit (optional): tagging with `userId` gives this metric essentially unbounded cardinality, which lines up with the Prometheus series limit issue we've been seeing. Might be worth dropping `.tag("userId", currentUserId())` and moving per-user latency to logs instead, if that data is still needed somewhere.
options.rationale: I flag it as optional because the author is already offering a sampling-flag alternative and I'd rather leave room for their own fix than dictate one.

review_action.comment: Nit (optional): tagging with `userId` gives this metric essentially unbounded cardinality, which lines up with the Prometheus series limit issue we've been seeing. Might be worth dropping `.tag("userId", currentUserId())` and moving per-user latency to logs instead, if that data is still needed somewhere.

options.agent_behavior: For cardinality-risk findings, the agent should frame the change as an optional nit and leave the remediation choice open to the author rather than mandating a specific fix.

options.label: B
options.text: Remove the `userId` tag from this timer. It has unbounded cardinality and will keep generating a new time series per user per path, which is already saturating Prometheus's series limit. If you need per-user latency, log it separately or sample it, but don't tag the metric with it.
options.rationale: I state the mechanism and the fix in one pass because the cardinality math is unambiguous and hedging around it just delays the correction.

review_action.comment: Remove the `userId` tag from this timer. It has unbounded cardinality and will keep generating a new time series per user per path, which is already saturating Prometheus's series limit. If you need per-user latency, log it separately or sample it, but don't tag the metric with it.

options.agent_behavior: For cardinality-risk findings, the agent should state the mechanism and required change directly in one comment without softening language or open questions.

options.label: C
options.text: With 500,000 active users, tagging this timer with `userId` means roughly that many new series per path — is that bounded anywhere downstream, or is that what's already pushing Prometheus past its cardinality limit? Would dropping the `.tag("userId", currentUserId())` line and logging per-user latency separately resolve it?
options.rationale: I pose it as a question because I want the author to connect the tag to the scrape-drop alerts themselves rather than just accepting my read of it.

review_action.comment: With 500,000 active users, tagging this timer with `userId` means roughly that many new series per path — is that bounded anywhere downstream, or is that what's already pushing Prometheus past its cardinality limit? Would dropping the `.tag("userId", currentUserId())` line and logging per-user latency separately resolve it?

options.agent_behavior: For cardinality-risk findings, the agent should surface the metric explosion as a question tied to observed system symptoms and let the author confirm the mechanism before prescribing the fix.

items.discriminates: politeness-framing preference (direct imperative vs socratic inquiry vs hedged optional nit) for delivering an identical cardinality diagnosis and identical remediation
items.bias_control: the author's PR description volunteers a plausible alternative mitigation (sampling flag) and CI is passing, so no framing reads as procedurally forced and the diagnosis itself is held constant across all three options

pr_context.title: Add email/tax/retry controls to createInvoice for dunning workflow

items.stack: Go microservice, gRPC-internal inventory reservation service, table-driven tests, GitHub PR review

pr_context.title: Fix batch reservation loop to include trailing warehouse zone
pr_context.description: Extends the batch reservation loop to iterate over all configured warehouse zones instead of stopping one short. Ran the existing table-driven tests locally and added a new fixture with five zones to confirm no regression. Did not add a case for the previous four-zone boundary since existing tests cover that.
pr_context.author_note: Figured this was worth a quick pass since it touches the reservation hot path.

items.scenario: This service handles warehouse stock reservations during checkout and runs roughly 400 requests per second at peak. The package has a single long-tenured maintainer who has owned it for four years and wrote the original zone-iteration logic. The diff under review changes a loop bound in the reservation batching function. CI is green and the new fixture passes, but the loop still stops one index short of the last configured zone, meaning that zone is silently never included in batch reservations. No ticket currently tracks this class of bug. The repository already has a helper, `AllZoneIndices` in `inventory/zones.go`, that computes the inclusive zone index range correctly and is used by two other batch paths.
items.prompt: You are reviewing this PR and confirm the loop bound still excludes the last configured zone. How do you communicate this finding to the author?

options.label: A
options.text: I leave a comment sketching the fix in pseudo-code, noting the loop needs to iterate through the entire zones slice, and ask the author to write and test the actual Go change themselves rather than applying a literal patch.
options.rationale: A pseudo-code nudge keeps the author actively engaged with the fix rather than just clicking apply, which matters to me even on a clear-cut bug.

review_action.comment: internal/reservation/batch.go:44 - looks like the last configured zone is never reserved because the loop stops one short. Something like `for i := 0; i < len(zones); i++` should cover it, but please write and test the actual change rather than copying this directly, since I haven't traced every caller.

options.agent_behavior: When the review agent wants the author to retain authorship of the fix, offer a pseudo-code sketch instead of a literal, directly-applicable patch.

options.label: B
options.text: I point to the existing zone-iteration helper in inventory/zones.go that already ranges correctly over all zones, and ask the author to reuse or model this loop after it instead of hand-writing the bound again.
options.rationale: We already solved this iteration pattern correctly elsewhere in the codebase, so pointing to that helper prevents the same class of bug from recurring in a third place.

review_action.comment: internal/reservation/batch.go:44 - this loop drops the last zone due to the `-1` bound. inventory/zones.go:22 already has a helper, `AllZoneIndices`, that ranges over the full zone set correctly and is used in two other batch paths. Worth reusing it here instead of restating the bound by hand.

options.agent_behavior: When a correct pattern already exists in the repo, point the author to it instead of authoring a local fix, favoring consistency over speed.

options.label: C
options.text: I post a GitHub suggestion block containing the exact corrected loop condition so the author can apply it with a single click, since the fix is a well-defined one-line change and there is no ambiguity about the correct form.
options.rationale: The fix has exactly one correct form, so a one-click suggestion removes friction without taking anything away from the author's judgment on this line.

review_action.comment:
internal/reservation/batch.go:44 - this still stops one zone short of the full set, dropping the last configured zone from batch reservations. Suggested fix below applies the corrected bound directly.
```suggestion
	for i := 0; i < len(zones); i++ {
```

options.agent_behavior: For single-fix, unambiguous line-level defects, offer a one-click suggestion block regardless of author tenure to minimize round trips.

options.label: D
options.text: I write a comment describing the off-by-one in prose, explaining that the loop should run through the full slice length, and leave the exact code change for the author to write themselves given their familiarity with this function.
options.rationale: He wrote this function and has fixed similar bounds before, so describing the problem is enough to let him apply the correct fix in his own idiom.

review_action.comment: internal/reservation/batch.go:44 - the loop bound `len(zones)-1` still excludes the last configured zone from batching, so any reservation request touching that zone silently drops it. Since this is a slice length check, the fix should make the loop cover every index in `zones`, not just up to the second-to-last one.

options.agent_behavior: For maintainers with deep ownership of the touched code, describe the defect precisely in prose and trust them to author the correction themselves.

items.discriminates: How the reviewer prefers to transmit a fully-diagnosed one-line fix: prose description, one-click suggestion block, guided pseudo-code, or redirection to an existing repo pattern.
items.bias_control: All four options identify the identical off-by-one, agree on its severity, and produce a correct fix if followed, so no mechanism is favored by differing diagnostic accuracy or urgency; only the delivery mechanism and its cost to author autonomy, review latency, or codebase consistency vary.

items.stack: TypeScript / Node.js, fetch-based internal HTTP client wrapper, monorepo with shared utils package

pr_context.title: Add retry wrapper for downstream pricing service calls
pr_context.description: This adds a small helper we can reuse instead of copy-pasting fetch calls to the pricing service. I tested it locally against the staging endpoint and confirmed retries fire on a 503. This is my first PR to this repo so please let me know if I'm missing conventions.
pr_context.author_note: Happy to adjust the retry count or backoff if there's a house standard I should match.

items.scenario: The pricing service this wrapper calls has occasionally taken 20+ seconds to respond under load, and nothing upstream currently bounds how long callers wait. The wrapper is being added to a shared utils package that two other teams have already said they plan to import next sprint. The contributor's git history shows this is their first merged change in this repository. CI is green and no reviewers have commented yet.
items.prompt: The five-line context-timeout-and-cancel fix is warranted here. How do you deliver it to this first-time contributor?

options.label: A
options.text: I post a suggestion block with the AbortController, timeout, and clearTimeout already written so the contributor can commit it with one click, and I explain in the same comment why it matters for a shared package.
options.rationale: This is going into a shared utils package that other teams depend on next sprint, so I'd rather guarantee the exact fix lands correctly than risk a partial or subtly wrong retry-timeout interaction going out under time pressure.
options.agent_behavior: For developers who respond well to fully worked suggestion blocks and treat them as a fast learning aid rather than an overwrite, the agent should default to complete, committable suggestions on shared-package code.

options.label: B
options.text: I merge a suggestion block into the thread but frame it explicitly as one option among several, inviting the contributor to push back or propose their own timeout value instead of committing mine as-is.
options.rationale: I still want to hand over a concrete, correct implementation given the shared-package stakes, but framing it as negotiable rather than final keeps the contributor's ownership of the decision intact.
options.agent_behavior: For developers who want concrete code but also want their own judgment respected on tunable details, the agent should provide a suggestion block explicitly marked as adjustable rather than final.

options.label: C
options.text: I describe the missing timeout and cancellation behavior in prose, name the AbortController API and roughly where it goes, but leave the contributor to write the actual five lines themselves.
options.rationale: I want this contributor's first PR to still feel like their own work, and describing the shape of the fix without writing it for them gives them the chance to internalize the AbortController pattern for next time.

review_action.comment: In pricingClient.ts around line 17, this fetch has no timeout, so a slow pricing response (we've seen 20s+ from this service) will block indefinitely, which matters more once other teams start importing this package. Can you wrap the request with an AbortController, set a timeout of a few seconds, and call clearTimeout once the response resolves?

options.agent_behavior: For developers who value working through the implementation themselves, the agent should describe the required mechanism in words and let the author produce the diff.

options.label: D
options.text: I leave a short comment naming the missing timeout as a blocking issue and offer to hop on a 15-minute call to pair on the AbortController fix if that's easier than iterating over comments for a first PR.
options.rationale: For a first-time contributor I'd rather offer a synchronous option than let an asynchronous comment thread stretch over a day, since the review latency costs more here than a short call would.

review_action.comment: In pricingClient.ts at line 17, the fetch call needs a timeout and cancellation since the pricing service has been slow (20s+) under load and this is heading into a shared package. Happy to jump on a quick call to add the AbortController together if that's faster than going back and forth in comments, otherwise glad to talk through it here.

options.agent_behavior: For developers who respond better to synchronous collaboration than to written review cycles, the agent should offer a short pairing session in place of an extended comment thread.

items.discriminates: whether the reviewer defaults to handing a first-time contributor a ready-to-commit suggestion block versus describing, offering to pair on, or softening the fix to preserve the newcomer's ownership of their first PR
items.bias_control: all four options both flag and require the fix at the same severity and urgency; they differ only in whether and how the concrete code is handed over, so no option reads as more diligent than another

items.category: Category 6: Review Interaction Habits
items.stack: Python/FastAPI microservice, SQLAlchemy async session, multi-tenant SaaS

pr_context.title: Add tenant usage export endpoint
pr_context.description: Adds a new endpoint that streams a CSV of per-tenant usage records for the billing team's monthly reconciliation. Tested locally against the staging DB with a tenant that has about 40k rows and confirmed the file downloads correctly. Did not test against a tenant with a much larger row count.
pr_context.author_note: Wanted to get this in before the end of the sprint since billing is asking for it, happy to follow up on anything.

items.scenario: The endpoint's route handler currently opens its own database session directly inside the function body instead of receiving one through FastAPI's dependency injection, and the call site that invokes the export helper passes that locally constructed session object rather than the one the framework would provide. This pattern bypasses the connection pool's lifecycle management and has previously caused connection leaks under sustained load in two other services owned by this team. The fix requires changing the dependency declaration in one file and updating the call site in a second file so both agree on the session lifecycle. The billing team is waiting on this for their monthly close, which is in three days.
items.code:
--- a/app/routers/exports.py
+++ b/app/routers/exports.py
@@ -1,10 +1,15 @@
 from fastapi import APIRouter
-from app.services.export_service import generate_usage_csv
+from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession
+from app.services.export_service import generate_usage_csv
+from app.db.session import async_session_factory
 
 router = APIRouter()
 
 @router.get("/tenants/{tenant_id}/usage-export")
 async def export_usage(tenant_id: str):
-    return await generate_usage_csv(tenant_id)
+    async with async_session_factory() as session:
+        return await generate_usage_csv(tenant_id, session)
--- a/app/services/export_service.py
+++ b/app/services/export_service.py
@@ -14,7 +14,7 @@ from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession
 from app.models.usage import UsageRecord
 
-async def generate_usage_csv(tenant_id: str, session: AsyncSession):
+async def generate_usage_csv(tenant_id: str, session: AsyncSession = None):
     query = select(UsageRecord).where(UsageRecord.tenant_id == tenant_id)
     result = await session.execute(query)
     rows = result.scalars().all()
items.prompt: You need to communicate that the session should come through FastAPI's dependency injection system rather than being constructed manually in the route handler, and that this touches both the router file and the service file. How do you convey this?

options.label: A
options.text: Push a small branch off the PR with both files corrected, link it in a comment, and ask the author to cherry-pick the commit or diff it against their branch, since GitHub's suggestion UI can't span two files as one atomic change.
options.rationale: For a change that only makes sense applied to both files at once, I'd rather hand over a working commit than risk the author applying one suggestion and not the other.

review_action.comment: exports.py / export_service.py - pushed a branch (fix/di-session-export) with the dependency-injected session wired through both files, since this needs to change in both places atomically and a single suggestion block can't express that. Feel free to cherry-pick the commit or just diff it against yours and copy what's useful.

options.agent_behavior: When a developer's profile favors receiving ready-to-merge alternatives, the agent should prepare and link a corrective branch rather than describing the change piecemeal in comments.

options.label: B
options.text: Post two GitHub suggestion blocks, one per file, each showing the exact replacement lines, tied together with a comment explaining that both must land in the same commit or the signature and call site will disagree.
options.rationale: I want the mechanical part of a two-file change to be zero-effort to apply correctly, so I give exact diffs for both spots and explicitly flag that they're coupled.

review_action.comment: exports.py:9 - suggestion: replace with `async def export_usage(tenant_id: str, session: AsyncSession = Depends(get_session)): return await generate_usage_csv(tenant_id, session)`. export_service.py:17 - suggestion: replace with `async def generate_usage_csv(tenant_id: str, session: AsyncSession):`. These two need to land together, otherwise the call site and signature disagree on where the session comes from.

options.agent_behavior: When a developer's profile favors exact, low-friction remediation, the agent should provide precise per-file suggestion blocks and explicitly call out that they must be applied together.

options.label: C
options.text: Comment that the session lifecycle needs to change across both files, note that it's easier to walk through live than in text, and propose a fifteen-minute pairing session before the PR moves forward, deferring the concrete edit until then.
options.rationale: Since this touches the session lifecycle pattern that's bitten two other services, I'd rather walk through it live so the author leaves understanding the pool-management reasoning, not just the diff.

review_action.comment: exports.py:9 - this needs the session to come through dependency injection rather than being opened manually here, and it touches export_service.py:17 too. Rather than write this up in prose across two files, can we grab fifteen minutes to pair on it? It'll be faster than iterating in comments and worth walking through given the leak pattern we've seen elsewhere.

options.agent_behavior: When a developer's profile favors synchronous collaboration over asynchronous comment threads, the agent should propose a short pairing session instead of drafting the remediation in writing.

options.label: D
options.text: Post a comment describing in prose what to change in each file: swap the manual context manager for a `Depends(get_session)` parameter in exports.py, and drop the default None in export_service.py so the signature stays required, without providing code for either edit.
options.rationale: I find that for a two-file structural change, prose forces the author to actually understand the dependency lifecycle rather than just applying a patch, and I'd rather spend the comment budget on the why.

review_action.comment: exports.py:9 and export_service.py:17 - the route should accept the session via `Depends(get_session)` instead of opening `async_session_factory()` directly, and export_service.py should keep `session: AsyncSession` required rather than defaulting to None so a caller can't accidentally skip injection. This avoids the pool-leak pattern we hit in two other services.

options.agent_behavior: When a developer's profile favors prose explanation, the agent should describe the cross-file dependency change conceptually and let the author write the edit rather than pre-drafting it.

items.discriminates: Whether the reviewer's default mechanism for a remediation that spans multiple files is written prose, exact per-file suggestion blocks with linking context, a ready-to-merge branch handoff, or a shift to synchronous pairing.
items.bias_control: All four mechanisms fully convey the same fix at the same severity and none skips or downgrades the finding; they trade off differently against author autonomy, thread noise, reviewer prep time, and merge latency, so no single option reads as the more diligent choice under a three-day deadline.

pr_context.title: Add retry policy to InvoiceExportClient

pr_context.author_note: Updated per the last round of comments, should be ready for a final look.

items.scenario: You are the second reviewer on a billing-service PR that has already gone through one full review round; the author addressed all four prior comments correctly and CI is green. The team's internal style guide, agreed in a retro six months ago, states that Spring beans should use constructor injection so dependencies are explicit and testable, but this class still uses field injection with @Autowired, a pattern still present in about a third of the codebase. items.prompt: You notice the new BackoffCalculator field follows the existing field-injection pattern in this class rather than the team's agreed constructor-injection convention. Given the finding is low severity and the author has already turned around four comments this round, what do you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve the PR and drop a comment on InvoiceExportClient.java:22 naming the field-injection versus constructor-injection convention, but describe the change in prose only and let the author decide when to make it.
options.rationale: I think naming the convention gap has teaching value even at low severity, but writing out the exact refactor myself would be overkill for something this mechanical and non-blocking.

review_action.comment: InvoiceExportClient.java:22: new fields here (backoffCalculator, and the two existing ones) are still using field injection; our style guide from the March retro calls for constructor injection so dependencies are explicit and mockable without reflection. Not blocking this PR, but worth converting when you're next in this class.

options.agent_behavior: For low-severity style deviations with an existing team convention, the agent should surface the rule in prose and leave the remediation effort to the author rather than authoring it.

options.label: B
options.text: Comment on InvoiceExportClient.java:22 with a full GitHub suggestion block that rewrites the constructor, converts all three fields to constructor injection, and removes the @Autowired annotations, ready for the author to accept in one click.
options.rationale: I'd rather hand over a one-click fix than ask for a fifth round of manual edits; minimizing the author's remaining effort matters more to me here than whether I'm the one who typed the diff.
options.agent_behavior: For low-severity mechanical refactors late in a review cycle, the agent should supply the exact suggestion block so the author's remaining effort is a single click rather than a manual rewrite.

options.label: C
options.text: Comment on InvoiceExportClient.java:22 pointing out the field-injection pattern and open a small tracked ticket for migrating this class, so the convention gap is recorded without adding scope to the current PR.
options.rationale: I prefer to separate the observation from the fix on a PR that's already gone through four rounds; a ticket keeps the finding from disappearing without forcing another diff cycle right now.

review_action.comment: InvoiceExportClient.java:22: this class continues the field-injection pattern rather than constructor injection per our style guide. I've filed BILL-1842 to migrate InvoiceExportClient's DI style separately so we don't hold up this export fix; feel free to pick it up whenever convenient.

options.agent_behavior: For low-severity but real convention gaps on PRs nearing merge, the agent should decouple the fix from the current diff by filing a ticket rather than blocking or silently dropping it.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave the class as field-injected and say nothing about it, reasoning that raising a fifth low-severity comment after four rounds of fixes is not worth the author's time on a non-critical-path job.
options.rationale: I weigh review fatigue heavily here; the finding is a stylistic convention gap with no functional risk, and I'd rather bank the goodwill for a round where it matters more.
options.agent_behavior: For low-severity convention drift on PRs with a high already-addressed comment count, the agent should default to silent approval rather than adding another round-trip.

items.discriminates: Whether the reviewer, facing a low-stakes convention finding late in an already-costly review cycle, resolves it by silence, prose-only comment, ticket deferral, or a ready-to-apply suggestion block.
items.bias_control: All four mechanisms are framed as reasonable responses to reviewer fatigue and low severity, and each carries an explicit cost (lost teaching moment, unresolved debt, ticket overhead, or authoring effort) so none reads as the obviously diligent choice.

pr_context.title: Fix goroutine leak in ingest worker pool shutdown
pr_context.description: Under load we saw worker goroutines stick around after Shutdown() returned, which was leaking memory in the staging cluster overnight. This patch changes how the done channel is closed so workers exit. I did not manage to reproduce the original leak locally, so I only have the staging metrics as evidence this helps.
pr_context.author_note: Staging has been leak-free for about 14 hours since I deployed this build, but I have not written a test that reliably triggers the leak.

items.scenario: You own the concurrency utilities package this worker pool is built on. The pool fans out jobs to N goroutines over a shared channel and closes a done channel to signal shutdown. Reading the diff, you see the same done channel could plausibly be closed twice under concurrent Shutdown() calls, which panics. You are about 70 percent confident the correct fix is to serialize the close with sync.Once rather than reordering when the channel gets closed relative to the job channel, but you have not run a race-detector reproduction yourself and the author's staging evidence is anecdotal, not a regression test. There is no hard deadline; this service processes billing events for two internal tenants.
items.prompt: Shutdown() now guards the done channel close with a select/default check to avoid a double-close panic if Shutdown() is called concurrently from two goroutines, but that check itself has a race window between the select and the close. Given you're fairly sure a race exists here but only moderately sure whether the right fix is reordering the channel closes or switching to sync.Once, how do you communicate this in the review?

options.label: A
options.text: Post a GitHub suggestion block at pool.go:41-46 replacing the select/default with sync.Once.Do(func(){ close(p.done) }), explicitly labeled in the comment text as one candidate fix rather than a directive.
options.rationale: A concrete suggestion block gets the author unblocked fastest and costs them almost nothing to accept or reject, as long as I'm honest in the wording that this is a candidate and not gospel.

review_action.comment: pool.go:41-46 - the select/default check doesn't close the race window between two concurrent Shutdown() calls. One candidate fix, not necessarily the only right one: wrap the close in a sync.Once so it's serialized regardless of call order. Suggestion block below shows the shape of that change; happy to discuss the channel-close-ordering alternative if you'd rather go that way.

options.agent_behavior: When the developer's profile shows heavy reliance on suggestion blocks, the agent should draft the most plausible fix as an literal suggestion diff while flagging it as provisional rather than certain.

options.label: B
options.text: Post a comment at pool.go:44 describing the double-close race in the select/default guard and stop there, leaving the choice of remedy entirely to the author without proposing either candidate fix.
options.rationale: I flag what I'm confident about and stop, since I'd rather not anchor the author on a fix I'm only 70 percent sure is right when they know this code path better than I do.

review_action.comment: pool.go:44 - the select/default guard around close(p.done) still has a race window: two concurrent Shutdown() calls can both pass the select before either executes close, so the panic isn't actually eliminated. This needs a real fix before merge; I'd like to see how you want to close it off.

options.agent_behavior: When the developer's profile shows low reliance on suggestion blocks, the agent should state findings plainly and leave remediation design to the author rather than drafting proposed diffs.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the author to first write a failing test that reproduces the double-close panic under `go test -race`, and defer picking between sync.Once and reordering until that test exists and can validate whichever fix lands.
options.rationale: Neither of us has actually reproduced this race, so I'd rather anchor the fix decision to a failing test under the race detector than have us debate two plausible patches without evidence either one closes the gap.

review_action.comment: pool.go:41-46 - before we pick between sync.Once and reordering the channel closes, can you add a test that spins up concurrent Shutdown() calls and runs under `go test -race`? Neither of us has reproduced the panic directly yet, and a failing test will tell us definitively which fix actually closes the window instead of us guessing from the diff.

options.agent_behavior: When the developer's profile shows high test-insistence, the agent should ask for a reproducing test before endorsing any specific fix rather than committing to a suggestion block on unverified reasoning.

options.label: D
options.text: Write out both the sync.Once approach and the channel-close-reordering approach in prose at pool.go:41-46, comparing their tradeoffs, without committing to either as the recommended path.
options.rationale: Laying out both options with their tradeoffs respects that I'm not fully sure which is right, and it gives the author enough context to make an informed call themselves without me pretending to certainty I don't have.

review_action.comment: pool.go:41-46 - two ways to close the double-close race window here. Option 1: sync.Once wrapping close(p.done), simplest and idiomatic, but adds a struct field. Option 2: reorder so p.jobs closes first and workers select only on that, avoiding p.done entirely, but changes shutdown semantics for anyone relying on immediate cancellation. Either resolves the panic; let me know which direction you'd rather take.

options.agent_behavior: When the developer's profile favors comparative exposition over prescriptive diffs, the agent should present multiple candidate fixes side by side and let the author choose, avoiding a single suggestion block.

items.discriminates: Separates reviewers who commit fix-candidates to a suggestion block under partial confidence from those who describe, compare in prose, or defer the fix decision to test-driven verification.
items.bias_control: All four mechanisms leave the actual remediation choice open to the author since the reviewer is only 70 percent sure of the fix, so no option reads as more diligent than another on that axis; they differ only in how directive the communication mechanism is.

items.stack: Python/asyncio service on Postgres, SQLAlchemy core, multi-tenant SaaS scheduling backend

pr_context.title: Use advisory lock for shift-slot claim instead of row lock
pr_context.description: This replaces the row-level locking on shift_slot with pg_advisory_xact_lock keyed on (tenant_id, slot_id) so we stop serializing on the row and avoid the deadlocks we saw under the old SELECT ... FOR UPDATE approach. Tested locally with two concurrent claim requests against the same slot and confirmed only one succeeds; also ran the existing claim test suite. One thing I didn't get to: the error message on a failed claim still says 'row locked' which is stale wording now.
pr_context.author_note: Happy to rename the error string in this PR or a follow-up, whichever is preferred.

items.scenario: This claim path is called whenever a worker taps to accept an open shift, and peak traffic hits several hundred claims per minute during morning shift-change windows across tenants. Three prior PRs from other engineers on this service attempted to fix claim contention by adjusting SELECT ... FOR UPDATE lock ordering, and each reintroduced deadlocks under load within a few weeks of merging. This PR is from a mid-level engineer and switches to a transaction-scoped advisory lock keyed on tenant and slot, sidestepping the row-lock contention pattern entirely. The only open item is a stale error string mentioned in the PR description.
items.code:
--- a/services/scheduling/claims.py
+++ b/services/scheduling/claims.py
@@ -40,17 +40,25 @@ async def claim_shift_slot(session: AsyncSession, tenant_id: str, slot_id: str, worker_id: str) -> ClaimResult:
-    slot = await session.execute(
-        select(ShiftSlot)
-        .where(ShiftSlot.tenant_id == tenant_id, ShiftSlot.id == slot_id)
-        .with_for_update()
-    )
-    slot = slot.scalar_one_or_none()
-    if slot is None or slot.claimed_by is not None:
-        raise ClaimError("row locked")
-    slot.claimed_by = worker_id
-    await session.commit()
-    return ClaimResult(success=True, slot_id=slot_id)
+    lock_key = advisory_lock_key(tenant_id, slot_id)
+    await session.execute(select(func.pg_advisory_xact_lock(lock_key)))
+    slot = await session.execute(
+        select(ShiftSlot)
+        .where(ShiftSlot.tenant_id == tenant_id, ShiftSlot.id == slot_id)
+    )
+    slot = slot.scalar_one_or_none()
+    if slot is None or slot.claimed_by is not None:
+        raise ClaimError("row locked")
+    slot.claimed_by = worker_id
+    await session.commit()
+    return ClaimResult(success=True, slot_id=slot_id)
items.prompt: You are reviewing this PR. The advisory-lock approach is a genuinely non-obvious improvement that avoids a deadlock pattern three prior PRs failed to fix, and there is one minor issue (the stale 'row locked' error string). How do you communicate on this PR?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a short inline reaction directly above the pg_advisory_xact_lock call reading 'nice, this avoids the row-lock deadlocks' with a thumbs-up emoji, then a separate comment on the stale error string.
options.rationale: A quick nod costs almost nothing and signals I noticed the change without turning the thread into a design discussion that isn't needed here.

review_action.comment: claims.py:47 - nice, this avoids the row-lock deadlocks 👍 claims.py:58 - separately, this error message still says 'row locked' but we're using an advisory lock now; worth updating the string before merge.

options.agent_behavior: For developers whose profile shows moderate preference for brief acknowledgement without extended discussion, the agent should insert short affirming reactions inline rather than expanding them into summary commentary.

options.label: B
options.text: In the review summary, write one sentence explaining that the advisory-lock choice correctly avoids the deadlock pattern the last three PRs hit, then comment on the error string inline.
options.rationale: Naming why a decision is good in the summary gives the author calibrated feedback on their judgment, not just their code, without turning a single line into a essay.

review_action.comment: Summary: switching to pg_advisory_xact_lock keyed on (tenant_id, slot_id) is the right call here; it sidesteps the row-lock contention that caused the last three attempts at this to reintroduce deadlocks under load. One small follow-up inline on the stale error string, otherwise this looks solid.

options.agent_behavior: For developers whose profile shows moderate preference for being told why a decision was good, the agent should place a single explanatory sentence in the review summary rather than inline or omitting it.

options.label: C
options.text: Leave a single inline comment at claims.py:58 asking the author to update the 'row locked' error string, and approve. No comment addresses the locking strategy change at all.
options.rationale: My job is to catch defects and unblock merges efficiently; the lock choice is correct and correct code doesn't need narration from me.

review_action.comment: claims.py:58 - This error message still says 'row locked' but we're no longer taking a row lock here. Can you update the string (or the ClaimError message) to something like 'slot already claimed' so it matches the new locking strategy?

options.agent_behavior: For developers whose profile shows low weight on recognition, the agent should default to terse issue-only comments and skip narrating correct design decisions.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave a detailed inline callout at claims.py:47 explaining the advisory-lock mechanism, why it avoids the deadlock pattern of the prior three PRs, and noting it as a reference pattern for other engineers reading this file later, in addition to the error-string comment.
options.rationale: This thread is discoverable by future engineers touching this file, so documenting why this pattern works and citing the prior failed attempts turns one good decision into institutional knowledge.

review_action.comment: claims.py:47 - Calling out why this works: pg_advisory_xact_lock keyed on (tenant_id, slot_id) takes the lock before the row read, so we serialize on intent-to-claim rather than on the row itself. The last three PRs that touched this function tried reordering the FOR UPDATE lock and each reintroduced deadlocks within weeks. Worth linking this thread from any future locking change to this file. Separately, claims.py:58's error string still says 'row locked' and should be updated to match.

options.agent_behavior: For developers whose profile shows high value on written rationale and archaeology, the agent should produce detailed inline explanations of non-obvious correct decisions addressed to future readers, not just the author.

items.discriminates: Whether the reviewer treats acknowledgement of a good, non-obvious decision as unnecessary overhead, a brief courtesy, calibrated feedback on judgment, or an investment in documentation for future readers of the code.
items.bias_control: All four options resolve the minor issue identically (a clear, actionable inline comment on the stale error string with remediation), so no option can be distinguished by whether it catches or handles the defect, only by how much and where it acknowledges the good decision.

pr_context.title: Add retry wrapper for invoice webhook delivery
pr_context.description: This is my first PR to the billing service. I added a retry wrapper around the webhook dispatch call with exponential backoff, based on the pattern I saw in the notifications service. I tested it locally by killing my dev server mid-request and confirming the retry fired, but I didn't get a chance to write an automated test for the backoff timing.
pr_context.author_note: Let me know if the backoff numbers look reasonable, I mostly guessed at them.

items.scenario: You own the billing service. This is a first-time external contributor's first merged-track PR. The webhook dispatch path fires on every invoice finalization across all tenants, roughly 40,000 times a day. The retry wrapper correctly distinguishes retryable network errors from non-retryable 4xx responses on the error path, which is the part contributors most often get wrong. Two moderate issues remain: the backoff multiplier is hardcoded rather than read from config, and there is no cap on total retry duration before the job is abandoned. Both are fixable in follow-up commits before this ships to production. CI is green and no deadline pressure exists on this PR.
items.prompt: Given that the error-path handling is solid and only the backoff config and retry cap need addressing, how do you communicate this review to the contributor?

options.label: A
options.text: Open the review with one sentence noting the retry approach is a reasonable fit for this codebase before listing the backoff config and retry cap as required changes underneath.
options.rationale: A brief framing sentence orients a new contributor to what direction is sound before they read the required changes, without turning the review into a narrative.

review_action.comment: The retry approach fits well with how the notifications service handles this. Two things to address before merge: src/webhooks/dispatch.ts line 27, the backoff multiplier should come from config rather than being hardcoded, and the loop needs a cap on retry attempts or elapsed time so a failing endpoint doesn't retry forever.

options.agent_behavior: For contributors early in ramp-up who benefit from directional confirmation, the agent should open with a short orienting note before the required changes.

options.label: B
options.text: Post a single comment that lists the two required changes, the hardcoded multiplier and the missing retry cap, without referencing the correct error-classification logic anywhere in the review.
options.rationale: I keep review threads focused on what needs to change so the contributor can act on a short, unambiguous list without parsing extra commentary.

review_action.comment: Two changes needed before merge: 1) src/webhooks/dispatch.ts line 27, move the backoff multiplier (500 * 2^attempt) into service config so it can be tuned without a deploy. 2) Add a maximum retry count or elapsed-time cap so a persistently failing endpoint doesn't retry indefinitely; abandon and log after the cap is hit.

options.agent_behavior: For contributors who value speed and dislike unsolicited commentary, the agent should keep findings terse and skip narrative framing entirely.

options.label: C
options.text: Leave an inline comment directly on the isClientError check calling out that the client/server error split is exactly right, in addition to the two separate comments requesting the config and cap fixes.
options.rationale: Pointing at the specific line where the contributor made a correct, non-obvious judgment call teaches them what to keep doing, which matters more for retention than a general compliment would.

review_action.comment: src/webhooks/dispatch.ts line 22, the isClientError check to avoid retrying 4xx responses is exactly the right call and a detail a lot of first PRs miss. Separately, line 27's backoff multiplier needs to move to config, and the loop needs a retry cap or max elapsed time before the job gives up.

options.agent_behavior: For contributors building domain judgment where reinforcing specific correct decisions accelerates learning, the agent should anchor praise inline at the exact line that shows good judgment.

options.label: D
options.text: Write a summary comment that opens by naming what the PR gets right, the error classification and the backoff pattern choice, then closes with the two required changes as a numbered list.
options.rationale: A first-time contributor's first review sets the tone for whether they come back; leading with what worked and closing with clear asks signals the two required changes are routine, not a rejection of their approach.

review_action.comment: This is a solid first PR. The error classification correctly separates retryable network failures from 4xx client errors, and following the notifications service's backoff pattern was the right instinct. Two things to fix before merge: 1) src/webhooks/dispatch.ts line 27, move the backoff multiplier into config. 2) Add a cap on retry attempts or elapsed time so the loop can't retry forever against a dead endpoint.

options.agent_behavior: For first-time or early-career contributors where retention and psychological safety are part of the review's purpose, the agent should lead the summary with concrete positives before the required changes.

items.discriminates: Whether and how explicitly a reviewer acknowledges correct work alongside required changes, ranging from silence about positives to a summary that leads with what worked.
items.bias_control: All four options request the identical two changes with identical severity and identical remediation; only the presence, placement, and specificity of acknowledgment of the correct error-handling logic differs, so no option can be picked by comparing thoroughness of the required-changes list.
