pr_context.title: Add bounded retry with jitter to tenant-config fetch client
pr_context.description: Wraps the outbound call to the tenant-config service with a capped exponential backoff plus full jitter so a downstream blip doesn't turn into a thundering herd on retry. Tested locally by killing the config service mid-load-test and watching retry spacing in the logs, and added a unit test that asserts the delay stays within bounds across 500 simulated attempts. No behavior change for the happy path.
pr_context.author_note: Happy to split the jitter helper into its own package if we end up using it elsewhere.

items.scenario: You own review rotation for the tenant-config client library, which every request-path service imports. The author is a senior engineer on the platform team who has shipped retry logic before. The PR touches one file, CI is green, and the unit test explicitly checks the jitter bounds. You have reviewed three other retry implementations this quarter that lacked jitter entirely and caused synchronized retry storms during a partial outage. There is no deadline pressure on this PR; it is not blocking anything else.
items.prompt: The retry-with-jitter change is correct, tested, and has zero findings. How do you close out this review?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve and call out in the comment that the bounded backoff with full jitter in fetch.go:43-52 is exactly the right pattern for a shared client, naming why it prevents synchronized retry storms.
options.rationale: Naming the specific decision that made this easy to review reinforces the exact behavior I want to see again, and it costs one sentence of thread noise against real reinforcement value for a pattern other services should copy.

review_action.comment: Approving. The bounded backoff with full jitter in fetch.go:43-52 is the right call here specifically because this client is shared across every request-path service; without jitter, a partial outage would have synchronized every caller's retry into the same window.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should name the specific design decision worth reinforcing when approving clean PRs from this developer, tying the praise to a concrete line rather than a generic compliment.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve with a note praising the jitter pattern and additionally ask the author to write it up as a short pattern doc in the team's shared retry-handling guide.
options.rationale: This pattern will keep coming up across services, so turning a good implementation into a documented team standard has more long-term value than praise in a single PR thread, even though it adds a follow-up ask on someone who wasn't expecting extra scope.

review_action.comment: Approving, this is a clean implementation of bounded retry with jitter. Given how often we reinvent this across services, would you be open to turning fetch.go:43-52 into a short pattern writeup in the retry-handling guide so other teams can copy it directly?

options.agent_behavior: The agent should pair praise with a documentation ask only when the developer has previously welcomed extra scope on clean PRs, since this adds real work beyond the review itself.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve with a short 'LGTM, thanks' comment so the author gets a visible acknowledgment in the thread before the merge.
options.rationale: A brief acknowledgment costs almost nothing and signals I actually read the diff rather than rubber-stamping, without turning the thread into a discussion the PR doesn't need.

review_action.comment: LGTM, thanks for the quick turnaround on this.

options.agent_behavior: The agent should default to a brief acknowledgment on clean PRs from this developer, keeping it to one line so approvals stay lightweight.

options.label: D
options.text: Click approve with no comment at all, letting the green check merge the PR without any written reaction to the change.
options.rationale: A clean PR with passing tests and no findings doesn't need my commentary to be mergeable; adding words here is thread noise that trains people to wait for my sign-off phrasing instead of trusting green CI.
options.agent_behavior: The agent should approve silently on zero-finding PRs from this developer, reserving written comments for cases with an actual finding or open question.

items.discriminates: How much verbal reinforcement, if any, a reviewer attaches to a zero-finding approval, ranging from silent merge to praise plus an added documentation task.
items.bias_control: All four options approve the PR outright with no blocking findings and no disagreement about code quality, so the only variable is how much commentary and follow-up scope accompanies the approval.

pr_context.title: Remove legacy invoice recalculation path and add proration flag to InvoiceService
pr_context.description: This PR deletes the old dual-write invoice recalculation code that was superseded by the ledger-based approach eighteen months ago. I traced every call site including the two scheduled jobs and the admin console endpoint before removing anything. Also added a small proration flag to the new path for mid-cycle plan changes. Ran the full invoicing regression suite locally and it passed.
pr_context.author_note: Took most of a day to confirm nothing else called the old path, wanted to be sure before deleting it.

items.scenario: The invoicing module has accumulated dead code for years because engineers are wary of deleting billing logic without full certainty, and two prior attempts stalled mid-review after reviewers raised call-site concerns the author could not immediately answer. This PR's author individually verified all seven call sites, including two cron jobs and an internal admin tool, before deleting the legacy path. The new proration flag is a small addition with one minor issue: it does not reset when a subscription is fully canceled mid-cycle, which would leave a stale flag value on reactivation, a low-severity data quality issue rather than a billing correctness one. The seven call sites the author checked are listed in the PR description (two cron jobs, the admin console, and four service callers); only the two that required code changes appear in this hunk.
items.prompt: You are reviewing this PR. The proration flag issue is minor and worth a comment, but how do you handle the fact that the author did a careful, verified 402-line dead code removal that the team has struggled to get anyone to do?

options.label: A
options.text: Post a single comment at InvoiceService.java:120-122 describing the proration reset gap and its fix, and add one sentence noting that the verified removal of the legacy path is exactly the kind of cleanup the team has been trying to get done.
options.rationale: I want the fix noted precisely where it lives, and I think naming the cleanup effort explicitly makes it more likely this kind of work keeps happening, since recognition is cheap and the team's problem is motivation, not skill.

review_action.comment: InvoiceService.java:120-122: the proration flag isn't reset when a subscription is canceled mid-cycle and later reactivated, so it can carry a stale true value. Worth clearing it in the cancellation handler. Separately, this is the kind of verified, call-site-by-call-site cleanup we've struggled to get people to actually do, so thank you for taking the day to confirm it was safe.

options.agent_behavior: When the developer's history shows they respond well to specific recognition of unrewarded maintenance work, the agent should name the cleanup effort explicitly alongside the technical note rather than treating the two as separate concerns.

options.label: B

pr_context.title: Fix duplicate row emission in tenant usage aggregator and add coverage for empty-partition path
pr_context.description: This closes the bug where tenants with zero events in a billing window got duplicated rows from the previous partition due to a stale merge key. I also added a test for the empty-partition case since it had no coverage at all. Ran the existing suite locally and it passes; I did not add a test isolating the merge-key fix itself since I was focused on getting the duplication stopped before the billing run tonight.
pr_context.author_note: Wanted to get eyes on this before the 6pm billing job kicks off, let me know if the merge key approach is wrong.

items.scenario: You own the billing aggregation module and are reviewing a same-day fix from a teammate on data platform. The merge-key change alters how partitions are joined when a tenant has no events, and the approach used (falling back to a left join on tenant_id alone) will silently reintroduce duplicates for tenants with multiple regions once multi-region billing ships next quarter, though it is correct for the current single-region schema. The new empty-partition test is well-constructed and covers a path the module had zero prior coverage on. The billing job runs in three hours.
items.code:
--- a/pipelines/billing/aggregator.py
+++ b/pipelines/billing/aggregator.py
@@ -41,13 +41,18 @@ def merge_partition_windows(current: pd.DataFrame, previous: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
-    merged = current.merge(
-        previous,
-        on=["tenant_id", "region_id", "window_start"],
-        how="outer",
-        suffixes=("", "_prev"),
-    )
+    if previous.empty:
+        merged = current.copy()
+        merged["row_source"] = "current_only"
+    else:
+        merged = current.merge(
+            previous,
+            on=["tenant_id"],
+            how="left",
+            suffixes=("", "_prev"),
+        )
+        merged["row_source"] = "joined"
     return merged
@@ -78,3 +83,15 @@ def test_merge_partition_windows_handles_overlap():
     assert len(result) == 3
+
+def test_merge_partition_windows_handles_empty_previous():
+    current = pd.DataFrame({"tenant_id": ["t1"], "window_start": ["2024-01-01"]})
+    previous = pd.DataFrame(columns=["tenant_id", "window_start"])
+    result = merge_partition_windows(current, previous)
+    assert len(result) == 1
+    assert result.iloc[0]["row_source"] == "current_only"
items.prompt: You need to REQUEST_CHANGES on the merge-key approach before the billing run, but the empty-partition test is genuinely good work on a path that had zero coverage before this PR. How do you handle acknowledging the test alongside the blocking feedback?

options.rationale: Keeping the praise in its own comment thread lets the author see the blocking issue and the positive note as distinct signals rather than one being buried in the other.

review_action.comment: aggregator.py:92-97: this empty-previous test is a good addition, that path had no coverage before. Separately, on the join change above: keeping tenant_id as the only join key at lines 47-52 will reintroduce duplicates once tenants can span multiple regions, so please restore region_id to the join keys and branch separately for the empty-previous case.

options.rationale: I like to open on something concrete and positive before delivering blocking feedback so the author reads the critique as part of a balanced review rather than a pure rejection.

review_action.comment: aggregator.py:47-52: the left join on tenant_id alone will reintroduce duplicate rows once a tenant can have multiple region_id values, since region_id is dropped from the join key. options.agent_behavior: For a developer with this profile, the agent should default to lean, single-purpose review comments and skip separate acknowledgement of adjacent good work unless the author asks.

items.discriminates: Whether and how a reviewer expresses acknowledgement of incidental good work (a well-built test) when it co-occurs with a blocking finding, ranging from no acknowledgement, to a separate in-thread comment, to team-visible recognition outside the PR, to a combined leading comment.
items.bias_control: All four mechanisms deliver the identical REQUEST_CHANGES blocking comment with the same diagnosis and remediation for the join-key defect, so the item isolates only whether and where acknowledgement of the test is expressed, not the rigor of the blocking review itself.
